    <title>IMF Warns Stablecoins Could Cut Payment Costs but Raise Currency Risks</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;article&gt;

&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgk3wTTGw0hyaDj-CqzqaU-hNddsJ3QACxEdlwOaWQEoavfmMueaNW2rj1UZEgPgXIVoc_4k_mpu4JpypcVnuxDOCrKpTIeSLPY8RPnf6mm2hlTgK3afZ7vsEzQbwl3Ae_08gBs8cHA4uW0inwqFHm5-xL0oKMrvRYtgNEdQBHELFIItHbl7r_upbZSoRDU/s1672/imf-stablecoins-cross-border-payments-currency-risks-2026.jpg%20(2).png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="IMF stablecoin analysis showing cheaper cross-border payments and currency risks in emerging markets" border="0" data-original-height="941" data-original-width="1672" height="225" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgk3wTTGw0hyaDj-CqzqaU-hNddsJ3QACxEdlwOaWQEoavfmMueaNW2rj1UZEgPgXIVoc_4k_mpu4JpypcVnuxDOCrKpTIeSLPY8RPnf6mm2hlTgK3afZ7vsEzQbwl3Ae_08gBs8cHA4uW0inwqFHm5-xL0oKMrvRYtgNEdQBHELFIItHbl7r_upbZSoRDU/w400-h225/imf-stablecoins-cross-border-payments-currency-risks-2026.jpg%20(2).png" title="IMF Stablecoin Warning: Cheaper Cross-Border Payments, Currency Risks" width="400" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;Stablecoins are moving into a new phase.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Once viewed mainly as a tool for cryptocurrency trading, dollar-backed digital tokens are increasingly being discussed as potential infrastructure for global payments. The technology could make some cross-border transactions faster and cheaper, but it could also create new challenges for countries trying to protect their currencies and maintain financial stability.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That tension was highlighted by International Monetary Fund Managing Director &lt;strong&gt;Kristalina Georgieva&lt;/strong&gt; in remarks at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium on August 28, 2026.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Georgieva said tokenization and stablecoins could help make global finance more fluid, with stablecoins showing potential to make &lt;strong&gt;large-value cross-border payments cheaper and faster&lt;/strong&gt;. At the same time, she warned that a more fluid financial system can transmit risks more quickly and create a greater penalty for policy mistakes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Primary source:&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href="https://www.imf.org/en/news/articles/2026/08/28/sp082826-md-navigating-a-financially-more-fluid-world" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;IMF — Kristalina Georgieva, “Navigating a Financially More Fluid World”&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Stablecoins Could Make International Payments Cheaper&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Cross-border payments remain one of the more complicated parts of the global financial system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A payment moving between countries can pass through banks, correspondent institutions, payment networks, foreign-exchange providers and other intermediaries. Each additional layer can add costs, processing time or operational complexity.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Stablecoins offer a different model.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A blockchain-based stablecoin can potentially move value across borders at any time without relying on every traditional payment layer to process the transaction in the same way.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That does not mean every stablecoin payment will automatically be cheaper. Users can still encounter blockchain fees, exchange-rate spreads, conversion costs, custody fees and other charges.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the underlying technology could reduce friction in some high-value international transactions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Georgieva Actually Said&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The IMF's position is more nuanced than simply being for or against stablecoins.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In her August 28 speech, Georgieva said financial innovation has historically improved domestic payments in terms of speed, convenience and cost. She also noted that progress in cross-border payments has been uneven, with many transactions remaining expensive and slow.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;She identified &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/how-do-companies-use-ai-today.html"&gt;stablecoins &lt;/a&gt;and tokenization as technologies that could potentially contribute to a broader transformation of cross-border payments.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But Georgieva also emphasized that the benefits come with risks that policymakers need to address.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The IMF's concern is therefore not that stablecoins are guaranteed to destabilize emerging markets. Rather, the concern is that widespread adoption—particularly of foreign-currency stablecoins—could create additional pressure on countries with weaker currencies or less resilient financial systems.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Currency-Substitution Problem&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;One of the biggest issues is &lt;strong&gt;currency substitution&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Imagine a country where inflation is high and people are losing confidence in the domestic currency.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Residents may already prefer to hold U.S. dollars as a store of value. A dollar-backed stablecoin could make that foreign-currency exposure easier to obtain, transfer and use digitally.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If enough people begin using the stablecoin for savings, payments or pricing, the domestic currency could gradually lose some of its traditional role.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is where the issue becomes important for central banks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Monetary policy works partly through demand for the domestic currency and the domestic financial system. If economic activity increasingly shifts toward a foreign-currency stablecoin, the transmission of monetary policy could become more difficult.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Emerging Markets Could Face Greater Pressure&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Not every country would experience the same effects.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Countries with strong currencies, deep &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/do-you-need-to-pay-public-blockchain-explorer-fee.html"&gt;financial markets&lt;/a&gt; and credible institutions may be better positioned to absorb the changes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Emerging markets and developing economies with weaker currencies, higher inflation or tighter capital controls could face greater pressure if foreign-currency stablecoins become widely adopted.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;According to Georgieva, stablecoins could potentially make capital controls more porous and contribute to several related risks, including:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Currency substitution&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Capital-flow volatility&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Exchange-rate instability&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Reduced monetary-policy effectiveness&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Pressure on monetary sovereignty&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Faster Payments Can Also Mean Faster Risk&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is one of the less obvious parts of the stablecoin debate.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The same infrastructure that makes payments move faster during normal conditions can also allow capital to move more quickly during periods of financial stress.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If investors can rapidly convert local assets into a dollar-backed &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/zcash-just-got-major-speed-boost-zakura.html"&gt;digital token&lt;/a&gt; and transfer those tokens abroad, capital outflows could potentially happen faster than they would through traditional channels.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That does not mean every stablecoin transaction represents capital flight. Most transactions may have perfectly legitimate commercial purposes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The concern is what could happen when large numbers of users react simultaneously to an economic shock.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Stablecoins: Potential Benefits vs. Potential Risks&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;table style="border-collapse: collapse; font-size: 16px; margin: 25px 0px; width: 100%;"&gt;
&lt;thead&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px; text-align: left;"&gt;Potential Benefit&lt;/th&gt;
&lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px; text-align: left;"&gt;Potential Risk&lt;/th&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/thead&gt;

&lt;tbody&gt;

&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Faster cross-border &lt;br /&gt;settlement&lt;/td&gt;

&lt;/tr&gt;

&lt;/tr&gt;

&lt;/tr&gt;

&lt;/tr&gt;

&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Potentially broader global &lt;br /&gt;financial access&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Greater exchange-rate and &lt;br /&gt;capital-flow volatility&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;

&lt;/tbody&gt;
&lt;/table&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Banking System Could Also Feel the Impact&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Stablecoins are not only a monetary-policy issue.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;They could also affect commercial banks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If consumers and businesses move significant amounts of money from traditional bank deposits into stablecoins, banks could potentially lose part of their deposit funding base.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That matters because bank deposits are an important source of funding for lending to households and businesses.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Georgieva therefore highlighted the importance of preventing excessive bank disintermediation while allowing competition and innovation to develop.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In other words, regulators need to make sure stablecoins improve financial competition without unintentionally weakening the banking system that supports the wider economy.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Reserve Management Matters&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is another issue that often gets overlooked when discussing stablecoins: the assets backing them.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A stablecoin is only as credible as the mechanism that allows users to trust its value and redemption process.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For a dollar-backed stablecoin, users need confidence that the issuer maintains appropriate reserves and that those reserves can support redemption at or close to the promised value.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is why Georgieva called for strong rules around reserve pools and international coordination.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Without transparency, liquidity and reliable redemption mechanisms, the promise of a stable digital dollar can quickly become a source of financial risk.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Could Stablecoins Strengthen the Dollar?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Most of the world's largest stablecoins are linked to the U.S. dollar.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That means stablecoin growth could potentially increase the global reach of dollar-denominated assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Someone who does not have easy access to traditional U.S. banking services may nevertheless be able to obtain a dollar-backed digital token through a crypto platform or other service.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For users, that can provide another way to hold and transfer dollar-denominated value.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For policymakers in other countries, however, the same development raises questions about the long-term role of their domestic currencies.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is why stablecoins are increasingly being discussed as part of the international monetary system rather than simply as another cryptocurrency product.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Regulation Will Be Critical&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The IMF's message points toward a regulatory challenge that will likely become more important as adoption grows.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Governments need to allow useful innovation without creating loopholes that encourage regulatory arbitrage.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Some of the questions regulators will need to address include:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;How should stablecoin reserves be regulated?&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;What standards should issuers follow?&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;How should users be protected?&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;How should cross-border transactions be monitored?&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;What happens if a major stablecoin experiences a loss of confidence?&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;How should stablecoin intermediaries interact with banks?&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;How should governments respond to widespread foreign-currency stablecoin adoption?&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;These are not questions that can be answered by technology alone.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;They involve monetary policy, banking regulation, taxation, consumer protection and international cooperation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Stablecoins Are Not Automatically Good or Bad&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The stablecoin debate is sometimes presented as a simple choice.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Either stablecoins are the future of payments, or they are a threat to traditional finance.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The reality is more complicated.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;They can potentially solve genuine problems in cross-border payments while simultaneously creating new risks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A payment system that is faster and cheaper can be extremely useful. But if the same system allows capital to move across borders almost instantly during a crisis, policymakers need safeguards capable of dealing with that speed.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is the balance the IMF is highlighting.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What This Means for Crypto and Traditional Finance&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For the cryptocurrency industry, Georgieva's remarks are another indication that stablecoins are being taken seriously as financial infrastructure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For banks, the message is equally important: digital payment technology could increase competition and force traditional institutions to modernize.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For emerging markets, however, the stakes may be higher.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The adoption of foreign-currency stablecoins could provide consumers with cheaper and more convenient ways to move money, but it could also challenge domestic currencies if adoption becomes widespread.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That means the next phase of stablecoin development will likely be shaped as much by regulation and monetary policy as by blockchain technology.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Stablecoins could make parts of the global payment system faster, cheaper and more competitive.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is the opportunity.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The risk is that greater financial fluidity also means greater speed when money moves out of a country, a bank or a domestic currency.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva's message is therefore not that stablecoins should be stopped. It is that the benefits of financial innovation need to be accompanied by strong regulation and sound macroeconomic policy.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;For emerging markets, the central question may ultimately be whether they can embrace the efficiency of digital dollars without allowing those digital dollars to weaken confidence in their own currencies.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Stablecoins may be part of the future of global payments. How that future affects monetary sovereignty, banks and exchange rates will depend heavily on the rules built around them.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;hr /&gt;

Unrealized gains have crossed $137,000, representing a return of roughly 65.36% on the trade.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="ds-markdown-paragraph" style="background-color: white; color: #0f1115; font-family: quote-cjk-patch, Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &amp;quot;Segoe UI&amp;quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, &amp;quot;Open Sans&amp;quot;, &amp;quot;Helvetica Neue&amp;quot;, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 16px 0px;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-weight: 600;"&gt;Why This Trade Stands Out&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="ds-markdown-paragraph" style="background-color: white; color: #0f1115; font-family: quote-cjk-patch, Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &amp;quot;Segoe UI&amp;quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, &amp;quot;Open Sans&amp;quot;, &amp;quot;Helvetica Neue&amp;quot;, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 16px 0px;"&gt;&lt;span class=""&gt;This isn't the first time a trader has made a splash on Aster. Earlier this year, another address opened a similar 5x long on Aster shortly after the platform launched perpetual contracts. That &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/the-business-is-gradually-back-to-usual.html"&gt;token &lt;/a&gt;went on to rally more than 510%. The pattern suggests that for some traders, Aster's newer listings and token updates have become opportunities for high-conviction leveraged bets.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="ds-markdown-paragraph" style="background-color: white; color: #0f1115; font-family: quote-cjk-patch, Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &amp;quot;Segoe UI&amp;quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, &amp;quot;Open Sans&amp;quot;, &amp;quot;Helvetica Neue&amp;quot;, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 16px 0px;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-weight: 600;"&gt;ASTER Price and Market Data&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="ds-markdown-paragraph" style="background-color: white; color: #0f1115; font-family: quote-cjk-patch, Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &amp;quot;Segoe UI&amp;quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, &amp;quot;Open Sans&amp;quot;, &amp;quot;Helvetica Neue&amp;quot;, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 16px 0px;"&gt;&lt;span class=""&gt;ASTER is currently trading in the $0.65 to $0.75 range, depending on the data source. The token is up approximately 6.6% over the past 24 hours.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="ds-markdown-paragraph" style="background-color: white; color: #0f1115; font-family: quote-cjk-patch, Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &amp;quot;Segoe UI&amp;quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, &amp;quot;Open Sans&amp;quot;, &amp;quot;Helvetica Neue&amp;quot;, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 16px 0px;"&gt;&lt;span class=""&gt;At current prices, ASTER carries a market capitalization of roughly $1.6–$2 billion, with a circulating supply of about 2.47–2.7 billion tokens. The maximum supply is capped at 8 billion.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="ds-markdown-paragraph" style="background-color: white; color: #0f1115; font-family: quote-cjk-patch, Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &amp;quot;Segoe UI&amp;quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, &amp;quot;Open Sans&amp;quot;, &amp;quot;Helvetica Neue&amp;quot;, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 16px 0px;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-weight: 600;"&gt;What Is Aster DEX?&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="ds-markdown-paragraph" style="background-color: white; color: #0f1115; font-family: quote-cjk-patch, Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &amp;quot;Segoe UI&amp;quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, &amp;quot;Open Sans&amp;quot;, &amp;quot;Helvetica Neue&amp;quot;, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 16px 0px;"&gt;&lt;span class=""&gt;Aster is a decentralized perpetual exchange formed in 2024 through the merger of Astherus and APX Finance. It supports trading across multiple chains — including BNB Chain, &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/valour-launches-zcash-etp-on-spotlight.html"&gt;Ethereum&lt;/a&gt;, &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/spacecoins-parent-company-signs-50m-pre.html"&gt;Solana&lt;/a&gt;, and Arbitrum — without requiring users to bridge assets.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="ds-markdown-paragraph" style="background-color: white; color: #0f1115; font-family: quote-cjk-patch, Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &amp;quot;Segoe UI&amp;quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, &amp;quot;Open Sans&amp;quot;, &amp;quot;Helvetica Neue&amp;quot;, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 16px 0px;"&gt;&lt;span class=""&gt;One of Aster's distinguishing features is its support for yield-bearing collateral. Traders can use asBNB (a liquid staking derivative of BNB) or USDF (Aster's yield-bearing stablecoin) as margin. These assets continue to earn yield while serving as trading collateral, which improves capital efficiency for active traders.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="ds-markdown-paragraph" style="background-color: white; color: #0f1115; font-family: quote-cjk-patch, Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &amp;quot;Segoe UI&amp;quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, &amp;quot;Open Sans&amp;quot;, &amp;quot;Helvetica Neue&amp;quot;, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 16px 0px;"&gt;&lt;span class=""&gt;Aster is backed by YZi Labs, formerly known as Binance Labs. The leveraged long position highlighted by Lookonchain is now profitable, but 5x leverage cuts both ways. A sharp reversal in ASTER's price would put that position under pressure quickly.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="ds-markdown-paragraph" style="background-color: white; color: #0f1115; font-family: quote-cjk-patch, Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, &amp;quot;Segoe UI&amp;quot;, Roboto, Oxygen, Ubuntu, Cantarell, &amp;quot;Open Sans&amp;quot;, &amp;quot;Helvetica Neue&amp;quot;, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; margin: 16px 0px;"&gt;&lt;span class=""&gt;Funding rates, open interest on Aster DEX, and broader crypto market sentiment will all play a role in what happens next.     <title>Why Can't Circle Reverse Stolen USDC on Arc? The Difference Between a Blockchain Rollback and a Token Freeze</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;article&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh04GngBgXLgrMm_J1HfigDqJmdNM2_2XVkiL3RRtkT1S9yjm_YUQgyODlI2FZuWg3ubbm1I1_Dyg8KWYLjXuBKCBv4wQJEMW9qmSU2Tt05XOSXm9Ok70UpqjskKDCJKvJeDLf_JrCJhJcTsQ5ALXx4ExI4AwnadasRhkHqThBog2eX3sJANApjaSwJvJbT/s1672/circle-usdc-arc-blockchain-rollback-freeze.webp.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="Circle USDC freeze versus Arc blockchain rollback explained" border="0" data-original-height="940" data-original-width="1672" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh04GngBgXLgrMm_J1HfigDqJmdNM2_2XVkiL3RRtkT1S9yjm_YUQgyODlI2FZuWg3ubbm1I1_Dyg8KWYLjXuBKCBv4wQJEMW9qmSU2Tt05XOSXm9Ok70UpqjskKDCJKvJeDLf_JrCJhJcTsQ5ALXx4ExI4AwnadasRhkHqThBog2eX3sJANApjaSwJvJbT/s1600/circle-usdc-arc-blockchain-rollback-freeze.webp.png" title="Circle USDC Freeze vs Arc Blockchain Rollback" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;By CoinAINews Editorial Desk&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;When Circle launched its Arc blockchain on September 16, 2026, one question arrived almost immediately: &lt;strong&gt;What happens if someone steals USDC on Arc?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The answer is more complicated than simply saying that Circle can freeze USDC.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle can use controls at the &lt;strong&gt;USDC token layer&lt;/strong&gt; to freeze certain addresses under its established procedures. But Arc itself is designed as an immutable blockchain, meaning Circle does not have a special button that allows it to rewrite the blockchain and send a confirmed transaction back to its original state.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction matters because a token freeze and a blockchain rollback are two completely different mechanisms.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Did Circle Say About Stolen USDC on Arc?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle Chief Product and Technology Officer Nikhil Chandhok addressed the issue in a September interview after Arc's mainnet launch. He said Circle is not interested in rolling back the Arc blockchain, even in the event of a major theft.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The reasoning is straightforward: if a company could simply rewrite blockchain history whenever a large transaction went wrong, users would have to trust that company to decide when the history should change.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Arc is instead designed so that transaction finality is part of the network's core architecture. Circle's own description of Arc positions it as a blockchain built for &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/zcash-ironwood-explained-why-80-of.html"&gt;stablecoin &lt;/a&gt;payments, financial applications and emerging machine-to-machine or AI-agent activity.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;So if someone sends USDC to the wrong address or a smart contract is exploited, the underlying blockchain record does not simply disappear because Circle operates the network's ecosystem.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;But Can Circle Freeze USDC?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Yes, and this is where the story becomes interesting.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle's ability to freeze USDC should not be confused with the ability to reverse an Arc transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A freeze can prevent an address from moving certain USDC. It does not necessarily erase the original transaction from the blockchain.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Think of it this way:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Rollback:&lt;/strong&gt; changes the blockchain's historical record.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Freeze:&lt;/strong&gt; restricts movement of tokens associated with an address.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Recovery:&lt;/strong&gt; requires the stolen assets to somehow be returned to their legitimate owner.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;These are three different concepts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle's published USDC terms also state that USDC transactions on supported &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/solana-yield-optimization-in-2026.html"&gt;blockchains &lt;/a&gt;are irreversible and that Circle does not have the ability to reverse or recall a transaction once it has been initiated. Circle separately maintains controls that can affect USDC accounts and transactions under applicable circumstances.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Doesn't Circle Simply Reverse the Blockchain?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The easiest answer is that doing so would undermine one of the fundamental properties of blockchain infrastructure: &lt;strong&gt;finality&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Imagine a bank database where an administrator can go back several hours and change the transaction history after deciding that an earlier payment should not have happened.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That model can be useful in some financial systems because there is a central authority responsible for correcting mistakes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Public blockchains generally take a different approach.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Once a transaction has been confirmed according to the network's consensus rules, the transaction becomes part of the chain's history. Applications may have additional controls, and token issuers may have their own administrative functions, but changing the underlying blockchain history is a much more significant action.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle's position on Arc is that the company does not want to establish itself as an authority capable of rewriting that history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Would a Rollback Actually Mean?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A blockchain rollback would mean reorganizing or rewriting a portion of the network's historical state.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For example, suppose an attacker stole $100 million worth of USDC through an exploited application.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A true rollback could theoretically attempt to return the blockchain to a state before the exploit occurred and then process the transactions again under a different outcome.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But that would create another problem: &lt;strong&gt;what happens to every legitimate transaction that occurred after the theft?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Other users could have deposited funds, traded assets, borrowed money, repaid loans or interacted with smart contracts after the original transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Rewriting history could therefore create a chain reaction across the entire ecosystem.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is one reason why blockchain finality matters to financial applications. Participants need to know when a transaction becomes final and can be relied upon.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Freeze vs Rollback: The Difference Explained&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;table style="border-collapse: collapse; border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); width: 100%;"&gt;
&lt;thead&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;So What Happens If Someone Steals USDC on Arc?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is no universal recovery button.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If an attacker obtains USDC through a compromised wallet, phishing attack or vulnerable smart contract, the first question is whether the relevant funds can be identified and whether token-level controls can prevent further movement.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That does not mean the original transaction can be erased.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The practical difference is important. A blockchain explorer could continue to show that the original USDC moved from one address to another even if the receiving address later becomes restricted from moving the tokens.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In other words, &lt;strong&gt;freezing an asset does not rewrite its history.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Is This Important for Banks and Institutions?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Arc was designed specifically with financial and institutional applications in mind.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle describes the network as an economic infrastructure layer for stablecoin payments, trading, treasury activity and other financial applications. The project launched with institutional validators, and Circle has also highlighted AI agents as an emerging category of economic participant.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That makes the question of transaction finality particularly important.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A bank or asset manager wants predictable settlement. At the same time, traditional financial systems often have mechanisms for fraud investigations, disputes and corrections.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Arc's approach does not attempt to make &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/solana-tests-alpenglow-upgrade-to-cut.html"&gt;blockchain transactions&lt;/a&gt; equivalent to a credit-card chargeback.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead, the network emphasizes blockchain finality while leaving token-level controls and application-level safeguards as separate layers.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Does Arc's Immutability Mean USDC Is Completely Unstoppable?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is another important distinction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Arc's blockchain immutability does not mean every USDC balance is immune from token-level restrictions.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;USDC is a centrally issued stablecoin. Circle maintains certain administrative controls over the token, including the ability to freeze addresses under its policies and applicable legal requirements.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Therefore, Arc combines two different ideas:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;The blockchain's transaction history is intended to remain immutable.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;The USDC token itself retains issuer-level controls.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Those two properties can coexist.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Would Circle Choose This Model?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Arc is targeting a different part of the market from blockchains designed primarily around speculative token trading.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle is positioning Arc around stablecoin payments, financial infrastructure, institutional activity and programmable economic applications.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For these users, predictable settlement can be more important than having a blockchain that can be manually reorganized after a major incident.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The trade-off is that users and applications have to take security seriously before transactions become final.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Smart-contract audits, wallet security, transaction simulation, access controls and operational safeguards therefore become especially important.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What About a Huge Hack?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is where the debate becomes more difficult.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A small mistaken transfer and a billion-dollar protocol exploit are obviously very different events, but an immutable system has to apply its rules consistently.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle's public position is that it does not want to roll back Arc even in response to a major hack.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That does not mean every stolen USDC case is hopeless. Token freezes, law-enforcement investigations, exchange cooperation and voluntary recovery agreements can potentially affect what happens after a theft.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But none of those mechanisms should be confused with rewriting Arc's blockchain history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Arc's Approach Is Different From Traditional Finance&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Traditional finance generally operates with centralized ledgers and institutions that can investigate, reverse, dispute or correct transactions under defined circumstances.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Blockchain networks move much of that responsibility toward software rules and consensus.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Arc is an interesting example because it is designed for institutional finance while still preserving blockchain-style finality.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That creates a practical compromise: the network can be used for regulated financial activity while the underlying blockchain does not give Circle unilateral authority to rewrite confirmed transactions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Does This Mean for Ordinary USDC Users?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For users, the lesson is simple: &lt;strong&gt;treat an Arc transaction as final.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Before sending USDC, users should verify the destination address, network, amount and application involved.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;They should also understand that sending funds to the wrong address is fundamentally different from making a payment through a traditional system that may offer a dispute or chargeback mechanism.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle's own documentation warns users that blockchain transactions can be irreversible and that funds sent incorrectly may not be recoverable.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This makes wallet security and transaction verification especially important when using a new blockchain.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bigger Question: Can Stablecoins Have Both Control and Immutability?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Arc highlights a broader question for the stablecoin industry.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Institutions want predictable settlement, compliance tools and mechanisms for dealing with illicit activity. Blockchain users, meanwhile, value transparency, finality and resistance to arbitrary changes in transaction history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle's architecture separates those responsibilities instead of putting them into one mechanism.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain can maintain its historical record while the issuer retains controls over the token itself.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Whether that model becomes common across institutional stablecoin networks will depend on how financial institutions, developers and users respond to the trade-off.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Circle cannot simply press a button and erase a confirmed Arc transaction because Arc is designed around immutable blockchain history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That does &lt;strong&gt;not&lt;/strong&gt; mean Circle has no control over USDC. Token-level controls, including freezing certain addresses, operate separately from the blockchain's consensus layer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The key distinction is therefore:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Circle can have controls over USDC without having the ability to rewrite Arc's blockchain history.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For users, the practical takeaway is even simpler: once an Arc transaction is confirmed, assume it is final and verify every transaction before signing it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Frequently Asked Questions&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Can Circle reverse a stolen USDC transaction on Arc?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Circle has said it does not intend to roll back Arc's blockchain to reverse transactions. Token-level controls such as freezing an address are different from rewriting blockchain history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Can Circle freeze USDC on Arc?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;USDC has issuer-level administrative controls, including mechanisms that can restrict certain addresses. A freeze does not erase the original blockchain transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Is Arc blockchain immutable?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Arc is designed around immutable transaction history and finality. Circle has publicly stated that it does not want to roll back the Arc blockchain.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What happens if USDC is sent to the wrong Arc address?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;The transaction may be irreversible. Users should verify the address and network before confirming a transaction because Circle does not generally provide a mechanism to reverse a completed blockchain transfer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Why did Circle create Arc?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Circle describes Arc as a blockchain designed for stablecoin payments and financial applications, with use cases including institutional finance and emerging AI-agent economic activity.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Does freezing USDC mean the blockchain transaction is reversed?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;No. Freezing affects the token's ability to move from an affected address. It does not rewrite the historical blockchain record.&lt;/p&gt;

DeFi Development describes CHAD as the first “SOL-backed Digital Credit” instrument, although that description is the company's own characterization of the product.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;DeFi Development Closes the CHAD Offering&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development Corp. announced on September 8 that it had completed its previously announced underwritten public offering of CHAD preferred stock.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The offering generated approximately &lt;strong&gt;$11 million in gross proceeds&lt;/strong&gt;. That figure is important because it is not the same as the amount that will ultimately be available for SOL purchases. Underwriting discounts, commissions and other offering expenses are deducted before the company deploys the net proceeds.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The company said substantially all of those net proceeds are expected to be used to acquire additional SOL.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That makes CHAD part of &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/strategy-skips-bitcoin-buy-as-strc.html"&gt;DeFi &lt;/a&gt;Development's broader strategy of raising capital through public markets and directing that capital toward a Solana-focused treasury.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What Is CHAD?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;CHAD is not a cryptocurrency token. It is a &lt;strong&gt;Variable Rate Series C Perpetual Preferred Stock&lt;/strong&gt; issued by DeFi Development Corp.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The shares were offered at &lt;strong&gt;$8 each&lt;/strong&gt; and have a stated amount of &lt;strong&gt;$10 per share&lt;/strong&gt;. The security trades on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the ticker symbol CHAD.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The initial annual dividend rate is 13%, which translates into an initial effective yield of approximately 16.25% when calculated against the $8 offering price.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Dividends are cumulative and accrue daily when and if declared by the company's board. The dividend rate can also change under the security's terms.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Why the $11 Million Matters for Solana&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The main reason the offering is attracting attention in crypto markets is its intended connection to SOL accumulation.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development said it expects to deploy substantially all of the net proceeds into additional SOL. In practical terms, the company is using a preferred-equity financing structure to raise capital that can then be allocated toward its &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/cronos-recovers-1112m-after-tectonic.html"&gt;digital-asset&lt;/a&gt; treasury.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The strategy differs from simply selling additional common shares. Because CHAD is non-convertible preferred equity, the company said the issuance does not increase its common share count.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development therefore expects the transaction to be accretive to its &lt;strong&gt;SOL per share (SPS)&lt;/strong&gt; metric once the proceeds are deployed into additional SOL.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;CHAD Does Not Mean $11 Million of SOL Was Bought&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;There is an important distinction between the size of the offering and the amount of SOL eventually purchased.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The company raised approximately $11 million &lt;strong&gt;before&lt;/strong&gt; underwriting discounts, commissions and offering expenses. The actual amount available for purchasing SOL will therefore be lower than the headline gross figure.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development has also not yet provided the final number of SOL acquired from these proceeds in the September 8 announcement. The company said it expects to provide an update on its SOL holdings and SPS after the offering proceeds are deployed.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That means the $11 million figure should be treated as a financing amount, not as a confirmed $11 million SOL purchase.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Why the Company Calls CHAD “Digital Credit”&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development describes CHAD as the first &lt;strong&gt;SOL-backed Digital Credit instrument&lt;/strong&gt;. That wording comes directly from the company and should not be interpreted as an independently established industry classification.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The company's argument is that CHAD expands the emerging digital-credit model beyond Bitcoin by using a Solana-focused treasury strategy.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development also points to one feature it considers important: SOL can generate native staking rewards. The company operates validator infrastructure and participates in staking and other Solana-related activities.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;In the company's model, capital raised through CHAD can be deployed into SOL, while the SOL held in the treasury can potentially generate staking-related income.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Tom Lee Participated in the Offering&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The CHAD offering also attracted participation from &lt;strong&gt;Thomas “Tom” Lee&lt;/strong&gt;, co-founder and head of research at Fundstrat Global Advisors and chairman of the board of BitMine.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development said Lee participated alongside other investors. The company did not state that Lee personally supplied the entire $11 million offering.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That distinction matters because the offering was a broader public financing rather than a single-investor capital injection.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;CHAD Is Designed as a Repeatable Funding Mechanism&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development is positioning CHAD as more than a one-time capital raise.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The company said establishing CHAD around its $10 stated amount and building liquidity in the security are near-term priorities. Management believes that a functioning market for CHAD could eventually provide a recurring source of capital for additional SOL purchases.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;This is effectively the company's proposed capital-markets flywheel: raise capital through preferred stock, deploy the proceeds into SOL, increase the company's SOL treasury and potentially improve its SOL-per-share metric without issuing additional common shares through this particular offering.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Whether that model can be repeated at scale will depend on investor demand, CHAD's trading performance, SOL's market conditions and the company's ability to access additional capital.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What Investors Should Watch Next&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The next important disclosure will be DeFi Development's update on its SOL holdings and SPS following deployment of the offering proceeds.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Investors will also be watching how CHAD trades relative to its $10 stated amount, how the company manages its variable dividend rate and whether the preferred stock can develop sufficient liquidity to support future offerings.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;At the same time, the strategy remains directly exposed to the risks associated with SOL. A decline in the price of Solana could reduce the value of the company's treasury and affect the economics of the strategy.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Key Risks Behind the Strategy&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;CHAD's structure does not eliminate market risk. DeFi Development's own filing warns that fluctuations in SOL's price, changes in market conditions, interest rates, regulatory developments and the company's ability to access capital could affect future results.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The company's statements about future SOL accumulation, SPS growth and CHAD becoming a recurring funding source are forward-looking statements rather than guarantees of future performance.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;For investors, the key question is therefore not simply how much money DeFi Development raised, but whether the company can deploy capital efficiently enough for the resulting SOL treasury growth to justify the cost of the preferred financing.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;How CHAD Fits Into DeFi Development's Solana Treasury Strategy&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development has built its corporate strategy around accumulating and compounding SOL. The company says the principal holding in its treasury reserve is allocated to Solana and that it also operates validator infrastructure.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;CHAD gives the company another &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/uniswap-processes-500m-in-tokenized.html"&gt;financing instrument &lt;/a&gt;alongside common equity and other potential sources of capital.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The key difference is that this particular issuance does not increase the common share count because CHAD is non-convertible preferred equity. If the company successfully deploys the capital into SOL, management believes that can improve SOL exposure on a per-common-share basis.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Frequently Asked Questions&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;What is CHAD stock?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;CHAD is DeFi Development Corp.'s Variable Rate Series C Perpetual Preferred Stock. It trades on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the ticker CHAD.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;How much did DeFi Development raise with CHAD?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development said the offering generated approximately $11 million in gross proceeds before underwriting discounts, commissions and offering expenses.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Will the entire $11 million be used to buy Solana?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;No. The $11 million figure is gross proceeds. The company expects to use substantially all of the net proceeds to acquire additional SOL after offering-related costs.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;What is CHAD's initial dividend rate?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;CHAD has an initial annual dividend rate of 13%. Based on the $8 offering price, DeFi Development says that represents an initial effective yield of approximately 16.25%.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Does CHAD dilute DFDV common shareholders?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;The company says the issuance does not increase its common share count because CHAD is non-convertible preferred equity.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Did Tom Lee invest the full $11 million?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;No. DeFi Development said Thomas “Tom” Lee participated in the offering alongside other investors. The company did not identify him as the sole investor or say that he provided the entire offering amount.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Has DeFi Development already announced how much SOL it bought with the proceeds?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;Not in the September 8 closing announcement. The company said it expects to provide an update on its SOL holdings and SOL per share after the proceeds are deployed.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;DeFi Development Corp.'s approximately &lt;strong&gt;$11 million CHAD offering&lt;/strong&gt; adds a new preferred-equity financing route to its Solana treasury strategy.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The most important facts are straightforward: CHAD was issued at $8 per share, carries an initial 13% annual dividend rate, is listed on Nasdaq under CHAD and is non-convertible preferred equity. The company expects substantially all net proceeds to be deployed into additional SOL.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The bigger test now is execution. DeFi Development will need to show how much SOL the capital ultimately purchases and whether the resulting increase in its SOL treasury translates into the SOL-per-share growth that management expects.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Sources&lt;/h2&gt;

    <title>Can a Blockchain Be Legally Considered a Person If It Controls Its Own Wallet? The Law Says No — For Now.</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;br /&gt;&lt;article&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgOCd6LyN9fZ_dXPEnxf8r1k9KUr_Omlr4WIapJbS_j9xgSuTrge1e9NKmIJXXXnrHbB1R8_kLwhJdx3ZEQf5MKeWZ3oZOSG8yxgkKZ_c6BPbSokewaiB3w_2iRxUhpAkmH0TaQJi55gP9P-KTXWDn1fwPJA9YKjm6Yohl8g52nFrYOSOxv_za-2h_-H3UD/s1672/blockchain-legal-personhood-ai-wallet.jpg.png" imageanchor="1" style="font-size: medium; margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;img alt="AI-powered blockchain wallet and digital legal system representing the question of blockchain legal personhood" border="0" data-original-height="941" data-original-width="1672" height="225" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgOCd6LyN9fZ_dXPEnxf8r1k9KUr_Omlr4WIapJbS_j9xgSuTrge1e9NKmIJXXXnrHbB1R8_kLwhJdx3ZEQf5MKeWZ3oZOSG8yxgkKZ_c6BPbSokewaiB3w_2iRxUhpAkmH0TaQJi55gP9P-KTXWDn1fwPJA9YKjm6Yohl8g52nFrYOSOxv_za-2h_-H3UD/w400-h225/blockchain-legal-personhood-ai-wallet.jpg.png" title="Can a Blockchain Become a Legal Person?" width="400" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: small;"&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: small;"&gt;By CoinAINews Staff |&amp;nbsp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: small;"&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A blockchain can hold assets, execute transactions and run code without anyone manually approving every step — but that doesn't automatically make it a legal person.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction is becoming harder to ignore as decentralized organizations, smart contracts and AI-powered agents gain the ability to control wallets and move digital assets with increasingly little human intervention.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Imagine a blockchain-based protocol with its own &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/bitcoin-reclaimed-four-major-moving.html"&gt;wallet&lt;/a&gt;. The wallet receives cryptocurrency, pays for infrastructure, moves funds according to smart-contract rules and continues operating automatically.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who, legally, is doing all of that?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The developers?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The people controlling the protocol?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Or the legal entity, if there is one?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is no general rule under which a blockchain automatically becomes a legal person simply because it can transact autonomously. But recent DAO litigation shows that courts can apply existing legal categories to decentralized organizations for specific purposes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction is important — and it is one reason the legal future of autonomous blockchain systems remains unsettled.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;A Wallet Doesn't Automatically Create a Legal Person&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The first distinction is the most important one.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A crypto wallet is essentially a mechanism for controlling blockchain assets through cryptographic keys. It can send and receive cryptocurrency, but having a wallet doesn't automatically create a legal identity.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The same is true for a smart contract.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A smart contract can automatically execute transactions when predefined conditions are met. That automation can make software appear to act independently, but the code itself doesn't automatically become a corporation, LLC or other legal entity.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Legal personality comes from the applicable legal system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That means a blockchain address can exist on-chain without necessarily having a corresponding legal person behind it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And that's where things become complicated.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;DAOs Are Already Testing the Boundary&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Decentralized autonomous organizations, or DAOs, provide one of the clearest examples.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A DAO can use smart contracts, governance mechanisms and blockchain wallets to manage a treasury and make collective decisions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the legal status of a DAO depends heavily on jurisdiction and structure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Wyoming provides an important example.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Under Wyoming law, a DAO can be organized as a limited liability company. The state's DAO statute provides a framework under the Wyoming Limited Liability Company Act and allows an LLC to elect DAO status. The framework also recognizes algorithmic management as one possible organizational model.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://wyoleg.gov/NXT/gateway.dll/Statutes%2F2021%20Titles%2F879%2F1045%2F1046" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;
Read the Wyoming DAO statute
&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is very different from saying that the blockchain itself has become a legal person.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The legal entity is the LLC.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain and smart contracts are part of the technology through which that organization operates.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction could become increasingly important as autonomous systems become more capable.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What If There Are No Human Decisions?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Now consider a more extreme scenario.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Suppose a DAO's treasury is controlled by smart contracts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI agent analyzes market conditions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It proposes a transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Another automated system evaluates the risk.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A governance mechanism approves the action according to predefined rules.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The transaction is then signed and broadcast automatically.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No human presses a button.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Does that mean nobody is responsible?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Not necessarily.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The absence of a human click doesn't automatically erase the legal relationships surrounding the system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Courts could look at who created the software, who controlled the infrastructure, who benefited from the activity, who had the ability to modify or stop the system and what legal structure surrounded the project.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The exact answer would depend on the facts and the jurisdiction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Courts Have Already Had to Ask Who Is Behind a DAO&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This isn't purely theoretical.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;U.S. courts have already dealt with cases involving the legal status and potential liability of DAOs.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The &lt;strong&gt;Ooki DAO&lt;/strong&gt; case is particularly important because it shows why an absolute statement about DAO legal personhood would be misleading.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In the CFTC's enforcement action, the court held that Ooki DAO could be sued as an unincorporated association and was a “person” under the Commodity Exchange Act for purposes of the case. The court subsequently entered a default judgment against the DAO.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/PressReleases/8715-23" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;
Read the CFTC's official statement on the Ooki DAO litigation
&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This does &lt;strong&gt;not&lt;/strong&gt; mean every DAO, blockchain or autonomous wallet is automatically a legal person.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The ruling concerned a particular DAO, a particular federal statute and a particular legal proceeding.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction matters.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It is more accurate to say that the Ooki case demonstrated that a decentralized organization can, under certain circumstances, fall within an existing statutory definition of “person.”&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is very different from creating a universal rule that software or blockchains have legal personhood.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Lido Case Added Another Layer&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The legal uncertainty became even more visible in litigation involving &lt;strong&gt;Lido DAO&lt;/strong&gt;, where a federal judge allowed claims to proceed under a general partnership theory.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The case was important because it raised a question that goes to the heart of decentralized governance: can participants in a DAO potentially face traditional legal obligations even when the organization operates through blockchain-based voting and smart contracts?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The answer isn't a universal “yes.”&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The ruling did not establish that every DAO is a general partnership, nor did it mean that every token holder automatically becomes personally liable for a DAO's activities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead, it showed how courts can attempt to apply existing legal concepts to organizations that operate in ways traditional corporate law did not anticipate.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/column-blow-crypto-collectives-judge-rules-venture-backers-must-face-claims-2024-12-02/" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;
Read Reuters' coverage of the Lido DAO ruling
&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For blockchain projects, that's a significant warning.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Decentralization can change how an organization operates technologically without necessarily eliminating the legal consequences associated with its activities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What About an AI-Controlled Wallet?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is where the question becomes even more interesting.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI agent can potentially operate a wallet, decide when to make transactions and interact with blockchain protocols.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But a cryptographic identity isn't the same thing as legal personhood.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A blockchain can recognize an address.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A protocol can recognize a wallet.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI system can identify itself through cryptographic credentials.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;None of those facts, by themselves, answer whether a court would recognize the software as a legal person.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The legal question is ultimately different from the technical one.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A machine can prove that it controls a private key.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That doesn't automatically prove that the machine has legal rights, obligations or capacity to enter into contracts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Legal Personhood Is More Than Having an Identity&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A legal person isn't simply something that can be uniquely identified.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Corporations, LLCs and other legal entities can have rights and obligations because the law recognizes them as entities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;They can enter contracts, own property, sue or be sued and incur liabilities, depending on the applicable legal framework.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An autonomous blockchain system doesn't automatically receive those rights simply because it has a unique wallet address.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That's why legal wrappers remain important for many DAOs.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A legal wrapper can connect on-chain activity with an entity recognized under existing law.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Wyoming's approach illustrates this model: rather than simply declaring autonomous software to be a person, the state provides a statutory framework through which an LLC can elect DAO status.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://wyoleg.gov/NXT/gateway.dll/Statutes%2F2021%20Titles%2F879%2F1045%2F1046" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;
View Wyoming's DAO statutory framework
&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Hardest Question: Who Is Responsible?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The real challenge may not be whether an AI or &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/taiwan-lawmaker-pushes-bitcoin-reserve.html"&gt;blockchain&lt;/a&gt; can be called a legal person.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It may be figuring out &lt;strong&gt;who is responsible when an autonomous system does something that causes harm&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Imagine an AI-controlled wallet makes a transaction that violates a contract.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Or an autonomous trading system causes a significant loss.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Or a smart contract controlled by an automated governance system transfers millions of dollars to the wrong address.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain can provide a permanent record of what happened.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the ledger doesn't necessarily explain why the decision happened or identify the legally responsible party.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That creates an accountability problem.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Investigators could potentially trace the transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The harder task would be tracing the authority behind it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Could the Law Eventually Recognize Autonomous Entities?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Possibly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Legal systems have created artificial legal persons before.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Corporations are the obvious example.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The concept exists because the law can assign rights, obligations and liabilities to an entity that isn't a human being.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That means the idea of legally recognizing an autonomous digital organization isn't inherently impossible.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But creating such a framework would require lawmakers to answer difficult questions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Would the entity be liable for its own actions?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who would pay damages?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Could it own cryptocurrency?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Could it sign contracts?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Could it be sued?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who would represent it in court?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;What happens if nobody has the technical ability to shut it down?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And perhaps the strangest question of all:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Can an entity be legally responsible when its decisions are generated by software that nobody fully controls?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Those are policy questions, not merely technical ones.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Wyoming's Approach Matters&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Wyoming's DAO framework is interesting precisely because it creates a legal structure around the technology rather than simply declaring autonomous software to be a person.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Under the statute, an LLC can elect DAO status, and the framework provides for both member-managed and algorithmically managed DAOs.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That approach effectively connects two worlds.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain provides automation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The legal entity provides a recognized structure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Whether this model becomes the dominant approach remains uncertain.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But it illustrates an important point: &lt;strong&gt;legal recognition can be built around autonomous technology without treating the technology itself as a human-like legal person.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Blockchain Could Become More Autonomous Without Becoming a Person&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This distinction may become increasingly important as &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/bill-gates-warns-ai-is-advancing-faster.html"&gt;AI agents&lt;/a&gt; become more capable.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Manage a crypto wallet&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Pay for computing resources&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Trade digital assets&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Interact with smart contracts&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Negotiate with other software agents&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Manage a protocol treasury&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Operate continuously without direct human intervention&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Technically, that could look remarkably similar to an independent economic actor.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Legally, however, the system could still be treated as software operating under the authority or responsibility of humans or legal entities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The gap between those two descriptions is where future regulation is likely to develop.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A blockchain having its own wallet and executing transactions autonomously does &lt;strong&gt;not automatically mean the blockchain becomes a legal person&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the law is not simply a blanket “no.”&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The Ooki DAO litigation demonstrates that, under the Commodity Exchange Act and the specific facts of that case, a DAO could be treated as a “person” and held liable. Wyoming, meanwhile, has created a statutory framework for DAOs operating through LLC structures, while the Lido litigation shows that courts are still testing how traditional legal concepts apply to decentralized organizations.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That doesn't establish a universal legal-personhood rule for blockchains or autonomous wallets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The next challenge could be even more complicated as AI agents begin controlling wallets and making increasingly independent decisions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain may know exactly which address signed the transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The law still has to answer a different question:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Who, exactly, was standing behind the wallet?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And if the answer eventually becomes “a machine,” lawmakers will have to decide whether that machine needs a legal identity of its own — or whether responsibility should remain with the humans and entities that created, funded or controlled it — &lt;strong&gt;because the blockchain can't answer a subpoena.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;This article discusses an emerging legal and technological question and is not legal advice. Laws governing DAOs, digital assets, corporations and autonomous systems vary by jurisdiction and can change over time.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
