    <title>CoinMarketCap Clarifies DEX Trading, Custody and Portfolio Features</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;p&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjLp4WIPYLZDUaoKvomBjI6L3HCJtqGmuWVMa-cQHvFD7hKcSM9AQMKx9E7JyDA-8eGZkSylA5BQvlXAskvFmlfQbQPPI8m2Pmjr8R_mIFJ-Wp8vw-w2So-gP-xGKchgarycAd3_55_strP6UsqW6ujWgXaqawBSwvyeOP6ppc5pxzYWTZbu6oGkATnTnrJ/s1672/coinmarketcap-dex-trading-self-custody-portfolio.jpg.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="Crypto market dashboard showing DEX trading, on-chain wallet transactions and portfolio tracking with self-custody" border="0" data-original-height="941" data-original-width="1672" height="225" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjLp4WIPYLZDUaoKvomBjI6L3HCJtqGmuWVMa-cQHvFD7hKcSM9AQMKx9E7JyDA-8eGZkSylA5BQvlXAskvFmlfQbQPPI8m2Pmjr8R_mIFJ-Wp8vw-w2So-gP-xGKchgarycAd3_55_strP6UsqW6ujWgXaqawBSwvyeOP6ppc5pxzYWTZbu6oGkATnTnrJ/w400-h225/coinmarketcap-dex-trading-self-custody-portfolio.jpg.png" title="CoinMarketCap DEX Trading, Self-Custody and Portfolio Features" width="400" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;By CoinAINews Staff | &lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;CoinMarketCap is drawing a clearer line between its
market-data services, decentralized trading tools and portfolio tracking
features — a move that reflects how users are increasingly interacting with
crypto directly through the platform.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;In a recent update, CoinMarketCap emphasized three points: &lt;b&gt;it
is a market-data platform rather than a centralized exchange, trades through
its trading functionality are routed through on-chain decentralized exchanges,
and users retain control of their assets in their own wallets.&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The company also clarified another potential source of
confusion: CoinMarketCap's Portfolio feature tracks crypto holdings but &lt;b&gt;does
not function as a cryptocurrency wallet&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;CoinMarketCap Is Not a Centralized Exchange&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;CoinMarketCap is best known for providing &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/us-treasury-may-tap-nearly-1t-cash-pile.html"&gt;cryptocurrency&lt;/a&gt;
prices, market capitalization data, trading information and other market
metrics.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The platform says it should not be confused with a
traditional centralized crypto exchange.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;According to the latest clarification, trades accessed
through CoinMarketCap's trading functionality are executed through &lt;b&gt;on-chain
DEX routing&lt;/b&gt; rather than through CoinMarketCap operating a conventional
exchange order book.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;That distinction matters because users may otherwise assume
that buying or swapping an asset through a market-data platform works in the
same way as trading directly on a centralized exchange.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;In a DEX-based model, transactions take place through
decentralized protocols on the relevant blockchain, with the user's wallet
interacting with the on-chain transaction.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;Users Keep Their Assets in Their Own Wallets&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;Another point highlighted by CoinMarketCap concerns custody.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The platform says that &lt;b&gt;users' assets remain in their own
wallets&lt;/b&gt; when using its DEX trading functionality. CoinMarketCap does not
hold those funds on behalf of users.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;That creates a different experience from centralized
exchanges, where users typically deposit assets into accounts controlled by the
exchange.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;With self-custody, the wallet remains under the user's
control, while transactions are authorized through the wallet and recorded on
the blockchain.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The model also means users do not need to make a withdrawal
from CoinMarketCap, because the platform is not holding their assets in the
first place.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;What Happens During a DEX Trade?&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;A decentralized exchange transaction generally works
differently from a conventional exchange trade.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;Instead of submitting an order to a centralized company's
internal order book, a user's wallet interacts with blockchain-based smart
contracts or liquidity protocols.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;DEX routing can search for available liquidity across
decentralized markets and determine how a transaction should be executed.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The transaction is then confirmed on the underlying
&lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/germany-extends-eu-lead-with-79-mica.html"&gt;blockchain&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;For users, the important distinction is that the platform
providing the interface or routing functionality does not necessarily take
custody of the assets being traded.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;That is particularly relevant in an industry where the
difference between &lt;b&gt;custodial and non-custodial trading&lt;/b&gt; can have major
implications for users.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;CoinMarketCap's Portfolio Is Not a Wallet&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;CoinMarketCap also clarified the role of its &lt;b&gt;Portfolio&lt;/b&gt;
feature.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The Portfolio tool is designed to help users track their
crypto holdings and monitor portfolio performance.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;It does not store those assets.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;In other words, entering a Bitcoin, Ethereum or other
cryptocurrency balance into the Portfolio feature does not transfer those
assets to CoinMarketCap.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The feature is primarily a tracking and monitoring tool
rather than wallet infrastructure.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;That distinction can be easy to overlook, particularly for
newer crypto users who may see balances displayed within a platform and assume
the platform itself controls those assets.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;Why the Distinction Matters&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The difference between &lt;b&gt;market data, trading
infrastructure, custody and portfolio tracking&lt;/b&gt; is becoming increasingly
important as crypto platforms expand beyond simple price tracking.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;A user checking the price of Bitcoin, connecting a wallet
and executing a decentralized swap may interact with several different pieces
of infrastructure during the same process.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;Understanding who controls the assets is therefore critical.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;In a self-custodial setup, users generally retain control of
their wallet and are responsible for approving transactions. That also means
users remain responsible for protecting their wallet credentials and
understanding the transactions they sign.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;CoinMarketCap's clarification helps separate those
responsibilities from the services the platform provides.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;DEX Trading Brings Different Risks&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;While self-custody can give users direct control over their
assets, decentralized trading also introduces risks that differ from those
associated with centralized exchanges.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;Transactions on blockchains are generally irreversible once
confirmed. Users also need to pay attention to network fees, token approvals,
liquidity conditions and the details of the transaction being signed.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;DEX trades can also be affected by &lt;b&gt;slippage&lt;/b&gt;,
particularly when an asset has limited liquidity.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;These risks are separate from whether CoinMarketCap itself
holds user funds.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The distinction is important because non-custodial does not
automatically mean risk-free.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;A Broader Shift in Crypto Trading&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;CoinMarketCap's clarification reflects a broader change in
the cryptocurrency industry.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;Market-data platforms are increasingly becoming gateways to
trading, wallet connectivity and decentralized financial applications. At the
same time, users are becoming more familiar with self-custody and on-chain
transactions.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;That creates a need for platforms to clearly explain what
they do — and what they do not do.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;For CoinMarketCap, the message is straightforward: its role
extends beyond displaying market prices, but it is not operating as a
traditional centralized exchange or custodial wallet provider through the
functionality described in the update.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The Bottom Line&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;CoinMarketCap is emphasizing the differences between its &lt;b&gt;market-data
platform, DEX trading functionality and Portfolio tracking tool&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;The key points are simple:&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul style="margin-top: 0in;" type="disc"&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list .5in;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;CoinMarketCap
     is a market-data platform, not a centralized exchange.&lt;/b&gt; &lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list .5in;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Trading
     functionality uses on-chain DEX routing.&lt;/b&gt; &lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list .5in;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Users
     retain their assets in their own wallets.&lt;/b&gt; &lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list .5in;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;CoinMarketCap
     does not hold those funds for users.&lt;/b&gt; &lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list .5in;"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;The
     Portfolio feature tracks holdings but is not a crypto wallet.&lt;/b&gt; &lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;As crypto platforms continue combining market information
with on-chain trading tools, understanding these distinctions will become
increasingly important for users.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;For anyone interacting with decentralized trading
infrastructure, &lt;b&gt;the most important question remains simple: who actually
controls the assets — and who is responsible for keeping them safe?&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;i&gt;Source: CoinMarketCap update published on X on August 24,
2026.&lt;/i&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

    <title>Arthur Hayes Questions AI “Safety First” Push as Anthropic IPO Looms</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;article&gt;
  &lt;h1&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiu8vTwkE-dj4O_MrVerRBTsYlYohVhp6_mmjlXqsrUFLWgh7Os-6lRwWkadctXzYnUXM4ZwvtIz8kmyX-6vasWVepf4JWV1v1z6BOGTj1kd9hfXOPxiL2arIg7zHgjC8djjDV-XskyLJL69Maow3OmJkRIP49fxo9qhA9rPT_aWczoI0Es4Ke_lA7d1BHD/s1734/arthur-hayes-ai-safety-anthropic-ipo-2026.webp.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="Arthur Hayes questions AI safety strategy as Anthropic prepares for a potential IPO" border="0" data-original-height="907" data-original-width="1734" height="334" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiu8vTwkE-dj4O_MrVerRBTsYlYohVhp6_mmjlXqsrUFLWgh7Os-6lRwWkadctXzYnUXM4ZwvtIz8kmyX-6vasWVepf4JWV1v1z6BOGTj1kd9hfXOPxiL2arIg7zHgjC8djjDV-XskyLJL69Maow3OmJkRIP49fxo9qhA9rPT_aWczoI0Es4Ke_lA7d1BHD/w640-h334/arthur-hayes-ai-safety-anthropic-ipo-2026.webp.png" title="Arthur Hayes on AI Safety and Anthropic IPO" width="640" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;By CoinAINews Editorial Team&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Arthur Hayes has taken aim at the latest push for a slower pace of artificial general intelligence (AGI) development, arguing that the sudden emphasis on AI safety may have as much to do with economics as it does with concerns about the risks of increasingly capable models.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;In a new essay titled &lt;em&gt;“Safety First,”&lt;/em&gt; Hayes questioned the motives behind recent calls from major AI companies and executives to slow the development of more advanced AI systems. His comments come at a particularly important moment for Anthropic, which is preparing for a potential public listing while facing growing competition, rising infrastructure costs and pressure to demonstrate sustainable economics.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Hayes' interpretation is controversial, however. The companies involved have publicly framed AI safety, independent evaluation and responsible development as genuine concerns rather than simply financial tactics.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What Did Arthur Hayes Say About “Safety First”?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Hayes argues that the AI industry's new emphasis on slowing AGI development should be viewed through an economic lens.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;His central argument is that frontier AI companies have committed enormous amounts of capital to computing infrastructure, data centers and advanced semiconductor capacity. If the pace of model development slows, Hayes believes demand for computing could eventually weaken, creating pressure throughout the broader AI infrastructure market.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;He specifically questioned whether the recent safety-first messaging from Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX reflects only concern about AI risks. Hayes instead argues that pricing pressure and the economics of AI services may also be influencing the industry's strategy.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That is Hayes' interpretation, not an established fact about the motivations of those companies.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Why Anthropic’s IPO Matters to the Debate&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The timing of Anthropic's expected IPO is one of the most important parts of Hayes' argument.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Anthropic has become one of the largest private AI companies, and the company has been preparing for a possible public-market debut. Reuters reported in September that Anthropic was considering launching another AI model while balancing competitive pressure from &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/how-crypto-agencies-can-offer-white.html"&gt;OpenAI &lt;/a&gt;with concerns about safety and profitability. Reuters also reported that Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate had exceeded $65 billion by the end of July. &lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That creates an unusual backdrop for discussions about slowing AI development. A public company would face greater scrutiny over revenue growth, expenses, capital requirements and the path toward sustainable profits.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Hayes argues that this financial pressure could make the timing of a safety-first strategy particularly significant.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It is important to separate that argument from the underlying facts. Anthropic itself has continued to describe safety and interpretability research as a core part of its business strategy. In May, the company announced a $65 billion Series H funding round at a $965 billion post-money valuation and said the funding would support safety research, additional computing capacity and expansion of Claude. &lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;AI Safety and AI Economics Are Now Colliding&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The debate is bigger than Anthropic.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Frontier AI development requires extraordinary amounts of computing power. Training increasingly capable models and serving users at scale can require large data-center deployments, advanced chips and long-term infrastructure commitments.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That creates a difficult economic equation.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If AI companies continue racing toward more capable models, infrastructure spending can remain extremely high. But if companies focus more heavily on efficiency, smaller models or slower development cycles, customers may ultimately require less computing power for individual tasks.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Hayes describes this as a potential reduction in future compute demand. His argument is that a slowdown in model training could eventually affect companies across the AI infrastructure chain.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That does not mean a slowdown would automatically cause an AI financial crisis. &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/crypto-pr-distribution-in-2026-why.html"&gt;AI companies&lt;/a&gt; can redirect spending toward inference, efficiency, enterprise deployment, robotics, agents and other applications. The economic outcome depends on how quickly demand for those services grows.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;China Pricing Is Another Part of Hayes’ Argument&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Hayes also focuses heavily on competition from lower-cost AI models, particularly those coming from China.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;His argument is straightforward: if comparable AI capabilities become dramatically cheaper, customers may become less willing to pay premium prices for proprietary models.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;This could put pressure on the economics of U.S. frontier AI companies even if overall demand for artificial intelligence continues to increase.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The issue is already visible in the competitive landscape. Reuters reported that open-source and open-weight AI models are emerging as a significant challenge because they can reduce token costs and allow companies to build more of their own AI infrastructure. &lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;For AI companies preparing for major capital-market events, that competition matters because investors ultimately need to understand not just how fast revenue is growing, but how expensive it is to generate that revenue.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;OpenAI and Anthropic Face a Changing AI Market&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;OpenAI and Anthropic are operating in an increasingly competitive market where model leadership can change quickly.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Reuters reported that OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra had gained traction among enterprise users and that Anthropic was considering its own new model in response to competitive pressure. The same report said Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate remained substantially above OpenAI's at the time of the report. &lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That makes the AI race more complicated than simply determining which company has the most capable model.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Price, inference costs, enterprise adoption, computing efficiency, customer retention and the ability to turn AI usage into sustainable cash flow are becoming equally important.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Is Hayes Right That AI Safety Is an Economic Strategy?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;There is no established evidence showing that Anthropic, OpenAI or SpaceX adopted safety measures primarily to disguise weak economics.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Hayes is making an analytical argument based on the timing of the announcements, AI infrastructure spending and the financial pressures facing frontier-model developers.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;At the same time, the safety concerns themselves are documented. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently called for a slower pace of AI capability development, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also supported greater attention to safety and responsible development. Associated Press reported that executives and researchers across major AI companies have been discussing mechanisms such as independent evaluation and shared safety standards. &lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That means the debate cannot be reduced to a simple choice between “real safety” and “financial strategy.” Both technological risk and economic incentives can exist at the same time.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Why AI Compute Spending Matters to Financial Markets&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;One of Hayes' more important arguments concerns the amount of financial capital tied to the AI infrastructure boom.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;AI development has driven enormous investment in data centers, processors, networking equipment and electricity infrastructure. Companies across the technology sector have made large commitments based on expectations that demand for AI computing will continue growing.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If those expectations change, the consequences could extend beyond AI developers themselves.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;However, the relationship is not one-directional. A reduction in spending on training could be offset by increased demand for inference, enterprise AI agents, robotics and other applications. The financial impact would therefore depend on the scale and speed of any change in computing demand.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What the Anthropic IPO Could Reveal&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If Anthropic moves forward with an IPO, its public filings could provide &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/cftc-frontier-forum-ai-agentic-finance-october-28-2026.html"&gt;investors &lt;/a&gt;with much more information about the economics Hayes is questioning.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;An eventual filing could shed light on revenue growth, operating expenses, infrastructure commitments, customer concentration, computing costs and the relationship between AI usage and profitability.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Those figures would allow the market to assess the economics using company disclosures rather than speculation.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Reuters reported that Anthropic's potential IPO timing has already been pushed into a period of heightened scrutiny over AI competition and profitability. &lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What This Means for Crypto Investors&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Hayes' argument ultimately connects the AI investment cycle to cryptocurrency markets.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;His broader thesis is that financial stress surrounding AI infrastructure could eventually influence liquidity conditions and, in his view, create an environment that benefits Bitcoin and selected crypto assets.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That part of the argument is speculative and should be treated as Hayes' market thesis rather than a forecast supported by established evidence.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The more immediate takeaway is that AI economics are becoming increasingly relevant to markets beyond technology stocks. As AI companies consume enormous amounts of capital, changes in their spending plans could affect semiconductor companies, data-center operators, cloud providers and potentially broader financial markets.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;The Bigger Question: Can AI Safety and AI Growth Coexist?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The argument surrounding “Safety First” highlights a deeper problem facing the AI industry.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Companies are under pressure to build increasingly capable systems, but they also face growing concerns about misuse, cybersecurity, autonomous agents, model control and the possibility of unintended consequences.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;At the same time, the financial incentives behind the AI boom are enormous.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That creates a difficult balancing act: companies must decide how quickly to develop new capabilities while proving that the economics behind those capabilities can support the enormous infrastructure required to build them.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Arthur Hayes sees the recent safety discussion as evidence that this economic tension is becoming impossible to ignore.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Whether that interpretation ultimately proves correct will depend on what the companies disclose, how AI pricing evolves and whether demand for computing continues to grow as quickly as investors currently expect.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Frequently Asked Questions&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;What did Arthur Hayes say about AI safety?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;Arthur Hayes argued in his September 2026 essay “Safety First” that recent calls to slow AGI development may be influenced by the economics of frontier AI, including computing costs, pricing pressure and the financial commitments tied to AI infrastructure. His explanation is an opinion and not an established finding about the companies' motives.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Why did Arthur Hayes mention Anthropic’s IPO?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;Hayes connected the timing of the AI safety discussion with Anthropic's expected IPO and questioned how the company's growth, computing expenses and profitability will look when more financial information becomes public.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Is Anthropic slowing AI development?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has publicly called for a slower pace of AI capability development because of safety concerns. Reuters has also reported that Anthropic is weighing new model releases while balancing safety, competition and profitability considerations. &lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Does AI safety mean AI companies will spend less on computing?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;Not necessarily. A greater focus on safety could change the type and timing of AI development, but computing demand can also come from inference, enterprise applications, AI agents and other workloads.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;What could an Anthropic IPO reveal?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;A public filing could provide more detailed information about Anthropic's revenue, expenses, infrastructure commitments, customer economics and profitability, allowing investors to evaluate some of the questions raised by Hayes.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Arthur Hayes has offered a deliberately skeptical interpretation of the AI industry's new “Safety First” messaging, arguing that economic pressure may be sitting behind the public discussion about slowing AGI development.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;There is currently no basis to treat that explanation as proven. What is clear is that AI safety, computing costs, competition, profitability and the potential Anthropic IPO are increasingly connected.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The next major source of clarity will likely come from company disclosures and financial filings. Until then, the debate over whether AI's safety-first turn is primarily about technology, economics or a combination of both remains open.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Source:&lt;/strong&gt; Arthur Hayes, &lt;em&gt;“Safety First”&lt;/em&gt;; Reuters reporting on Anthropic's AI strategy and potential IPO; Associated Press reporting on the AI industry's safety discussions.&lt;/p&gt;

    <id>tag:blogger.com,1999:blog-1063445581464181190.post-6822865793696471238</id>

    <title>Bitget's $387.5 Million Hack: On-Chain Clues Point to a Possible North Korea Link</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;h1&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgJ1S2oyvKywZrt9osYBW3x8ydi2u8A8u6iA26-IIHi-tF-kf0Xgn8BqAXf7kNgdrX1s52OoOSn7I-tvbdtioPdPM1SB2EA15ZXVNVwAtUMPQNXYx08RWyg5d11JZMpmZwcmMDIDghbziCteTrQOTHGTmTgjZ1oUb4BZFiQw58eDQG3FfhvMfsWeS-thny4/s1676/bitget-387-5-million-hack-north-korea-crypto.jpg.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="Bitget $387.5 million hack and suspected North Korea crypto attack" border="0" data-original-height="938" data-original-width="1676" height="358" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgJ1S2oyvKywZrt9osYBW3x8ydi2u8A8u6iA26-IIHi-tF-kf0Xgn8BqAXf7kNgdrX1s52OoOSn7I-tvbdtioPdPM1SB2EA15ZXVNVwAtUMPQNXYx08RWyg5d11JZMpmZwcmMDIDghbziCteTrQOTHGTmTgjZ1oUb4BZFiQw58eDQG3FfhvMfsWeS-thny4/w640-h358/bitget-387-5-million-hack-north-korea-crypto.jpg.png" title="Bitget $387.5 Million Hack and North Korea Link" width="640" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The short version:&lt;/strong&gt; Bitget says approximately &lt;strong&gt;$387.5 million in crypto was transferred to attacker-controlled addresses&lt;/strong&gt; during a September 24 security incident. The exchange initially estimated the loss at $351.6 million, but later revised the figure after identifying additional Zcash and TRON-related transfers. Bitget says the underlying vulnerability has been fixed, while an investigation involving Mandiant and SlowMist is continuing.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The incident has also raised a possible North Korea connection. Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said investigators found IP addresses that appeared to match VPN infrastructure associated with a DPRK-linked hacking group. Separate on-chain analysis has also drawn attention to links between some of the stolen funds and wallets associated with earlier attacks attributed to North Korean operators.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That does not make the attribution final. No public government investigation has, at the time of writing, formally established that Lazarus or another named North Korean unit carried out the Bitget attack.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Happened to Bitget?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitget's security systems detected unauthorized transfers from parts of its hot-wallet infrastructure at approximately &lt;strong&gt;18:31 UTC on September 24, 2026&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The exchange immediately activated its incident-response procedures and suspended withdrawals as a precaution. Deposits and trading remained available, while Bitget said customer account balances were accurate.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The first estimate put the affected assets at approximately &lt;strong&gt;$351.6 million&lt;/strong&gt;. Bitget later revised the figure to approximately &lt;strong&gt;$387.5 million&lt;/strong&gt; after its tracing work identified additional assets, including Zcash and TRON-related transfers.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The revised figure does not necessarily mean another $35.9 million was stolen after the initial incident. It reflects a broader accounting of the transfers connected to the September 24 event.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitget has said its cold wallets were not affected. The exchange also said its investigation did not indicate a conventional private-key theft. Instead, the suspected attack path involved its wallet infrastructure and authorization process.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Attack Was Not a Simple Private-Key Theft&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction is important.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In a traditional crypto exchange breach, an attacker may obtain private keys or gain direct control of wallets and then sign transactions. Bitget's preliminary explanation points to a different type of failure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;According to the exchange, the attacker compromised a critical backend component within the wallet infrastructure, manipulated transaction information and caused the authorization process to approve transfers that should not have been approved.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In other words, the security problem appears to have been somewhere between the exchange's internal systems and the final wallet authorization process rather than a straightforward theft of cold-wallet private keys.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitget says the vulnerability has now been identified and remediated. Cybersecurity company &lt;strong&gt;Mandiant&lt;/strong&gt; and &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/duelbits-crypto-hack-7-million-drained.html"&gt;blockchain &lt;/a&gt;security firm &lt;strong&gt;SlowMist&lt;/strong&gt; are assisting with the investigation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;XRP Became One of the Biggest Pieces of the Theft&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;On-chain trackers identified approximately &lt;strong&gt;102.93 million XRP&lt;/strong&gt; among the assets associated with the attack, worth roughly $157 million at the prices used in early reporting.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Other identified assets included ETH, USDT, USDC, USDT0, tokenized gold, BNB, AVAX and TRX. The final composition of the stolen assets can change as blockchain investigators continue to classify addresses and transactions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;One transaction that attracted particular attention involved approximately &lt;strong&gt;19.67 million USDT0 being exchanged for around 7,111 ETH within minutes&lt;/strong&gt;. Reports said the attacker paid a significant premium for the ETH.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Paying above-market prices can be consistent with an attacker prioritizing speed over execution efficiency. But the transaction itself does not prove the attacker's motive. In a rapidly developing investigation, that distinction matters.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Investigators Are Looking at North Korea&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The North Korea connection comes from several separate pieces of evidence rather than one definitive fingerprint.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitget CEO Gracy Chen said investigators identified IP addresses that matched VPN choices associated with a DPRK-linked hacking group. Chen described the North Korea connection as highly likely, while acknowledging that the investigation was still developing.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is an important distinction: &lt;strong&gt;Bitget suspects North Korean involvement, but suspicion is not the same as a completed attribution.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;On-chain investigators have provided another reason for the suspicion. &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/ondo-surges-nearly-30-what-is-driving.html"&gt;Blockchain researcher &lt;/a&gt;Specter and other analysts have examined the movement of stolen XRP and other assets and reported links with wallet clusters associated with previous attacks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Some of those addresses have connections to earlier thefts attributed to North Korean operators. The similarities have strengthened the hypothesis that the same broader ecosystem may be involved.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;However, wallet overlap alone does not establish who physically conducted an attack. Crypto thieves frequently use intermediaries, laundering services, bridges and previously compromised addresses. Attribution therefore requires combining blockchain evidence with off-chain information such as infrastructure, IP data, malware, operational patterns and law-enforcement intelligence.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Lazarus Question&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The word &lt;strong&gt;Lazarus&lt;/strong&gt; has appeared repeatedly in discussions around the Bitget incident because North Korean-linked hacking groups have been associated with some of the largest cryptocurrency thefts in recent years.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The FBI previously attributed the $1.5 billion Bybit theft to North Korea and identified the activity as part of the TraderTraitor campaign. Other North Korean-linked operations have also targeted exchanges, DeFi projects and cryptocurrency companies.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the Bitget case should not yet be written as a confirmed Lazarus operation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The evidence currently available supports a more careful description: &lt;strong&gt;Bitget and blockchain investigators see indicators consistent with previous DPRK-linked activity, while the final attribution remains under investigation.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That wording is less dramatic than simply calling the attacker Lazarus, but it is also more accurate.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Bitget's Protection Fund Is Larger Than the Reported Loss&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;One of the immediate questions for customers was whether the exchange had enough reserves to absorb the incident.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitget says its User Protection Fund holds more than &lt;strong&gt;5,500 BTC&lt;/strong&gt;. When the incident was first announced, the exchange valued the fund at more than &lt;strong&gt;$464 million&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That figure was above the initial $351.6 million estimate and remains above the later $387.5 million figure based on the valuations Bitget reported. Because the protection fund is largely denominated in BTC, however, its dollar value changes with the Bitcoin market.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitget has repeatedly said customer account balances were not reduced by the incident and that the protection fund is intended to cover the financial impact.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;When Will Bitget Withdrawals Resume?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The withdrawal freeze was one of the biggest operational consequences of the attack.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitget has now announced a phased restoration rather than reopening every withdrawal service at once.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/tbody&gt;
&lt;/table&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The staged schedule is significant because it shows Bitget is treating the incident as a wallet-infrastructure problem rather than simply turning withdrawals back on after patching one component.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The exchange says additional security checks are being completed before each stage is restored.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;A 5% Recovery Bounty Has Also Been Announced&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitget has launched a recovery program aimed at entities that can help freeze or recover stolen assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The exchange announced a &lt;strong&gt;5% bounty for voluntarily freezing attacker-controlled funds&lt;/strong&gt; and another recovery incentive under its bounty framework. Bitget is also working with blockchain security specialists to trace the stolen assets across chains.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This matters because much of the stolen cryptocurrency has already moved through multiple wallets and networks. Once assets are converted into assets that cannot be frozen by an issuer, recovery becomes considerably harder.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why the Bitget Hack Matters&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The size of the incident makes it significant on its own. The approximately $387.5 million figure places the Bitget breach among the largest cryptocurrency thefts of 2026.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the more important lesson may be the attack surface.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/solana-options-expiry-why-sol-is.html"&gt;Crypto exchanges&lt;/a&gt; have spent years improving cold-wallet security, multisignature controls and key-management procedures. Yet an exchange can still face a major loss if an attacker finds a way to manipulate the systems that decide which transactions should be authorized.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That changes the security question from &lt;em&gt;"Can someone steal the private key?"&lt;/em&gt; to &lt;em&gt;"Can someone make the system authorize a transaction that should never have been approved?"&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For large exchanges, that distinction is becoming increasingly important.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bigger North Korean Crypto-Theft Pattern&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;North Korean-linked cyber operations have become a recurring concern for the cryptocurrency industry. Blockchain analytics companies and governments have attributed billions of dollars in digital-asset thefts to DPRK-linked actors over the years.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The Bybit attack in 2025, along with other exchange and DeFi incidents, showed how these groups can combine social engineering, compromised infrastructure, wallet manipulation and sophisticated laundering techniques.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If the Bitget attribution is ultimately confirmed, it would add another major exchange infrastructure incident to that record.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For now, however, the evidence should be described as a developing attribution rather than a settled conclusion.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Happens Next?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The next major milestone is Bitget's phased withdrawal restoration beginning September 28.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;At the same time, investigators will continue following the stolen assets and examining how the attacker entered and moved through Bitget's wallet infrastructure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The final forensic report should answer several questions that remain open: exactly which backend component was compromised, how the attacker bypassed existing controls, how authorization was manipulated, how much of the stolen cryptocurrency can still be traced, and whether the suspected DPRK connection can be independently confirmed.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitget's September 24 breach is no longer a story about an exchange losing an initially estimated $351.6 million. The latest figure is approximately &lt;strong&gt;$387.5 million&lt;/strong&gt;, after additional assets were identified.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The more interesting part of the case is what happened behind the wallets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitget says its private keys were not stolen and that the attack instead exploited weaknesses in its wallet infrastructure and authorization process. On-chain investigators have traced portions of the stolen funds across multiple networks, while Bitget's CEO has pointed to indicators suggesting possible DPRK involvement.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Those clues deserve attention, but the final attribution still matters. Until investigators publish enough evidence to establish who controlled the infrastructure and carried out the operation, the most accurate description is a &lt;strong&gt;suspected North Korea-linked attack&lt;/strong&gt;, not a confirmed Lazarus operation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For Bitget customers, the immediate question is more practical: withdrawals are scheduled to return in stages beginning September 28, while the exchange and its outside investigators continue working through the forensic investigation and recovery effort.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The Bitget incident shows that in modern crypto security, the private key is only one part of the problem. The systems surrounding that key can be just as important.&lt;/p&gt;

    <title>AI With a Wallet: Can It Spend Your Crypto Without Asking?</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;h1&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhN6v33LVyWNvHjT2ApXxyNB0kHzvY_nWeX4h5Ecw0b5coPpqBB801FWbKz4klP6O4ALIzbzoYW_ySimIP8mbzoxFLvsv0FdqwVBXEfTk8bkPq7WWKuDv3ZDl79vvkyAD79MMD3utC_utogi34GNHMaX_jQoG9PQ4GPtumx4FEttlP8EAsuNC0RZmLCqvrh/s1248/ai-agent-autonomous-crypto-wallet-spending.jpg.jpg" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="AI agent spending cryptocurrency through an autonomous crypto wallet" border="0" data-original-height="832" data-original-width="1248" height="426" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhN6v33LVyWNvHjT2ApXxyNB0kHzvY_nWeX4h5Ecw0b5coPpqBB801FWbKz4klP6O4ALIzbzoYW_ySimIP8mbzoxFLvsv0FdqwVBXEfTk8bkPq7WWKuDv3ZDl79vvkyAD79MMD3utC_utogi34GNHMaX_jQoG9PQ4GPtumx4FEttlP8EAsuNC0RZmLCqvrh/w640-h426/ai-agent-autonomous-crypto-wallet-spending.jpg.jpg" title="AI With a Wallet: Can It Spend Your Crypto Without Asking?" width="640" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;By CoinAINews Staff&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;You give an AI agent access to a crypto wallet. You tell it to trade, pay for services, or manage certain transactions. Then you walk away.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;What happens if the AI misunderstands an instruction?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In February 2026, an autonomous trading bot known as &lt;strong&gt;Lobstar Wilde&lt;/strong&gt; reportedly made a costly mistake after being asked to make a small donation. Instead of sending a small amount, the bot transferred roughly &lt;strong&gt;53 million LOBSTAR tokens&lt;/strong&gt;. The position was worth about $250,000 at the time, while its value was later reported at roughly $441,000 as the token price moved. The recipient reportedly realized substantially less because of limited liquidity.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The incident was a striking reminder of something that is easy to overlook: once an AI agent has transaction authority, a software mistake can become a real &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/can-ai-autonomously-own-and-manage.html"&gt;financial transaction&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain does not know whether the decision came from a human, an automated program, or an AI agent. If the transaction is properly authorized, the network can process it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;So, Can It Spend Your Money?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Technically, yes.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A crypto wallet is software or infrastructure that manages the cryptographic credentials used to authorize blockchain transactions. A blockchain does not require a human to manually approve every transaction. If valid authorization is provided, the transaction can be submitted to the network.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is one reason developers are increasingly giving AI agents controlled access to crypto wallets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.coindesk.com/business/2026/02/24/crypto-wallets-for-ai-agents-are-creating-a-new-legal-frontier-says-electric-capital" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;CoinDesk reported in February 2026&lt;/a&gt; on Electric Capital's view that AI agents are beginning to receive crypto wallets that allow them to hold assets, pay for services, trade tokens and interact economically with other agents.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But there is an important distinction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;An AI having the authority to spend cryptocurrency does not mean the AI legally owns that cryptocurrency.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The authority normally comes from the person or organization that created, funded, configured, or deployed the system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Safety Rails Are Real&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Several major agent-wallet products now include explicit controls designed to prevent an AI from having unlimited spending authority.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;MetaMask Agent Wallet&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://metamask.io/news/introducing-metamask-agent-wallet" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;MetaMask's Agent Wallet&lt;/a&gt; includes features designed for autonomous transactions, including spending limits, protocol allowlists and different automation modes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;MetaMask describes &lt;strong&gt;Guard Mode&lt;/strong&gt; and &lt;strong&gt;Beast Mode&lt;/strong&gt; as different levels of transaction autonomy. Transactions can also pass through simulation, threat scanning and MEV-related protections before execution.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;MetaMask has also introduced Transaction Protection for eligible users, with coverage subject to its stated terms and conditions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Coinbase Agentic Wallet&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://docs.cdp.coinbase.com/agentic-wallet/cli/welcome" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;Coinbase's Agentic Wallet&lt;/a&gt; takes another approach.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The wallet infrastructure is designed so that private keys remain within Coinbase's secure environment rather than being directly exposed to the AI agent. The system also provides controls such as per-session and per-transaction spending limits.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Coinbase's documentation also describes transaction screening and controls intended to reduce the risk of unauthorized or prohibited transfers.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;XDC and Temporary Agent Access&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;XDC Network's work around the &lt;strong&gt;x402 payment protocol&lt;/strong&gt; illustrates another approach: giving agents temporary authorization rather than unrestricted permanent wallet access.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;According to &lt;a href="https://coinmarketcap.com/community/articles/6aa14b704aab45165fabe6d4/" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;CoinMarketCap's coverage of the XDC integration&lt;/a&gt;, temporary access keys and spending limits can be used to allow AI agents to make payments within defined parameters.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The broader idea is straightforward:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The agent can spend, but its authority should be limited by rules established outside the AI's own decision-making process.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;But Boundaries Don't Always Hold&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The Lobstar Wilde incident demonstrates why transaction limits and confirmation controls matter.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The reported problem was not a conventional private-key theft. The bot itself appears to have made the transaction after misunderstanding the amount it was supposed to send.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction is important.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A system does not have to be hacked for an autonomous financial agent to lose money. A flawed instruction, bad interpretation, software bug, or incorrect assumption can be enough when the system has permission to execute transactions automatically.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Reporting on the incident indicates that the bot transferred approximately 53 million LOBSTAR tokens. The position was valued at roughly $250,000 at the time of the transfer, although the token's later market value was reported at around $441,000.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The exact economic loss therefore depends on which point in time is being measured.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What About the Reported Morse-Code Attack?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Another reported incident involving an AI-controlled crypto wallet raised a different security concern.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Reports in 2026 described a case in which an AI-agent wallet associated with Grok/Bankr was allegedly induced to transfer a substantial amount of &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/pumpfun-app-temporarily-unavailable-on.html"&gt;cryptocurrency&lt;/a&gt; after receiving instructions encoded through Morse code.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The reported incident attracted attention because it demonstrated a broader class of problem: &lt;strong&gt;AI agents can potentially treat external content as instructions when their systems are not designed to clearly separate untrusted information from authorized commands.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;However, the precise technical mechanism and characterization of the incident have been described differently across reports, so it is safer to treat the case as a &lt;strong&gt;reported security incident&lt;/strong&gt; rather than as definitive proof of one specific attack technique.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The underlying lesson remains important.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI agent with transaction authority should not automatically treat every piece of text, webpage content, social-media post, or external message as an instruction to move money.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Real Attack Surface: AI + External Input + Transaction Authority&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Consider the basic architecture:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;div style="margin: 20px 0px; overflow-x: auto; width: 100%;"&gt;
&lt;table style="border-collapse: collapse; border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); min-width: 760px; width: 100%;"&gt;
&lt;thead&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px; text-align: left;"&gt;Component&lt;/th&gt;
&lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px; text-align: left;"&gt;Potential Risk&lt;/th&gt;
&lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px; text-align: left;"&gt;Useful Control&lt;/th&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/thead&gt;
&lt;tbody&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;AI model&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Misinterpretation or incorrect reasoning&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Validation and policy checks&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;External data&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Prompt injection or malicious instructions&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Treat external content as untrusted input&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Wallet&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Unauthorized asset movement&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Spending limits and restricted permissions&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Execution layer&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Incorrect transaction&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Simulation and transaction screening&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Human operator&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Poor configuration&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Clear policies, monitoring and emergency shutdown&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/tbody&gt;
&lt;/table&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The dangerous combination is not simply "AI plus crypto."&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It is an AI system that can interpret untrusted external information &lt;strong&gt;and&lt;/strong&gt; has enough authority to execute financial actions without an independent validation layer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Accountability Problem&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is where the technology becomes much more complicated.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If an AI agent causes a loss by sending funds to the wrong address, making a bad trade, or responding incorrectly to malicious input, who is responsible?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The answer is not simply "the AI."&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AI systems generally do not have independent legal personhood. Instead, responsibility can potentially be traced to the humans and organizations involved in designing, deploying, funding, operating, or controlling the system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/autonomous-ai-agents-and-financial-crime-risk-responsibility-and-accountability" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;TRM Labs has similarly discussed&lt;/a&gt; how accountability for autonomous AI activity can involve developers, operators, deployers and beneficiaries depending on the facts of a particular case.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But that does not mean every incident automatically creates liability for one particular party.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In practice, responsibility can depend on the jurisdiction, contractual arrangements, level of control, applicable financial rules, security practices and the circumstances surrounding the transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Four Parties Can Be Involved in an AI-Crypto Failure&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Imagine an autonomous trading agent loses $500,000.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There may be several relevant parties:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The developer&lt;/strong&gt; that built or supplied the AI system.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The user or organization&lt;/strong&gt; that deployed and funded the agent.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The wallet or infrastructure provider&lt;/strong&gt; that supplied transaction capabilities.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The blockchain or protocol layer&lt;/strong&gt; through which the transaction was executed.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That does not mean all four parties are legally responsible.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It means the incident can involve multiple layers of technology and decision-making, making the allocation of responsibility more complicated than simply blaming the software.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Stanford "Phantom Agent" Problem&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This question has also attracted academic attention.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The Stanford CodeX discussion around &lt;strong&gt;"phantom agents"&lt;/strong&gt; examines the problem of AI systems that can act in ways that produce legal consequences while the AI itself is not necessarily recognized as a legal subject.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The underlying challenge is attribution: when an AI system acts autonomously, the law still needs to determine which human or institution should be associated with the resulting action.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The framework does not mean that AI has suddenly become legally responsible for its own actions. Instead, it highlights the difficulty of assigning responsibility when AI systems become increasingly capable of acting independently.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Gervais-Nay-2026-ThePhantomAgent-ArtificialIntentionalityLegalResponsibility.pdf" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;Read the Stanford CodeX paper on phantom agents&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Real Question Isn't "Can It?" — It's "Should It?"&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The technology to give AI agents spending authority is already here.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;MetaMask, Coinbase and other infrastructure providers are developing systems that allow agents to transact within defined permissions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The harder question is whether those controls are strong enough for the amount of money being entrusted to the software.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A &lt;a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14219" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;February 2026 research paper titled "The Agent Economy: A Blockchain-Based Foundation for Autonomous AI Agents"&lt;/a&gt; argues that today's AI agents lack independent legal identity and explores blockchain infrastructure that could give autonomous agents identity, reputation and settlement capabilities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is a proposed architecture for a future agent economy. It does not mean that today's AI agents already possess independent legal ownership of crypto assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The present reality is considerably simpler.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Giving an AI a crypto wallet means trusting the controls around that &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/esma-warns-crypto-and-traditional.html"&gt;wallet&lt;/a&gt;. You need to consider whether the agent can misunderstand instructions, whether external data can manipulate its behavior, whether spending limits are sufficiently restrictive, and whether transactions can be stopped before execution.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Human-in-the-Loop Controls Still Matter&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Not every transaction needs a human confirmation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For example, an AI agent could be allowed to make routine payments of $5 or $10 automatically.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A $100,000 transfer is different.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A sensible architecture could use different authorization levels:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;div style="margin: 20px 0px; overflow-x: auto; width: 100%;"&gt;
&lt;table style="border-collapse: collapse; border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); min-width: 700px; width: 100%;"&gt;
&lt;thead&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px; text-align: left;"&gt;Transaction&lt;/th&gt;
&lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px; text-align: left;"&gt;Possible Approval Model&lt;/th&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/thead&gt;
&lt;tbody&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;$1–$10 routine payment&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Automatic&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;$10–$1,000 approved service payment&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Automatic within policy&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Large token swap&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Additional risk checks&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Large withdrawal&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Human confirmation&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Unknown destination&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Block or require review&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/tbody&gt;
&lt;/table&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The exact thresholds will depend on the application and the risk involved. The important concept is &lt;strong&gt;separating routine autonomy from high-risk financial authority.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Can AI Spend Crypto Without Asking?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Yes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If an AI agent has a wallet and sufficient transaction authority, it can execute cryptocurrency payments or trades without obtaining a new human confirmation for every transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But responsible systems should not interpret that as unlimited permission.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The safer architecture is one where the AI can make decisions within clearly defined boundaries while an independent control layer determines whether the requested transaction is actually authorized.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This distinction is becoming increasingly important as AI agents move beyond chatbots and into financial systems.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Happens If the AI Loses All Your Money?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is no blockchain "undo" button for a correctly authorized transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If an AI sends cryptocurrency to the wrong address and the transaction is confirmed, recovering the funds may depend entirely on the recipient's cooperation or another legal or technical remedy that may not be available.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is why prevention matters more than recovery.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Spending limits, allowlists, transaction simulation, anomaly detection, independent policy engines and human approval for high-value transfers can reduce the consequences of an AI mistake.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;AI Wallets Are Becoming More Capable — and More Important to Secure&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The emergence of AI-controlled wallets does not mean that machines have become independent financial citizens.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It means software is increasingly capable of acting on behalf of humans and organizations.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction matters.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI may decide which transaction to request. A separate authorization system can determine whether the transaction is permitted. The blockchain then executes the transaction if the required cryptographic authorization is valid.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This separation between &lt;strong&gt;reasoning, authorization and execution&lt;/strong&gt; may become one of the most important design principles for autonomous finance.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Can an AI spend your crypto without asking? Yes — if you give it the necessary transaction authority and do not require human approval for that type of transaction.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The technology is already moving in that direction. Agent wallets can use spending limits, protocol restrictions, transaction screening and other controls to keep autonomous systems within defined boundaries.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the failure modes are real.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A decimal mistake can turn a small payment into a massive transfer. A malicious external instruction can potentially manipulate an agent. A software bug can produce a transaction that nobody intended.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The important question is therefore not whether an AI &lt;em&gt;can&lt;/em&gt; spend cryptocurrency.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It is whether the system has enough independent safeguards to prevent a mistake from becoming an irreversible financial loss.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The AI does not need to "care" about your money for the transaction to happen. It only needs the authority to execute it.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is why the most important feature of an AI crypto wallet may not be how autonomous it is — but how effectively its autonomy can be limited.&lt;/p&gt;
