    <title>What Happens to Bitcoin If Satoshi-Linked Wallets Suddenly Move?</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhhE9VHdYEeGOdcIsd7qpBGzyqrRoWs0DEq-6dINlCW4iKbgnuOv9H0yHKUzCLCo8gAJLowHg3GYlI60Zb_JT4-qDOYbHU3r0tV_XbSqhqzAXcODYt7v6mrw9-AlWUfDW942Fw6YnV8oSlNggI7erhGJWhI8uEGtUYSDSJZmeBttG7qgFRZKyAoPay6TntG/s1536/What%20Happens%20to%20Bitcoin%20If%20Satoshi-Linked%20Wallets%20Suddenly%20Move.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="Satoshi Nakamoto Bitcoin wallets 1.1 million BTC Patoshi pattern dormant coins movement |" border="0" data-original-height="1024" data-original-width="1536" height="213" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhhE9VHdYEeGOdcIsd7qpBGzyqrRoWs0DEq-6dINlCW4iKbgnuOv9H0yHKUzCLCo8gAJLowHg3GYlI60Zb_JT4-qDOYbHU3r0tV_XbSqhqzAXcODYt7v6mrw9-AlWUfDW942Fw6YnV8oSlNggI7erhGJWhI8uEGtUYSDSJZmeBttG7qgFRZKyAoPay6TntG/w320-h213/What%20Happens%20to%20Bitcoin%20If%20Satoshi-Linked%20Wallets%20Suddenly%20Move.png" title="What Happens to Bitcoin If Satoshi-Linked Wallets Suddenly Move? | CoinaiNews |" width="320" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Aug 14, 2026&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;– On-chain analysis has associated
roughly 1.1 million BTC across approximately 22,000 early-mining addresses with
what is commonly known as the Patoshi pattern, although attributing all of
those coins to &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/crypto-scam-alert-what-to-do-if-youve.html"&gt;Satoshi Nakamoto &lt;/a&gt;remains an analytical estimate rather than a
cryptographically proven fact. Those coins represent more than&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;5% of
the total supply that will ever exist&lt;/b&gt;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;One of Satoshi's final known communications came in April
2011, when he indicated that he had "moved on to other things."&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;What would happen if that changed? What if one of those
wallets suddenly moved?&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;The answer depends entirely on how the movement happens.&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;The Critical Distinction: Signed Message vs. Moving Coins&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;A reveal could span a wide range. At one end, Satoshi signs
a message and proves control without spending a single satoshi. Michael Saylor
set the bar when he said that until someone signs with Satoshi's keys, every
theory is just an educated guess.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;At the more severe end of the spectrum: coins move, an
exchange deposit appears, and trading bots read the transaction before any
human does.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Those two events share a name and little else. One is a line
of cryptography and the vanilla version of the reveal.&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;The other is 1.1
million BTC walking toward the order book&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;— which could trigger
extreme market volatility.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Scenario 1: The Bull Case — Proof Without Movement&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;The friendliest version would see Satoshi prove their
identity and then sit still.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;In May 2026, Paradigm's Dan Robinson published a method
called PACTs that could allow a holder to create a timestamped proof of control
without moving the coins. However, PACTs remain a proposed system and would
require additional Bitcoin protocol infrastructure before such a mechanism
could be implemented.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;One potentially bullish outcome would be evidence that the
person controlling the coins is unable or unwilling to sell them. If the keys
were permanently inaccessible, those coins could effectively become unspendable
and behave economically like lost supply. Jameson Lopp has argued that freezing
dormant coins is closer to burning them than to confiscation. Fewer coins
within reach and steady demand tend to push the price in one direction.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;A live reveal could also be bullish if the identified person
publicly committed to holding the coins rather than selling them. In that
scenario, the market reaction could depend heavily on the person's reputation,
credibility and intentions.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Scenario 2: The Bear Case — A Sale or a State Project&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;The ugly version hinges on who returns and how.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;If control were unexpectedly traced to a government or
another centralized organization, the market could reassess Bitcoin's
historical narrative and assumptions about its origins. Such a discovery could
create uncertainty around the asset's perceived independence from centralized
institutions.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;A confirmed identification of a living Satoshi could also
create significant personal-security and reputational consequences for whoever
was identified, particularly if the person suddenly became the focus of global
attention. Naming a living founder ends the myth and marks them.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Scenario 3: The Nightmare — 1.1 Million BTC Headed to
Exchanges&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;If the coins actually move toward an exchange, the response
would be fundamentally different.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;The Numbers That Should Keep You Awake:&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul style="margin-top: 0cm;" type="disc"&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;1.1
     million BTC&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;— Estimated Patoshi-associated holdings&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Approximately
     22,000 addresses&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;from the early mining pattern&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;**At
     $80,000 Bitcoin** (illustrative price): ~$88 billion&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;5.3%
     of all Bitcoin that will ever exist&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;That would make the holdings exceptionally large by Bitcoin
market standards.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Phase One — The Discovery:&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;A blockchain analyst
notices a 2009 vintage address broadcasting a transaction. Within minutes,
blockchain analysts, exchanges and trading desks would likely monitor the
transaction closely. Derivatives markets could react by reducing risk exposure,
while traders could rapidly price in the possibility of future selling
pressure. Bitcoin could experience sharp volatility even before any coins were
actually sold.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Phase Two — The Confirmation:&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;The coins hit OTC
desks first. A transfer of that scale would be extraordinarily large relative
to normal Bitcoin market activity and could create substantial volatility if
traders interpreted it as preparation for a sale. The bigger effect could come
from changing expectations about &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/schwab-exec-cryptos-next-big-bet-may-be.html"&gt;Bitcoin's&lt;/a&gt; long-term supply distribution and
potential future selling pressure.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;A major part of Bitcoin's scarcity narrative has been the
long dormancy of coins associated with Satoshi.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Phase Three — The Structural Breakdown:&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;A large
release of previously dormant Bitcoin could significantly change market
expectations about supply distribution and future selling pressure.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Why the Coins May Never Move&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Despite the fear, there are strong reasons to believe the
coins will remain untouched.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;1. A Theory About Quantum Risk&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;One recent theory suggests that the distribution of early
Bitcoin across thousands of addresses may have had a security rationale,
potentially including future quantum-computing risks. However, this remains a
theory and has not been established as Satoshi's actual motivation. Bitwise
Head of Research André Dragosch and analyst Marco Battistoni have proposed this
interpretation of the 22,000-address structure, with archived correspondence
supporting the view that the arrangement was a deliberate security strategy
rather than a coincidence from early mining.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;According to Battistoni, breaking into every wallet would
require repeating an extremely demanding computational process more than 22,000
times — likely exceeding the value attackers could recover.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;2. BIP-361&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;BIP-361 is a draft proposal that would introduce a staged
migration away from quantum-vulnerable legacy signatures if adopted. The
proposal would eventually reject older signature formats after a specified
deadline. If such a proposal were adopted and its proposed rules eventually
took effect, some inactive Bitcoin using vulnerable legacy signature schemes
could become difficult or impossible to spend without an approved migration
path. Blockstream CEO Adam Back and other critics argue that freezing legally
owned Bitcoin would conflict with one of the network's core principles.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Satoshi's own 2010 response on the Bitcointalk forum stated
that the network would have enough time to adopt stronger protection if such
threats emerged gradually.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;3. Market Context&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Bitcoin from the Satoshi era has continued to move in some
cases during 2025 and 2026, but movements from individual early addresses do
not by themselves establish a connection to Satoshi or the broader Patoshi
cluster.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;The Bottom Line&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;If Satoshi-linked coins move, the outcome isn't
predetermined — it's determined by how they move. A signed message and a sold
coin are worlds apart.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;For Bitcoin's market narrative, one potentially bullish
outcome would be evidence that the coins are permanently inaccessible or that
their controller has no intention of selling them. For the market, the most
terrifying outcome would be 1.1 million BTC walking toward the order book.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Either way, the network itself remains unaffected. Bitcoin's
core design doesn't rely on who holds the coins, only on math, cryptography,
and consensus.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;The biggest effect would be on market psychology and
Bitcoin's narrative — not its technical capabilities.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;div align="center" class="MsoNormal" style="text-align: center;"&gt;

    <title>Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse Says Crypto Could Transform How Central Banks Move Value</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;article&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi_gAGihpXArC0yqHFffhAHCyRDzQG_pO0oJ3eqV-sFSrMObwCQh3u-Fl4r8OoPRgIYcbw3_dUVCp6W18_0wog8YULAqMJau662UKsgad6VAYfNQwgDFBdcA7QKgUj8TVvLLVLLivkKJ_0FIh0_pmWS-tiLttlZpV26TEIce0-J91gz0Av8mJvWLwMM7Dyd/s1672/Brad%20Garlinghouse%20on%20Crypto%20and%20Central%20Bank%20Value%20Transfers.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="Brad Garlinghouse on Crypto and Central Bank Value Transfers" border="0" data-original-height="941" data-original-width="1672" height="360" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEi_gAGihpXArC0yqHFffhAHCyRDzQG_pO0oJ3eqV-sFSrMObwCQh3u-Fl4r8OoPRgIYcbw3_dUVCp6W18_0wog8YULAqMJau662UKsgad6VAYfNQwgDFBdcA7QKgUj8TVvLLVLLivkKJ_0FIh0_pmWS-tiLttlZpV26TEIce0-J91gz0Av8mJvWLwMM7Dyd/w640-h360/Brad%20Garlinghouse%20on%20Crypto%20and%20Central%20Bank%20Value%20Transfers.png" title="Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse says crypto could transform global value transfers" width="640" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;By CoinAINews Staff&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;
September 7, 2026&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Ripple CEO &lt;strong&gt;Brad Garlinghouse&lt;/strong&gt; is arguing that cryptocurrency could give central banks a faster and potentially more efficient way to store and move value across borders, as traditional financial infrastructure continues to face practical limitations.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Garlinghouse made the argument while commenting on a recent move by the &lt;strong&gt;De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB)&lt;/strong&gt;, the Dutch central bank, to relocate part of its gold reserves from North America to the United Kingdom.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In a post on X, Garlinghouse described the episode as a reminder of how finance still operates and said crypto could provide an alternative for &lt;strong&gt;storing and moving value instantly, securely and globally at little to no cost&lt;/strong&gt;. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Garlinghouse Points to the Dutch Central Bank’s Gold Move&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The immediate trigger for Garlinghouse’s comments was DNB’s decision to move gold reserves from locations in the United States and Canada to the United Kingdom.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;DNB moved around &lt;strong&gt;86 tonnes of gold&lt;/strong&gt; between March and August, according to reporting on the operation. The relocation was intended to make the reserves more accessible and easier to use if they were needed during a crisis. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the physical movement of gold was only part of the story.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Reports indicate that approximately 59 tonnes were sold in New York and subsequently repurchased in London. As a result, only around 27 tonnes physically crossed the Atlantic during the broader operation. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction is what made the transaction interesting to Garlinghouse.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;From his perspective, the episode illustrates the friction involved when large amounts of value are tied to &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/china-unveils-45-billion-bank-and.html"&gt;physical assets&lt;/a&gt; and traditional financial infrastructure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Did Brad Garlinghouse Actually Say?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Garlinghouse did not say that central banks are already replacing gold with cryptocurrency.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead, he presented crypto as a potential solution for moving and storing value in a digital environment.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;His argument is that digital assets can be transferred across borders without physically transporting the underlying asset, potentially reducing some of the time, logistical complexity and costs associated with traditional value transfers.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction is important because the post is fundamentally a &lt;strong&gt;technology and financial-infrastructure argument&lt;/strong&gt;, rather than an announcement of a central-bank crypto adoption program.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why the Argument Matters for Crypto&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;One of the biggest challenges facing &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/polands-crypto-bill-veto-survives-after.html"&gt;cryptocurrencies&lt;/a&gt; has always been proving that blockchain technology can solve problems beyond speculative trading.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Cross-border settlement is one area where the industry has increasingly focused its attention.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Traditional international financial transactions can involve multiple institutions, currencies, compliance checks and settlement systems. Digital assets can potentially reduce some of those layers by allowing value to move on blockchain networks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That does not mean every blockchain transaction is automatically cheaper or faster than every traditional payment. Network fees, liquidity, compliance requirements, custody and transaction finality still matter.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the potential to transfer digital representations of value across borders without physically moving an underlying asset is one of the strongest arguments blockchain companies make for institutional adoption.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Ripple’s Broader Push Into Financial Infrastructure&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Garlinghouse’s comments also fit with Ripple’s broader strategy of positioning blockchain technology as financial infrastructure rather than simply as a cryptocurrency trading system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Ripple currently markets infrastructure for moving money across stablecoins, crypto assets and local currencies, while also offering digital-asset custody services. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The company's focus has expanded beyond the original cross-border payments narrative to areas including stablecoins, custody and institutional financial services.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That broader strategy reflects a shift taking place across the digital-asset industry: companies are increasingly trying to sell blockchain technology to banks and financial institutions as infrastructure for settlement, liquidity and asset management.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Could Central Banks Really Use Crypto to Move Reserves?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That remains a much bigger question.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Central banks manage reserves under strict legal, operational and risk-management frameworks. Any digital asset used for reserve management would need to satisfy requirements around security, liquidity, governance, custody, market depth and regulatory treatment.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For that reason, Garlinghouse’s statement should be viewed as a proposal about what blockchain technology could enable rather than evidence that central banks are preparing to hold large amounts of cryptocurrency.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is also a major difference between using &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/why-is-my-bitcoin-transaction-still.html"&gt;blockchain&lt;/a&gt; rails to transfer or represent value and holding a volatile cryptocurrency as a reserve asset.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Stablecoins, tokenized assets and blockchain-based settlement systems can address different problems from holding assets such as Bitcoin or XRP directly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Tokenization Could Be the More Immediate Use Case&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For traditional financial institutions, tokenization may be a more practical starting point than replacing conventional reserves with cryptocurrencies.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Tokenization allows an asset or financial claim to be represented digitally on a blockchain. In theory, that can make transfers, settlement and ownership records more programmable and easier to coordinate across systems.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The broader financial industry is already exploring tokenized deposits, stablecoins, tokenized securities and other blockchain-based financial instruments.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That means the debate is increasingly shifting from &lt;strong&gt;“Will banks use crypto?”&lt;/strong&gt; to a more specific question: &lt;strong&gt;“Which parts of financial infrastructure can benefit from blockchain-based settlement?”&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Speed Alone Is Not Enough&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Garlinghouse’s emphasis on speed and low-cost transfers highlights one potential advantage of blockchain networks, but speed is only one part of institutional finance.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Financial institutions also need reliable settlement finality, regulatory compliance, deep liquidity, cybersecurity and clear legal ownership.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A transaction that settles quickly is not necessarily useful to a central bank if the asset being transferred is highly volatile or difficult to liquidate at scale.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is why stablecoins and tokenized traditional assets have attracted significant attention alongside cryptocurrencies such as XRP and Bitcoin.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why the Gold Example Is Interesting&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The Dutch gold relocation illustrates an important distinction between &lt;strong&gt;moving an asset&lt;/strong&gt; and &lt;strong&gt;moving economic value&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Gold itself is physical. Moving it between countries requires transportation, security, insurance, storage and logistical coordination.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But ownership of gold can also be represented through financial claims and transactions that do not require every ounce of metal to physically cross a border.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Garlinghouse’s argument is that blockchain-based assets take that concept much further by making the digital transfer of value native to the system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Whether that becomes a mainstream central-bank use case remains uncertain, but it is one reason financial institutions continue to examine tokenization and blockchain settlement.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What This Could Mean for XRP&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Garlinghouse is the CEO of Ripple, a company closely associated with XRP and blockchain-based payments, so his comments naturally attract attention from the XRP market.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;However, his statement should not be interpreted as a prediction that central banks are about to adopt XRP as a reserve asset.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The broader argument is about &lt;strong&gt;crypto and blockchain infrastructure&lt;/strong&gt; and its potential role in moving value internationally.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Ripple has continued to build products around payments, custody and digital assets, but actual adoption by central banks would depend on regulatory decisions, institutional requirements and individual central-bank policies.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Traditional Finance Is Also Evolving&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is another side to the debate that is easy to overlook.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Traditional financial institutions are not standing still. Banks and payment networks are also investing in faster settlement systems, stablecoins, tokenized deposits and blockchain-based infrastructure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Recent moves by major financial institutions to explore bank-issued stablecoins show that blockchain technology is increasingly being considered inside mainstream finance rather than only within the crypto industry. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This could eventually produce a financial system in which traditional banks and blockchain networks coexist rather than one completely replacing the other.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bigger Question for Central Banks&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The most important question is not whether cryptocurrency can move value quickly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It is whether blockchain-based assets can provide the combination of &lt;strong&gt;speed, security, liquidity, regulatory certainty and operational reliability&lt;/strong&gt; required by central banks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If they can, the potential market is enormous.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Central banks manage some of the world's largest pools of financial assets. Even a limited role for tokenized assets or blockchain-based settlement could have implications for international payments, foreign-exchange markets and reserve management.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But that transition would likely take years rather than happen overnight.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Key Takeaways&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse says crypto could allow value to be stored and moved globally with greater speed and potentially lower costs.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;His comments came after the Dutch central bank relocated part of its gold reserves to the UK.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;About 86 tonnes of gold were moved during the broader relocation, while much of the transaction involved selling gold in one location and repurchasing it in another.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Garlinghouse presented the episode as an example of the limitations of traditional financial infrastructure.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;His comments do not mean central banks are currently preparing to replace gold with cryptocurrency.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Tokenization, stablecoins and blockchain settlement may offer more immediate institutional use cases.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;For XRP, the comments reinforce Ripple’s long-running focus on blockchain-based financial infrastructure, but they are not evidence of imminent central-bank XRP adoption.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Frequently Asked Questions&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What did Brad Garlinghouse say about crypto and central banks?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Garlinghouse said crypto could be an ideal use case for storing and moving value instantly and securely around the world at little to no cost. He made the comments while discussing the Dutch central bank’s gold relocation. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Why did Brad Garlinghouse mention the Dutch central bank?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;He pointed to the relocation of Dutch gold reserves as an example of the logistical complexity associated with moving large amounts of value through traditional financial systems.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Did the Dutch central bank move $11 billion in gold?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Reporting on the relocation has valued the broader gold transfer at roughly $11 billion. Around 86 tonnes were moved from North America to the UK, although much of the transaction involved selling and repurchasing gold rather than physically transporting every tonne. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Does Garlinghouse think central banks will adopt XRP?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;His statement does not establish that central banks will adopt XRP. His broader argument concerns the potential of crypto and blockchain technology for moving and storing value.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Could blockchain replace traditional financial infrastructure?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Blockchain technology could replace or improve some parts of financial infrastructure, particularly settlement and asset transfer. However, regulatory requirements, liquidity, custody, security and legal frameworks remain important barriers to widespread institutional adoption.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Why is tokenization important for banks?&lt;/h3&gt;
&lt;p&gt;Tokenization can represent assets or financial claims digitally on blockchain networks, potentially making settlement and transfers more programmable and efficient.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Brad Garlinghouse’s latest comments highlight one of crypto’s biggest potential advantages: &lt;strong&gt;the ability to move digital representations of value without physically moving the underlying asset&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Whether central banks ultimately adopt blockchain-based systems at scale is still an open question. But as banks and financial institutions increasingly experiment with stablecoins, tokenization and digital settlement, the debate is moving beyond cryptocurrency speculation and toward the infrastructure of global finance itself.&lt;/p&gt;

They should not be interpreted as confirmation that central banks have adopted, or are preparing to adopt, XRP or another cryptocurrency as a reserve asset.&lt;/p&gt;

    <title>AI Insider Trading: The New Market-Abuse Risk Nobody Talks About</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;h1&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEj6yn0L9uX9H-q_tr1jdF7PqcnblPz7YD2LsBdjHE1VwH8j6lW_dsg5wWOdqfJFiYWtghI0YiVf5cPry7Xyk9ye2jCFfVsLwizFhwDt5A-3qBub_18fBHfKyJi2CTuDYNsNVn_QJeouxNnuYt_7tX1NWKxD-5Br7kFrHzxIhjZirBw05SiJqHOq2Tki8euf/s1672/ai-insider-trading-crypto-market-abuse.jpg.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="AI trading agent analyzing confidential crypto market information before an automated trade" border="0" data-original-height="940" data-original-width="1672" height="360" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEj6yn0L9uX9H-q_tr1jdF7PqcnblPz7YD2LsBdjHE1VwH8j6lW_dsg5wWOdqfJFiYWtghI0YiVf5cPry7Xyk9ye2jCFfVsLwizFhwDt5A-3qBub_18fBHfKyJi2CTuDYNsNVn_QJeouxNnuYt_7tX1NWKxD-5Br7kFrHzxIhjZirBw05SiJqHOq2Tki8euf/w640-h360/ai-insider-trading-crypto-market-abuse.jpg.png" title="AI Insider Trading: The New Market-Abuse Risk" width="640" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;By CoinAINews Staff&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Imagine an AI trading agent connected to a crypto exchange.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It monitors blockchain activity, exchange flows, governance proposals, project announcements and thousands of other signals. Then it receives information that has not yet been made public.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Maybe a major token listing is about to be announced. Maybe a crypto company is preparing a deal. Maybe a protocol has discovered a serious vulnerability.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI understands what the information could mean.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It buys.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Minutes later, the information becomes public and the token jumps.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Did the AI just commit insider trading?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The answer depends on the information, the applicable law, the asset and the people or entities behind the trading system.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The machine may have executed the order, but that does not automatically place the activity outside market-abuse rules. The harder question is how the AI obtained the information, what authority it had, and who was responsible for the account and trading system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Insider Trading vs. Insider Dealing: What Is the Difference?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The terminology varies by jurisdiction. The United States commonly uses the term &lt;strong&gt;insider trading&lt;/strong&gt;, while the European Union and several other jurisdictions use &lt;strong&gt;insider dealing&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This article uses both terms to describe broadly similar conduct involving trading on material, non-public information, while recognizing that the precise legal definitions differ between jurisdictions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For crypto, the distinction matters because there is no single global insider-trading rule covering every digital asset and every exchange.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Can an AI Commit Insider Trading in Crypto?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI system can technically execute a trade using non-public information. Whether that conduct legally constitutes insider trading or insider dealing depends on the applicable regulatory framework.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI agent can potentially:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;receive information from multiple data sources;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;identify information that may affect an asset's price;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;compare it with historical market data;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;calculate a trading opportunity;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;place an order automatically; and&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;close or adjust the position after the information becomes public.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The important point is that &lt;strong&gt;automation changes how the trade happens, not necessarily whether the underlying conduct is regulated.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Crypto Already Has Insider-Dealing Rules&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The idea that crypto markets simply have no insider-trading rules is no longer accurate.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In the European Union, the Markets in &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/ai-borrowing-from-ai-who-writes-contract.html"&gt;Crypto-Assets&lt;/a&gt; Regulation, or &lt;strong&gt;MiCA&lt;/strong&gt;, contains specific market-abuse provisions. Article 89 prohibits insider dealing involving covered crypto-assets, including using inside information to acquire or dispose of crypto-assets directly or indirectly. It also covers recommending or inducing another person to trade on the basis of inside information.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-89-prohibition-insider-dealing" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;Read ESMA's MiCA Article 89 guidance on insider dealing&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;MiCA also requires certain persons professionally arranging or executing crypto transactions to have systems and procedures aimed at preventing and detecting market abuse and to report reasonable suspicions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-92-prevention-and-detection-market-abuse" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;Read ESMA's MiCA Article 92 market-abuse requirements&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Counts as Inside Information?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Not every secret, prediction or early market signal is automatically inside information.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The applicable legal framework matters, but the concept generally focuses on information that is sufficiently specific, not public and capable of materially affecting the price or investment decision concerning the relevant asset.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Crypto makes this particularly complicated because information can come from many places:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;blockchain transactions;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;governance proposals;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;developer communications;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;private investor discussions;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;exchange data;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;token issuers;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;social-media channels; and&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;internal company systems.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI may also combine dozens of individually public signals and reach a conclusion that other traders have not reached.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction is critical.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Public Blockchain Analysis Is Not Automatically Insider Trading&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Suppose an AI notices that several large wallets are moving tokens toward exchange addresses.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/can-ai-own-its-own-crypto-wallet-law.html"&gt;blockchain&lt;/a&gt; data is public.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI concludes that selling pressure may be coming and opens a short position.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is very different from receiving a confidential message saying that the project is about to announce a major problem.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The first scenario is automated analysis of public information.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The second involves potentially non-public information.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Being faster or better at analysing public information does not automatically make an AI an insider trader.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This distinction could become increasingly important as AI systems become better at analysing public blockchain data.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What If the AI Receives a Private Tip?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Now consider a different situation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An employee of a crypto project gives an AI trading system access to an internal document before a major announcement.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The document contains information that could materially affect the token's price.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI reads it, calculates the likely market reaction and buys the token.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No human manually enters the order.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The trading system does it automatically.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The absence of a human pressing the buy button does not by itself answer the legal question. In the EU, MiCA expressly prohibits using inside information to acquire or dispose of covered crypto-assets. The investigation would still need to examine the circumstances surrounding the information, the transaction and the relevant parties.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-89-prohibition-insider-dealing" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;ESMA: MiCA Article 89 — Insider Dealing&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Who Is Responsible When the AI Makes the Trade?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is the central accountability problem.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Suppose a company owns an autonomous trading system. The company gives the system access to a trading account and instructs it to seek profitable opportunities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An employee then provides confidential information to the system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI buys the relevant token.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Several actors could become relevant to an investigation, depending on the jurisdiction and facts:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;the person who improperly disclosed the information;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;the person who authorized or instructed the trade;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;the company operating the AI system;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;the person or entity controlling the trading account; and&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;other parties that knowingly participated in or benefited from the conduct.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI's autonomy does not, by itself, identify the legally responsible party.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What If Nobody Told the AI to Buy?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Suppose the company never explicitly tells the AI to buy the token.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead, the system has a standing instruction:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;“Trade whenever your models identify an opportunity with a sufficiently high probability of profit.”&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI receives confidential information through a connected data source and independently decides to trade.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That scenario makes the attribution question harder, but it does not automatically make the transaction lawful.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Investigators would need to look at the AI's permissions, data sources, system design, trading account, internal controls and the conduct of the people who supplied or controlled those systems.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Autonomous execution can complicate attribution without eliminating the underlying market-abuse rules.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Could an AI Be the “Insider”?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That may not be the most useful legal question.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI can technically receive, store and process information. But the legal system applicable to a transaction may instead focus on the human or legal entity that controls the account, supplied the information, authorized the activity or benefited from the transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The practical question is therefore:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Who had the relevant information, who had authority over the trading system, and on whose behalf did the AI act?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That framework is more useful than assuming that the software itself must become the legal “insider.”&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;AI Could Make Market Abuse Much Faster&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Traditional insider trading already creates an information advantage. An autonomous AI system could potentially make that advantage much faster.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A human trader might need minutes to read a document, understand it and place an order.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An automated system could potentially process information, compare it with historical patterns and execute a transaction almost immediately.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It could also monitor hundreds of assets and multiple venues simultaneously.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That creates a difficult surveillance problem.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;By the time investigators identify the suspicious information, an automated system may already have opened a position, changed its exposure or moved assets between wallets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Blockchain data can provide valuable forensic evidence, but investigators may still need to reconstruct the information pipeline that led to the trade.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What About the United States?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The U.S. regulatory picture is more complicated because the treatment of a crypto asset can determine which federal framework applies.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is, however, an important 2026 development that should not be overlooked.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;On &lt;strong&gt;March 17, 2026&lt;/strong&gt;, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission issued an interpretation clarifying how federal securities laws apply to certain crypto assets and transactions involving crypto assets. The CFTC joined the interpretation and provided guidance on administering the Commodity Exchange Act consistently with it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026-30-sec-clarifies-application-federal-securities-laws-crypto-assets" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;SEC: Federal Securities Laws and Crypto Assets — March 17, 2026&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/PressReleases/9198-26" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;CFTC: Crypto Asset Regulatory Interpretation — March 17, 2026&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The SEC interpretation does not create one universal U.S. insider-trading rule for every cryptocurrency. The relevant asset, transaction, market and applicable federal or state law still matter.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction is important when discussing AI because a trading agent could operate across different types of crypto markets, each with different regulatory characteristics.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What About the UK?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The United Kingdom is also building a dedicated &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/ai-made-millions-in-crypto-who-pays-tax.html"&gt;cryptoasset &lt;/a&gt;market-abuse regime.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;On &lt;strong&gt;June 30, 2026&lt;/strong&gt;, the FCA published final rules and guidance for its cryptoasset admissions, disclosures and market-abuse regime. The framework is designed to address abusive practices including insider dealing and market manipulation in qualifying cryptoasset markets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.fca.org.uk/publications/policy-statements/cryptoasset-regime" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;FCA: UK Cryptoasset Regime and Market-Abuse Rules&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The FCA has also specifically described cryptoasset insider dealing, including situations involving confidential information and transactions ahead of events such as an unannounced airdrop.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.fca.org.uk/publications/consultation-papers/cp25-41-regulating-cryptoassets-admissions-disclosures-market-abuse-regime-cryptoassets" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;FCA: Cryptoasset Market-Abuse Regime&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For AI trading systems operating in or connected to the UK regime, the key issue will again be how automated decisions, inside information and accountable persons or entities fit together.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What About the UAE?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Dubai provides another useful example because its Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority, or VARA, has explicit market-offence provisions for virtual assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;VARA identifies &lt;strong&gt;insider dealing, unlawful disclosure and market manipulation&lt;/strong&gt; as market offences. Its insider-dealing rules cover transactions involving virtual assets when an entity possesses inside information and uses it directly or indirectly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://rulebooks.vara.ae/rulebook/c-insider-dealing" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;VARA: Insider Dealing&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://rulebooks.vara.ae/rulebook/e-prohibition-insider-dealing-and-unlawful-disclosure" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;VARA: Prohibition of Insider Dealing and Unlawful Disclosure&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is particularly relevant to AI because VARA's rules also contemplate situations involving legal entities and internal arrangements designed to limit access to inside information and prevent insider dealing.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://rulebooks.vara.ae/rulebook/f-legitimate-behaviour-treating-inside-information" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;VARA: Legitimate Treatment of Inside Information&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;And What About India?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;India's crypto regulatory framework is different from the dedicated market-abuse regimes discussed above.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The Financial Intelligence Unit–India currently plays an important AML/CFT/CPF role for virtual digital asset service providers. Its 2026 guidelines cover areas such as customer due diligence, transaction monitoring, suspicious transaction reporting and record-keeping.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://fiuindia.gov.in/pdfs/downloads/VDA08012026.pdf" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;FIU-IND: AML/CFT/CPF Guidelines for VDA Service Providers&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That should not be presented as an Indian crypto insider-trading regime equivalent to MiCA or VARA. Instead, it shows that Indian authorities already require regulated VDA service providers to maintain monitoring and compliance systems.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;India is also developing an agentic-payment framework. Reuters reported in September 2026 that the National Payments Corporation of India was developing a registry to verify and monitor AI agents conducting UPI transactions, with questions around liability for unauthorized or erroneous AI-driven payments still being worked through.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/india/india-plans-ai-registry-it-looks-roll-out-agentic-payments-sources-say-2026-09-10/" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;Reuters: India Plans AI Registry as It Develops Agentic Payments&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That development is not an insider-trading rule, but it is relevant to the broader question of how regulators may identify and hold accountable autonomous financial systems.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Happens If AI Discovers the Information Itself?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Now consider a harder case.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Nobody gives the AI a confidential document.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead, it analyses thousands of public blockchain transactions, wallet movements, governance discussions and market signals.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI predicts a major announcement before almost everyone else.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It trades.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The prediction is correct.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is not automatically insider trading.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The fact that an AI can identify a market-moving pattern before human traders does not by itself prove that it possessed inside information.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is one reason regulators will need to distinguish between &lt;strong&gt;automated intelligence based on legitimate public information&lt;/strong&gt; and &lt;strong&gt;automated trading based on confidential information&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;AI Market Manipulation Is a Separate Risk&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Insider trading is only one possible form of AI-driven market abuse.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI system could also potentially be used to generate misleading information, coordinate trading activity or create artificial market signals.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;MiCA separately prohibits market manipulation involving covered crypto-assets, including conduct capable of giving false or misleading signals about supply, demand or price.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32023R1114" rel="noopener" target="_blank"&gt;EUR-Lex: Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 (MiCA)&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That means the broader question may eventually be bigger than AI insider trading. Regulators may have to deal with systems capable of using speed, scale and automation to create or exploit market conditions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Which AI Trading Scenarios Carry the Most Legal Risk?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;div style="margin: 20px 0px; overflow-x: auto; width: 100%;"&gt;
&lt;table style="border-collapse: collapse; border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); min-width: 760px; width: 100%;"&gt;
&lt;thead&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px; text-align: left;"&gt;Scenario&lt;/th&gt;
&lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px; text-align: left;"&gt;Information Source&lt;/th&gt;
&lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px; text-align: left;"&gt;Legal Risk Level&lt;/th&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/thead&gt;
&lt;tbody&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;AI analyses public blockchain data&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Public information&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Low&lt;/strong&gt; — not automatically insider dealing&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;AI receives confidential project information&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Non-public information&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;High&lt;/strong&gt; — market-abuse rules may apply&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;AI trades after an employee supplies inside information&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;Unauthorized or restricted disclosure&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Very High&lt;/strong&gt; — information source and authorization become critical&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;AI disseminates false &lt;br /&gt;information to move a &lt;br /&gt;token&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;AI-generated or manipulated information&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(119, 119, 119); padding: 10px;"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;High&lt;/strong&gt; — potential market-manipulation issues&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/tbody&gt;
&lt;/table&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Risk levels above are a general editorial illustration, not a legal classification. The applicable law and facts determine the actual legal exposure.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Real Issue Isn't Whether a Computer Can Press the Buy Button&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The difficult part is reconstructing &lt;strong&gt;why the AI made the decision&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Imagine an investigator asks an AI trading system:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;“Why did you buy this token?”&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The system answers:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;“My model calculated a 94% probability of a positive announcement.”&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The next question is more difficult:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;“Where did that probability come from?”&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The answer could involve thousands of data points, multiple APIs, blockchain addresses, internal messages and model-generated inferences.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That creates an evidence problem.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Future investigations may need to examine not only the final transaction but also the information pipeline that influenced the AI's decision.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Crypto Companies Should Be Watching&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Companies deploying autonomous trading systems should not assume that giving a machine decision-making authority removes their compliance responsibilities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Depending on the jurisdiction and business model, sensible controls can include:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;restricting which information sources an AI can access;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;separating confidential information from trading systems;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;limiting which assets an AI can trade;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;setting wallet and account permissions;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;maintaining detailed decision logs;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;monitoring unusual orders and transfers;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;controlling who can modify the agent's permissions; and&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;preserving records that allow a trade to be reconstructed later.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The exact compliance requirements depend on the relevant law, but the principle is straightforward: &lt;strong&gt;an autonomous trading system still needs an accountable operating structure.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Frequently Asked Questions&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Can an AI commit insider trading in crypto?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI can technically execute a crypto trade using non-public information. Whether that conduct legally constitutes insider trading or insider dealing depends on the applicable jurisdiction, asset, market and facts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Is AI insider trading illegal?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is no single global law called “AI insider trading.” Existing market-abuse rules can apply to conduct carried out through automated systems. For example, EU MiCA prohibits insider dealing involving covered crypto-assets, while Dubai's VARA rules prohibit insider dealing involving virtual assets within its regulatory framework.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Can an AI be the legal insider?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That depends on the applicable legal framework. The more practical question is usually which person or legal entity supplied the information, controlled the system, authorized the transaction or benefited from the trade.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What if the AI only uses public blockchain data?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Analysing public information is different from trading on confidential inside information. An AI that identifies a market signal from public blockchain data is not automatically an insider trader simply because it reaches the conclusion faster than other market participants.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Can AI manipulate crypto markets?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Technically, an AI could be used to generate misleading information, coordinate trading or create artificial market signals. Whether specific conduct constitutes market manipulation depends on the applicable law and facts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What should companies do if they use AI for crypto trading?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Companies should consider access controls, information segregation, trading limits, audit logs, monitoring and clear authorization structures. Firms operating in regulated markets should also obtain jurisdiction-specific legal and compliance advice.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Note: Replace the three internal-link URLs above with the exact live CoinAINews post URLs if the slugs on your site differ.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AI does not need to become a legal person to create a serious market-abuse problem.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It only needs access to information, a trading account and enough authority to act.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If an AI analyses public blockchain data and finds a profitable signal, that is fundamentally different from receiving confidential information and trading before the market learns about it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And when an autonomous system does receive inside information, saying &lt;em&gt;“the bot did it”&lt;/em&gt; is unlikely to answer the real questions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Investigators will want to know where the information came from, who controlled the system, what authority the AI had and who stood behind the transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The machine may place the trade. The people and entities behind the machine may still have to answer for it.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

It is not a substitute for advice from a qualified lawyer or compliance professional. If you operate, design, fund or control an AI trading system, consult qualified legal counsel and compliance advisers in the jurisdictions where the system, operator, exchange or relevant crypto assets are located or regulated. Laws and regulatory frameworks can change.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
