    <title>REX Launches ASSX: 2X Leveraged ETF Gives Traders Amplified Exposure to Bitcoin Treasury Firm Strive</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;h1&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjd3NlkzL0zdG8dmjTkxm6uBB-nA5eoExDdv_R6vSzOnvtODZVkmqRja9T0dj-dQSmMze0LfyjJnNwfBfqa0jTbjkSETvnrQKVMhcb1FViNTHHA0Ob4YppM3m6e4wtbFb-CS4ULgAyP3n1WlC7ok96pdXYVr78CbBXqOBOI8vrcwINjYG5Yb-o4Mfyz-R3S/s1733/rex-tuttle-assx-2x-strive-bitcoin-treasury-etf.webp.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="REX and Tuttle launch ASSX 2X leveraged ETF tied to Bitcoin treasury firm Strive" border="0" data-original-height="907" data-original-width="1733" height="334" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjd3NlkzL0zdG8dmjTkxm6uBB-nA5eoExDdv_R6vSzOnvtODZVkmqRja9T0dj-dQSmMze0LfyjJnNwfBfqa0jTbjkSETvnrQKVMhcb1FViNTHHA0Ob4YppM3m6e4wtbFb-CS4ULgAyP3n1WlC7ok96pdXYVr78CbBXqOBOI8vrcwINjYG5Yb-o4Mfyz-R3S/w640-h334/rex-tuttle-assx-2x-strive-bitcoin-treasury-etf.webp.png" title="REX and Tuttle Launch ASSX 2X Leveraged Strive ETF" width="640" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;REX Shares and Tuttle Capital Management have launched a new leveraged ETF tied to Strive, one of the public companies building a large Bitcoin treasury.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The new fund, called the &lt;strong&gt;T-REX 2X Long ASST Daily Target ETF&lt;/strong&gt;, trades under the ticker &lt;strong&gt;ASSX&lt;/strong&gt; on Cboe. The ETF is designed to deliver &lt;strong&gt;200% of the daily performance of Strive's common stock, ASST, before fees and expenses&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The launch gives traders a new way to take an amplified short-term position on a Bitcoin-focused public company without directly buying Bitcoin or ASST shares themselves.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But there is an important detail that could easily get lost in the headline: &lt;strong&gt;ASSX is not a 2X Bitcoin ETF.&lt;/strong&gt; It does not hold Bitcoin and does not attempt to deliver twice Bitcoin's daily return. Instead, its target is based on the daily performance of Strive shares. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;ASSX Starts Trading on Cboe&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;REX and Tuttle launched ASSX on September 18, 2026, with the fund beginning trading on Cboe under the ticker &lt;strong&gt;ASSX&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;REX describes the product as the &lt;strong&gt;first U.S. ETF offering 2X daily long exposure to Strive&lt;/strong&gt;, a Bitcoin-treasury company. The fund's investment objective is specifically tied to ASST's daily performance rather than the price of Bitcoin. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That makes ASSX part of a growing market for leveraged &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/saudi-arabia-withdraws-from-china-led.html"&gt;ETFs &lt;/a&gt;built around publicly traded companies with significant exposure to digital assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For traders who already follow Bitcoin treasury companies, the product adds another layer to an increasingly complex market: instead of simply buying a Bitcoin-related stock, investors can now use an ETF designed to magnify its &lt;em&gt;daily&lt;/em&gt; moves.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;How the 2X Exposure Actually Works&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The basic idea behind ASSX is straightforward.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If ASST gains 5% during a trading day, ASSX seeks to gain approximately 10%, before fees, expenses and other factors affecting the fund's performance.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If ASST falls 5%, the same mechanism works in reverse, with ASSX targeting approximately a 10% decline for that day.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;However, the word &lt;strong&gt;“daily”&lt;/strong&gt; is critical.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;REX states that the fund does not seek to achieve its investment objective for a period different from a single trading day. Its leverage is reset each day, which means an investor should not assume that holding ASSX for several days will simply produce twice ASST's total return. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why ASSX Is Not the Same as a 2X Bitcoin ETF&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This distinction matters because Strive is closely associated with Bitcoin.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Strive has adopted a Bitcoin-focused corporate strategy and holds a substantial amount of BTC. That gives its stock exposure to developments in the Bitcoin market, but &lt;strong&gt;ASST remains a company's stock rather than Bitcoin itself&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There are several factors between Bitcoin's price and ASSX's eventual performance.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Bitcoin's price can influence the value of Strive's &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/coinbase-ceo-says-sec-and-cftc-rules.html"&gt;Bitcoin holdings&lt;/a&gt;.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Changes in Bitcoin sentiment can influence demand for ASST shares.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Strive's corporate decisions and capital structure can affect the stock.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;ASST can move independently of Bitcoin on some trading days.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;ASSX then targets 2X the daily move of ASST.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That means the relationship can be thought of as &lt;strong&gt;Bitcoin exposure through Strive, followed by daily leverage on Strive's stock&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It is therefore inaccurate to describe ASSX as simply “2X Bitcoin.”&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Strive Holds 25,000 Bitcoin&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The launch is attracting attention because of the size of Strive's Bitcoin treasury.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;According to Cointelegraph, Strive currently holds approximately &lt;strong&gt;25,000 BTC&lt;/strong&gt;, making it the fifth-largest publicly traded corporate Bitcoin holder based on BitcoinTreasuries.NET data cited in the report. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The company also recently added &lt;strong&gt;469 BTC&lt;/strong&gt;, with the purchase financed through sales of SATA, its perpetual preferred stock, according to the report.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That treasury strategy is one of the main reasons Strive has become an increasingly watched stock among investors looking for equity-market exposure to Bitcoin.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the value of Strive shares is not determined solely by the market value of its Bitcoin holdings.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Investors also have to consider the company's financing strategy, capital structure, future Bitcoin purchases and the valuation that the stock market assigns to the business.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Strive Stock Jumped 6.4% on Friday&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The timing of the ASSX launch also comes as ASST has been attracting market attention.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Strive shares rose &lt;strong&gt;6.4% on Friday to close at $30.09&lt;/strong&gt;, according to the Cointelegraph report, which cited Yahoo Finance data.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The report also noted that the closing price was slightly above the &lt;strong&gt;$29.40 average 12-month analyst price target&lt;/strong&gt; tracked by S&amp;amp;P Global. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That single-day move also illustrates why a leveraged product such as ASSX can attract active traders. A sizeable move in ASST can translate into a substantially larger percentage move in the leveraged ETF.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Of course, the same mechanism works when the stock falls.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Daily Reset Is the Part Traders Need to Understand&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;One of the biggest differences between ASSX and simply holding ASST is the daily reset.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Suppose ASST rises sharply on one day and then gives back part of that gain the following day. A 2X daily ETF does not simply take the total two-day return of ASST and multiply it by two.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead, the fund resets its exposure after each trading session.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That creates what is commonly known as &lt;strong&gt;path dependency&lt;/strong&gt;. The sequence of gains and losses can materially affect the final result when a leveraged ETF is held for longer than one day.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;REX specifically warns that performance over periods longer than a single trading day can differ significantly from 200% of ASST's cumulative performance because of daily compounding and the fund's reset mechanism. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For that reason, ASSX is fundamentally designed around a daily trading objective rather than a promise of delivering 2X ASST's long-term return.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Traders May Find ASSX Interesting&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The attraction is easy to understand.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A trader who expects ASST to move sharply higher during a particular session can use ASSX to seek approximately twice that daily move.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That provides a way to express a short-term bullish view on Strive without directly purchasing the underlying shares.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;At the same time, the leverage makes the product considerably more sensitive to adverse moves.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A trader who gets the direction wrong can see losses accumulate much faster than they would from holding the underlying stock without leverage.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;REX says the fund is intended for knowledgeable investors who understand the consequences of daily leveraged products, understand leverage risks and are willing to monitor their portfolios frequently. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;ASSX Adds Another Layer to the Bitcoin Treasury Trade&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The bigger story behind ASSX is not just the launch of one ETF.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It is the continued expansion of financial products built around companies that hold Bitcoin on their balance sheets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Over the past few years, investors have gained several different ways to obtain Bitcoin-related exposure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;They can hold BTC directly, use a spot &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/brazil-securities-regulator-launches-tokenization-working-group.html"&gt;Bitcoin ETF&lt;/a&gt;, buy shares in a Bitcoin treasury company or trade financial products based on those companies.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;ASSX takes that structure another step further by adding daily leverage to the stock of a Bitcoin treasury company.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The result is a product that sits somewhere between traditional equity trading and crypto-market speculation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;REX and Tuttle Are Expanding Their Leveraged ETF Lineup&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;ASSX is also not an isolated product from REX and Tuttle.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;According to the companies, their lineup includes other 2X ETFs connected to crypto-related publicly traded companies, including &lt;strong&gt;Strategy, BitMine, Cipher Mining, Circle and SharpLink&lt;/strong&gt;. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That suggests the issuers see continued demand for leveraged exposure to individual companies that are closely connected to the digital-asset market.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The approach gives traders a packaged ETF structure instead of requiring them to use traditional margin strategies or options to obtain amplified exposure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For sophisticated traders, that can create another tool. For inexperienced investors, however, the mechanics can be much less intuitive than a conventional unleveraged ETF.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Happens if Bitcoin Moves Sharply?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin's price could become an important driver of ASST, but investors should not assume that every Bitcoin move will produce a matching move in the stock.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Strive's stock can react to Bitcoin's price, but it can also respond to company-specific news, capital raises, changes in its treasury strategy, investor demand and broader equity-market conditions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;ASSX then magnifies the daily move of that stock.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That creates a chain of exposure that can produce very different results from simply buying BTC.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For example, Bitcoin could rise while ASST performs differently because of stock-specific factors. In that situation, ASSX would follow ASST rather than Bitcoin.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is why the underlying asset named in the fund's objective matters more than the broader “Bitcoin ETF” label sometimes attached to the story.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bigger Trend Behind Bitcoin Treasury Companies&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin treasury companies have become an increasingly visible part of the crypto-finance market.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The basic strategy is to hold Bitcoin as a significant corporate treasury asset while using the company's equity and other financing instruments to support its broader strategy.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Strive is one example of that model, and its approximately 25,000-BTC position has made ASST a stock that can attract both traditional equity investors and crypto-focused traders. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Products such as ASSX show how Wall Street-style financial engineering is developing around that trend.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead of only asking whether Bitcoin will rise or fall, traders can now take positions based on how a Bitcoin treasury company's shares react to the same market environment.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Investors Should Watch With ASSX&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Several factors will be important as ASSX develops a trading history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;ASST volatility:&lt;/strong&gt; Larger daily moves in Strive can produce larger moves in ASSX.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Bitcoin volatility:&lt;/strong&gt; Changes in BTC can influence sentiment around Bitcoin treasury companies.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Daily compounding:&lt;/strong&gt; Multi-day performance can differ significantly from simply doubling ASST's cumulative return.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Company-specific events:&lt;/strong&gt; Financing, treasury purchases and corporate announcements can move ASST independently of Bitcoin.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Liquidity and trading conditions:&lt;/strong&gt; The ETF's market price can be affected by trading activity and market conditions.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;These factors make ASSX a very different instrument from a traditional Bitcoin ETF.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;REX Shares and Tuttle Capital Management have launched ASSX, a 2X daily leveraged ETF built around Strive's ASST shares.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The ETF began trading on Cboe on September 18, 2026, and seeks to deliver 200% of ASST's daily performance before fees and expenses. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The most important point for crypto investors is that &lt;strong&gt;ASSX is not a leveraged Bitcoin ETF&lt;/strong&gt;. It does not hold BTC and does not target twice Bitcoin's return. Its exposure is to Strive's stock, and Strive's Bitcoin treasury is only one factor that can influence that stock.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;With Strive holding approximately &lt;strong&gt;25,000 BTC&lt;/strong&gt; and continuing to build its Bitcoin-focused strategy, ASST has become an increasingly visible bridge between traditional equities and the crypto market. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;ASSX takes that connection one step further by adding daily leverage. That could make it attractive to active traders looking for amplified short-term exposure, while the daily reset and compounding effects make it a product that requires a clear understanding of how leveraged ETFs work.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In short, the launch is another sign that the Bitcoin treasury trend is moving beyond simply buying and holding BTC. Financial markets are increasingly creating products around the companies, stocks and strategies that sit around the Bitcoin ecosystem.&lt;/p&gt;

Leveraged ETFs can experience substantial losses, and performance over periods longer than one trading day can differ significantly from the stated daily multiple because of compounding and daily resets. must now disclose their AI status, &lt;a data-preview="" href="https://www.google.com/search?ved=1t:260882&amp;amp;q=define+deepfakes&amp;amp;bbid=1063445581464181190&amp;amp;bpid=8661312994647279272" target="_blank"&gt;deepfakes&lt;/a&gt; require clear labeling, and all &lt;a data-preview="" href="https://www.google.com/search?ved=1t:260882&amp;amp;q=AI-generated+content+examples&amp;amp;bbid=1063445581464181190&amp;amp;bpid=8661312994647279272" target="_blank"&gt;AI-generated content&lt;/a&gt; must carry &lt;a data-preview="" href="https://www.google.com/search?ved=1t:260882&amp;amp;q=define+machine-readable+marks&amp;amp;bbid=1063445581464181190&amp;amp;bpid=8661312994647279272" target="_blank"&gt;machine-readable marks&lt;/a&gt;.     <title>Italy Tightens Crypto Sanctions Checks as Banca d’Italia Demands Stronger Transfer Controls</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;article&gt;

&lt;h1&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEgeFZtDpd3KVUAk7SFNjWljx3L8E8LPRgmH6RgQJAu1PE6vLNUvEFkA2PaLquIGI2UAKpmQNx3X5FGczG3YmlJDbbnpF20-a__QI8KpcRVIIaPuJP8NEvkGeaWP_UPoZUYx5k0L53ad1zpCSEwJ3fRkVZYbvfOJkSBUkEQ1MJLosZE77RUsmzAFJQW075wS" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="Banca d’Italia tightens sanctions screening controls for crypto transfers in Italy" data-original-height="941" data-original-width="1672" height="360" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/a/AVvXsEgeFZtDpd3KVUAk7SFNjWljx3L8E8LPRgmH6RgQJAu1PE6vLNUvEFkA2PaLquIGI2UAKpmQNx3X5FGczG3YmlJDbbnpF20-a__QI8KpcRVIIaPuJP8NEvkGeaWP_UPoZUYx5k0L53ad1zpCSEwJ3fRkVZYbvfOJkSBUkEQ1MJLosZE77RUsmzAFJQW075wS=w640-h360" title="Banca d’Italia Tightens Crypto Sanctions Screening" width="640" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;By CoinAINews Staff&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;Italy is putting stronger compliance pressure on the country's regulated crypto sector as &lt;strong&gt;Banca d’Italia&lt;/strong&gt; reminds supervised firms that their systems must be capable of detecting relationships and transactions involving sanctioned individuals and entities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The central bank published its communication on &lt;strong&gt;September 7, 2026&lt;/strong&gt;, focusing on procedures for complying with European Union and national restrictive measures. It also pointed supervised intermediaries toward European Banking Authority guidance covering controls on customers and transfers of funds and crypto-assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The development was highlighted by &lt;strong&gt;CoinMarketCap&lt;/strong&gt;, which reported that Banca d’Italia had ordered crypto service providers to screen transfers for sanctioned entities and strengthen internal controls against illicit flows.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But there is an important distinction behind the headline: &lt;strong&gt;Italy has not banned crypto transfers.&lt;/strong&gt; The regulatory move is about sanctions compliance, screening systems and internal controls—not a blanket prohibition on Bitcoin, &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/us-bank-usbdc-stablecoin-stellar-cross-border-payments.html"&gt;Ethereum &lt;/a&gt;or other digital assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Did Banca d’Italia Actually Say?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Banca d’Italia's September 7 communication concerns compliance with &lt;strong&gt;EU and Italian restrictive measures&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The central bank said supervised intermediaries need adequate safeguards for detecting relationships and transactions involving sanctioned persons and entities. It specifically referenced &lt;strong&gt;EBA Guidelines 2024/15&lt;/strong&gt;, which cover policies and controls concerning customers and transfers of funds and crypto-assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The guidance also addresses the configuration and calibration of screening systems, making the technical side of sanctions compliance an important part of the regulator's message.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In practical terms, regulated firms need systems capable of identifying potential sanctions exposure rather than relying on a basic or poorly configured screening process.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Crypto Transfers Are Under the Microscope&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Crypto networks can move digital assets across borders without following traditional banking hours. That is one of their biggest advantages for legitimate users and businesses.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It also creates a compliance challenge.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;When a regulated &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/hunter-biden-laptop-memecoin-crash-86-5-percent.html"&gt;crypto provider&lt;/a&gt; processes a transfer, it needs to consider whether the customer, counterparty or transaction creates exposure to applicable restrictive measures.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is why sanctions screening has become an increasingly important part of the infrastructure surrounding regulated crypto services.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The objective is not to stop ordinary crypto activity. The objective is to prevent regulated intermediaries from facilitating transactions that fall within applicable sanctions restrictions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Does Sanctions Screening Mean for Crypto Firms?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Sanctions screening generally involves comparing relevant customer and transaction information against applicable sanctions information and investigating potential matches.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For crypto firms, that process can be more complicated because digital-asset transactions involve blockchain addresses, pseudonymous accounts and transfers that can cross jurisdictions quickly.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A modern compliance operation may therefore combine customer information, transaction monitoring and blockchain analytics.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;div style="margin: 20px 0px; overflow-x: auto; width: 100%;"&gt;
&lt;table style="border-collapse: collapse; min-width: 700px; width: 100%;"&gt;
&lt;thead&gt;

&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/thead&gt;
&lt;tbody&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(136, 136, 136); padding: 10px;"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Customer screening&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(136, 136, 136); padding: 10px;"&gt;Helps identify potential exposure to sanctioned &lt;br /&gt;individuals and entities.&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;tr&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(136, 136, 136); padding: 10px;"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Transfer screening&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(136, 136, 136); padding: 10px;"&gt;Allows firms to assess applicable transactions &lt;br /&gt;before processing them.&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;

&lt;/tr&gt;

&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/tbody&gt;
&lt;/table&gt;
&lt;/div&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Does Italy Now Screen Every Small Crypto Transfer?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is where the social-media headline needs some context.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;CoinMarketCap summarized the development as Banca d’Italia ordering crypto providers to screen transfers for sanctioned entities. However, the central bank's official communication is framed around the adequacy of safeguards and compliance with restrictive measures, including the EBA's guidance on the configuration and calibration of controls.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Therefore, it would be too broad to describe the announcement as a brand-new Italian law stating that &lt;strong&gt;every single crypto transaction of every size must automatically be screened&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The stronger and more accurate takeaway is that regulated providers are expected to maintain effective sanctions controls and cannot treat crypto transfers as outside the scope of restrictive-measures compliance.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Is Italy Banning Bitcoin or Crypto?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;No.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Banca d’Italia's communication does not announce a ban on Bitcoin, Ethereum, &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/blog-post.html"&gt;stablecoins&lt;/a&gt; or other cryptocurrencies.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It also does not say that ordinary users will lose access to crypto transfers simply because they are using blockchain networks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The issue is compliance with applicable restrictive measures. If a transaction creates a legitimate sanctions concern, a regulated provider may need to investigate or take appropriate action under the relevant rules.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is very different from a nationwide cryptocurrency ban.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why EBA Guidelines 2024/15 Matter&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Banca d’Italia's reference to &lt;strong&gt;EBA Guidelines 2024/15&lt;/strong&gt; is particularly important because it connects the Italian communication to a broader European supervisory framework.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The guidelines address policies, procedures and controls concerning restrictive measures, including customers and transfers of funds and crypto-assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;They also emphasize the configuration and calibration of screening systems.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For crypto companies, that means compliance is increasingly becoming a technology problem as well as a legal one.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A provider needs systems that can process large volumes of transactions while identifying potentially relevant sanctions exposure without overwhelming compliance teams with meaningless alerts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Blockchain Analytics Could Become More Important&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Traditional sanctions screening often focuses heavily on names and other customer information.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Crypto adds another layer because transactions occur through blockchain addresses.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Blockchain analytics can help regulated firms identify links between addresses, transactions and entities that may present elevated risk.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But an important distinction remains: an address associated with a sanctioned entity is not necessarily the same thing as every address that has ever interacted with it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is why compliance teams need investigation and risk-based controls rather than treating blockchain exposure as automatic proof of wrongdoing.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What This Means for Crypto Exchanges and CASPs&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The development matters most for &lt;strong&gt;crypto-asset service providers&lt;/strong&gt;, exchanges and other regulated firms operating within Italy's financial system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;These businesses need to make sure their compliance infrastructure can support the applicable restrictive-measures requirements.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That can involve:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Maintaining current sanctions information.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Screening relevant customers and counterparties.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Monitoring applicable crypto transfers.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Reviewing potential sanctions matches.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Maintaining appropriate internal procedures.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Testing and calibrating screening systems.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;Keeping compliance decisions and relevant records auditable.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The exact requirements can vary depending on the firm's activities, authorization and applicable regulatory framework.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Does MiCA Change the Situation?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;MiCA—the &lt;strong&gt;Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation&lt;/strong&gt;—is the European Union's framework for covered crypto-asset activities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But MiCA compliance does not eliminate separate sanctions obligations.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A crypto business can operate within the European regulatory framework while still having to comply with applicable EU restrictive measures.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is part of a broader shift in European crypto regulation: digital-asset companies increasingly need the same kind of compliance infrastructure expected from other regulated financial businesses.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Could Stronger Screening Affect Crypto Users?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Potentially, yes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Users of regulated crypto platforms may encounter additional transaction reviews if a transfer generates a sanctions-related alert.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A review does not automatically mean that the user has done anything wrong. Screening systems can produce potential matches that require additional information or investigation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For most users, the immediate impact is likely to be limited to compliance checks when a transaction or account triggers a relevant risk indicator.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Italy's Move Matters for European Crypto&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Italy is not operating in isolation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Across Europe, regulators are attempting to bring crypto services further into the regulated financial system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That means the industry is increasingly being evaluated not only on technology and innovation but also on its ability to prevent money laundering, sanctions evasion and other forms of financial crime.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Banca d’Italia's latest communication fits into that wider regulatory direction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The message is straightforward: &lt;strong&gt;blockchain-based money movement still has to operate within the rules governing regulated financial activity.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bigger Story: Crypto Compliance Is Becoming Infrastructure&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For years, the crypto industry largely focused on wallets, exchanges, smart contracts and blockchain networks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Now another layer is becoming equally important: compliance infrastructure.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;As banks and regulated financial institutions move more assets and payments onto blockchain networks, they need tools capable of combining on-chain information with conventional customer and transaction data.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Italy's latest regulatory communication shows how that transition is happening at the supervisory level.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The future regulated crypto market will therefore depend on more than faster blockchains. It will also depend on whether firms can build compliance systems that work at blockchain speed without sacrificing regulatory controls.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Happens Next?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Banca d’Italia's communication does not announce a new blanket enforcement campaign against specific crypto exchanges.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead, it reminds supervised intermediaries about the need for appropriate safeguards and points them toward the applicable European guidance.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The immediate implication is therefore operational: firms should review whether their sanctions controls are appropriately designed, configured and maintained.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Any enforcement action involving a particular crypto provider would be a separate matter.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Frequently Asked Questions&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What did Banca d’Italia announce about crypto?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Banca d’Italia published a September 7 communication concerning compliance with EU and national restrictive measures and highlighted the need for supervised firms to maintain adequate safeguards for detecting relationships and transactions involving sanctioned persons and entities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Does Italy ban crypto transfers?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No. The communication does not announce a blanket ban on crypto transfers or cryptocurrencies. It concerns sanctions compliance and internal controls.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Do Italian crypto firms need sanctions screening?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Regulated crypto-asset service providers are subject to applicable restrictive-measures and financial-crime compliance requirements. Banca d’Italia's communication specifically points to EBA guidance covering customers and transfers of funds and crypto-assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Does this apply to Bitcoin?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The communication is not a Bitcoin-specific rule. It concerns applicable restrictive-measures compliance for supervised financial activity, including controls relevant to crypto-assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Is this a new MiCA rule?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It should not be described simply as a new MiCA rule. Banca d’Italia's communication focuses on restrictive measures and references EBA Guidelines 2024/15 concerning relevant controls.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Will Italian crypto users have every transaction blocked?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;No. There is no indication of a blanket block on crypto transactions. Regulated providers may conduct additional reviews when transactions or customers trigger relevant compliance alerts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Italy is tightening the compliance spotlight on crypto transfers, with Banca d’Italia emphasizing the need for supervised firms to maintain effective controls against sanctioned individuals and entities.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The September 7 communication does not amount to a cryptocurrency ban. Instead, it reinforces the importance of sanctions screening, internal controls and properly configured compliance systems within the regulated financial sector.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For crypto companies, the message is becoming increasingly clear: &lt;strong&gt;moving assets on a blockchain does not remove the need to comply with sanctions rules.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And as digital assets become more integrated with European finance, the quality of that compliance infrastructure could become just as important as the blockchain technology underneath it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Disclaimer:&lt;/strong&gt; This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal, financial or investment advice. Regulatory requirements can change, and crypto businesses should consult qualified professionals regarding their specific obligations.&lt;/p&gt;

    <title>If an AI Writes a Smart Contract That Exploits a Loophole, Who Is Legally Liable? The Answer Isn't Simple.</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;br /&gt;&lt;article&gt;&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh4JqvzyY8jdc-K9W8qD5zpktbHnDUVpKr38X9zXILI2Ix6BO81kdCWV2SsFQkOHDiK8VxbFexj2BsS4Qz8cNs1ikavSaRLxi-dDJwvaQUbykEXnXX8FJBwiDFO9o1SsLdpi53mxpU-sWiuhZxhGBAyyM4BeFU_1P80A4Uo8PtIaqDTAgkOueYwCSeDEt8J/s1672/ai-smart-contract-legal-liability-blockchain.jpg.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="AI generating smart contract code beside a crypto wallet and legal scales representing blockchain liability" border="0" data-original-height="941" data-original-width="1672" height="225" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh4JqvzyY8jdc-K9W8qD5zpktbHnDUVpKr38X9zXILI2Ix6BO81kdCWV2SsFQkOHDiK8VxbFexj2BsS4Qz8cNs1ikavSaRLxi-dDJwvaQUbykEXnXX8FJBwiDFO9o1SsLdpi53mxpU-sWiuhZxhGBAyyM4BeFU_1P80A4Uo8PtIaqDTAgkOueYwCSeDEt8J/w400-h225/ai-smart-contract-legal-liability-blockchain.jpg.png" title="Who Is Liable for an AI-Generated Smart Contract?" width="400" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;By CoinAINews Staff |&amp;nbsp;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;What happens when an AI writes a smart contract, the code gets deployed, and someone discovers a loophole that lets money drain from it? The easy answer is to blame the machine. The legal answer is much harder.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AI coding tools are becoming increasingly capable of generating, reviewing and modifying software. In crypto, that development carries an obvious attraction: developers can use AI to move faster, experiment with ideas and automate parts of the development process.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But there is a catch.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A smart contract doesn't just run on a computer. It can control real digital assets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If AI-generated code contains a vulnerability, a seemingly small mistake can become a financial problem once the contract is deployed on a public blockchain.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And when money disappears, the question quickly changes from &lt;strong&gt;"Who wrote the code?"&lt;/strong&gt; to something much more difficult:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Who was legally responsible for putting that code in control of the money?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;AI Can Write Smart Contracts. That Doesn't Make AI Legally Responsible&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Large language models can generate Solidity and other programming code, but generating code and being legally responsible for that code are two very different things.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Recent research has demonstrated that large language models can generate code capable of identifying or exploiting vulnerabilities in smart contracts. Other research has also highlighted security weaknesses in LLM-generated smart contracts, showing why generated code should not simply be treated as production-ready software.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2508.01371v3" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;
Read the research on automated exploit generation for smart contracts
&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That's an important distinction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI model might produce a function that passes basic tests but fails under an unusual sequence of transactions. It might misunderstand an access-control requirement or overlook an interaction between two parts of a protocol.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Once deployed, the blockchain doesn't ask whether an AI wrote the code.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It simply executes the contract according to its rules.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That is why the AI itself isn't necessarily the obvious legal target.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Current legal discussions around autonomous AI generally focus on the humans and organizations that developed, deployed, controlled or benefited from the system rather than treating the AI model itself as the automatic bearer of liability.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/who-is-liable-when-ai-goes-rogue-lawyers-see-new-risks-2026-08-07/" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;
Read Reuters' analysis of liability when autonomous AI systems cause harm
&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Imagine the Contract Loses Millions&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Consider a hypothetical example.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A developer wants to create a decentralized lending protocol.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead of writing every function manually, the developer asks an AI coding agent to build the core smart contracts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI generates the code.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The developer reviews it, runs tests and deploys it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The protocol attracts users.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Several months later, a security researcher discovers that a particular sequence of transactions can bypass an important check.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An attacker exploits the vulnerability.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Millions of dollars leave the protocol.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain records every transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the ledger doesn't answer the most important question:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Who is responsible?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI generated the vulnerable function.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The developer deployed the contract.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The user may have authorized the AI to write the code.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI company supplied the model.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain executed the resulting transactions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Suddenly, what looked like a technical bug has become a legal puzzle.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Could the Developer Be Liable?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Potentially, depending on the circumstances and applicable law.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If a developer deploys financial software without reasonable security testing, an injured party could potentially argue that the developer failed to take appropriate precautions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But that doesn't mean every developer automatically becomes liable whenever AI-generated code contains a bug.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Software vulnerabilities can occur even after professional development and security review.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The legal question would depend on the specific facts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;What did the developer know?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;What security measures were reasonable?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Was the vulnerability foreseeable?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Was the code independently audited?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Did the developer make representations about the protocol's security?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who controlled deployment?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Could the developer have prevented the loss?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Those details could matter enormously.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The important point is that &lt;strong&gt;using AI doesn't automatically erase the responsibilities that may already exist around software development and deployment.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What If the User Was the One Giving the Instructions?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Now change the scenario.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The person deploying the protocol isn't a professional developer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;They simply tell an autonomous AI agent:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;"Build a yield protocol, deploy it and manage the treasury."&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The agent generates the code, interacts with development tools, deploys the contracts and begins operating the system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The human approves the initial setup.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Later, something goes wrong.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Would the user automatically be responsible?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Again, there is no universal answer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But the user's role could become extremely important.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A legal analysis could examine who instructed the system, who authorized the deployment, who controlled the wallet and who had the ability to stop the operation.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The more authority a person gives an AI system, the more important questions of control and oversight may become.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That doesn't mean a user automatically becomes legally responsible for every unexpected action of an AI.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It means &lt;strong&gt;authorization and control are likely to matter.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The AI Provider Could Face Questions Too&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is another possible participant in the chain: the company that provides the AI system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Suppose a company develops a powerful coding model.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A customer uses that model to generate smart-contract code.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The model produces a vulnerability.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The customer deploys the contract.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An attacker exploits it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Could the AI provider be responsible?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That depends on the facts and the applicable law.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Legal analysis could examine the provider's terms, representations, warnings, intended use of the product and the degree of control it exercised over the customer's activity.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is a major difference between providing a general-purpose coding assistant and actively operating or controlling an autonomous financial system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction could become increasingly important as AI agents move from simply suggesting code to actually executing tasks.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Recent legal analysis of autonomous AI has already highlighted questions around developer, deployer and other participant liability when agents act with limited human oversight.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/who-is-liable-when-ai-goes-rogue-lawyers-see-new-risks-2026-08-07/" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;
Reuters — Who Is Liable When AI Goes Rogue?
&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Responsibility Chain Is Bigger Than "AI vs. Human"&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The future may therefore look less like a simple question of &lt;strong&gt;"AI versus human"&lt;/strong&gt; and more like a chain:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;AI provider → developer → deployer → user → smart contract → blockchain&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Each link can represent a different type of involvement.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI provider creates the underlying model.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The developer may use that model to create or modify the code.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The deployer puts the contract on-chain.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The user may authorize the deployment or provide the economic objective.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The smart contract executes the programmed rules.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain records and validates the resulting transactions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If something goes wrong, investigators and courts may have to work backward through that chain.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who had control at each stage?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who could reasonably have detected the problem?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who had a duty to act?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who benefited?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And perhaps most importantly, &lt;strong&gt;where did human responsibility actually end?&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;As AI systems become more autonomous, those questions could become much harder to answer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Smart Contracts Make Mistakes Especially Expensive&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AI-generated code is not unique to crypto.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But smart contracts introduce a feature that makes mistakes particularly dangerous: once deployed, some contracts can be difficult or impossible to change.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Traditional software can often be patched after a vulnerability is discovered.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A smart contract may have an upgrade mechanism, but not every contract does.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If the code is immutable and controls valuable assets, discovering a vulnerability after deployment can be very different from finding a bug in an ordinary application.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There may be no simple "undo" button.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Recent research into smart-contract security also shows that automated systems can generate or identify exploitable contract behavior, reinforcing why security review remains important even as AI-assisted development becomes more common.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://arxiv.org/html/2508.01371v3" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;
Review the smart-contract exploit-generation research
&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In other words:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;AI can accelerate coding. It cannot eliminate the need for verification.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Happens When an Attacker Finds the Loophole First?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is where the legal and technical problems collide.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Suppose an attacker notices a vulnerability before the developer does.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The attacker interacts with the contract.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The contract follows its programmed rules.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Funds move.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain confirms the transactions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;From a technical perspective, the transaction may have been valid under the protocol's rules.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;From a legal perspective, however, the circumstances surrounding the transaction could still raise questions about unauthorized access, fraud, theft or other potential violations, depending on the jurisdiction and facts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction is crucial.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;"The smart contract allowed it" doesn't automatically mean "the law allowed it."&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Code determines what a blockchain system will execute.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Law determines how human conduct surrounding that system may be treated.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Those are not always the same thing.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Does an Audit Solve the Problem?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An independent security audit can reduce risk, but it doesn't create a guarantee that a contract is safe.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Auditors can miss vulnerabilities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;New attack techniques can emerge after an audit.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The contract can also change after the audit.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And an audit doesn't necessarily settle legal responsibility if something later goes wrong.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Still, independent review can be important evidence that a developer or operator took reasonable security precautions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For AI-generated code, that may become particularly significant.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If an organization knows that substantial portions of its financial software were generated automatically, relying solely on the model's output could be difficult to defend if serious problems were foreseeable and avoidable.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The practical lesson is simple:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Treat AI-generated financial code as untrusted until it has been properly tested and reviewed.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Could Liability Be Shared?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It could be.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A single incident may involve several participants with different responsibilities.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A developer could potentially face questions about code review.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A deployer could face questions about authorization.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A user could face questions about instructions and control.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An AI provider could face questions about its role and representations.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;An attacker could face separate legal consequences for deliberately exploiting a vulnerability.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is no reason to assume that one participant must automatically carry the entire legal burden.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The final outcome would depend on the jurisdiction, contracts, evidence and precise facts.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That's one reason sweeping claims such as &lt;strong&gt;"AI is liable"&lt;/strong&gt; or &lt;strong&gt;"the developer is always liable"&lt;/strong&gt; can be misleading.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bigger Problem: Autonomous AI Agents&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The situation becomes even more complicated when the AI isn't merely writing code.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Imagine an agent that can:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li&gt;write a smart contract;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;test the contract;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;deploy it;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;control a wallet;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;interact with DeFi protocols;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;monitor market conditions;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;change supporting infrastructure; and&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li&gt;make decisions without asking a human every time.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;At that point, the system starts looking less like a coding assistant and more like an autonomous economic operator.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That doesn't automatically give the AI legal personhood.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But it does make the question of human control much more difficult.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If a human gave an agent broad authority six months ago and the agent has been making thousands of decisions since then, how should responsibility be allocated when one of those decisions causes significant harm?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There is no universally settled answer.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Recent reporting on autonomous AI liability shows that lawyers are already examining negligence, authorization and other existing legal theories as AI systems become capable of taking actions with less direct human oversight.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/who-is-liable-when-ai-goes-rogue-lawyers-see-new-risks-2026-08-07/" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;
Read Reuters' reporting on autonomous AI liability
&lt;/a&gt;
&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Developers Should Do Now&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The legal debate may take years to develop.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Security practices cannot wait that long.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Developers using AI for smart contracts should treat the model as an assistant rather than a final authority.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That means reviewing generated code, running automated tests, using independent security reviews for high-value contracts, limiting permissions and monitoring transactions after deployment.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Where appropriate, developers can also consider emergency controls and upgrade mechanisms.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;None of these measures guarantees that a contract will never fail.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;They can, however, reduce the likelihood that a single unnoticed coding error turns into a catastrophic loss.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If an AI writes a smart contract that contains a loophole, the AI itself doesn't automatically become legally liable.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The real legal questions are likely to revolve around the people and organizations surrounding the system.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who instructed the AI?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who wrote or reviewed the code?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who deployed the contract?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who controlled the wallet?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Who had the ability to detect or prevent the problem?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And who benefited from the resulting activity?&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The answers could vary significantly depending on the jurisdiction and circumstances.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;What is becoming clear is that AI doesn't make traditional questions of responsibility disappear.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It adds another layer to them.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The AI may write the code.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The blockchain may execute it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But neither one necessarily answers the legal question of who was responsible for putting that code in control of real money.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The hardest question may not be who wrote the smart contract. It's who had the responsibility to make sure it was safe before billions of dollars were allowed to trust it — because the blockchain won't answer for the mistake.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Laws concerning AI, software, cryptocurrency, smart contracts and liability vary by jurisdiction and can change over time.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
