    <title>Bitcoin and Gold Are Moving Together Again — Ki Young Ju Says Institutions Are Taking Notice</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;article&gt;

  &lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg9C1sdBNONxgAL5EcA8V-Zxpja6CKq2x7WCFHjqjolIP2ooWq-wjdFZiKKF0z_tgIEDYtz049jNxNwktIsVsaGVffHRdcg9O99rk-4eLawotU8kT-ch1kKiYMfT-2j3Wg4oc5VqfyBFzLAe1XE0yF-mIMBTsMdeJjrdE3wFVULGJwzQLtvmEX62qABmlDZ/s1672/bitcoin-gold-institutional-investor-interest-2026.webp.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="Bitcoin and gold moving together as institutional investors take renewed interest in BTC" border="0" data-original-height="941" data-original-width="1672" height="225" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEg9C1sdBNONxgAL5EcA8V-Zxpja6CKq2x7WCFHjqjolIP2ooWq-wjdFZiKKF0z_tgIEDYtz049jNxNwktIsVsaGVffHRdcg9O99rk-4eLawotU8kT-ch1kKiYMfT-2j3Wg4oc5VqfyBFzLAe1XE0yF-mIMBTsMdeJjrdE3wFVULGJwzQLtvmEX62qABmlDZ/w400-h225/bitcoin-gold-institutional-investor-interest-2026.webp.png" title="Bitcoin and Gold Move Together as Institutional Interest Returns" width="400" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;div style="text-align: left;"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;By CoinAINews Staff |&amp;nbsp;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/div&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Bitcoin is once again behaving a little more like gold — and this time, institutional investors may be driving the connection.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;CryptoQuant founder and CEO &lt;strong&gt;Ki Young Ju&lt;/strong&gt; told Coinage that institutional investors are once again viewing Bitcoin as a &lt;strong&gt;“very attractive asset”&lt;/strong&gt;, helping explain why Bitcoin and gold have recently been moving in the same direction.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The comment, highlighted by &lt;a href="https://www.facebook.com/CoinMarketCap/posts/latest-cryptoquant-founder-ki-young-ju-told-coinage-that-institutional-investors/1492860212871367/" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;CoinMarketCap&lt;/a&gt;, comes as both assets have attracted renewed attention from investors looking beyond traditional fiat assets.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The renewed relationship between Bitcoin and gold is more than a familiar “digital gold” narrative.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It points to a broader change in how some investors may be treating Bitcoin: less as a purely speculative technology trade and more as part of a wider allocation to scarce or alternative assets.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Recent market data has also highlighted a strengthening relationship between Bitcoin and gold. At the same time, Bitcoin investment products have recorded significant inflows, giving the institutional-demand argument more weight.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;But correlation alone does not tell investors where Bitcoin goes next.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The more interesting question is &lt;strong&gt;why the two assets are moving together again — and what institutional demand could mean for BTC from here.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Bitcoin's Relationship With Gold Has Changed Before&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Bitcoin and gold have never maintained a permanent relationship.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;There have been periods when they moved together, periods when they moved in opposite directions and periods when the correlation was weak enough to make the “digital gold” comparison look questionable.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That is why the latest change matters.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Ki Young Ju has previously pointed to &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/trump-linked-real-trump-coins-promoted.html"&gt;Bitcoin's&lt;/a&gt; changing relationship with gold, with CryptoQuant data showing periods in which BTC's correlation with the precious metal strengthened significantly.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;A positive correlation simply means the two assets have recently shown a greater tendency to move in the same direction.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It does &lt;strong&gt;not&lt;/strong&gt; mean Bitcoin has become equivalent to gold.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Gold remains a centuries-old monetary and reserve asset, while Bitcoin is a relatively young digital asset with substantially higher volatility.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Still, the market's behavior can reveal something about investor preferences.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;When investors become concerned about currency debasement, fiscal risks, inflation or the durability of traditional financial assets, both Bitcoin and gold can appear in the same conversation.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That appears to be happening again.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Why Institutions Could Be Looking at Bitcoin Differently&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Ki Young Ju's comments are particularly interesting because institutional investors do not necessarily approach Bitcoin the same way retail traders do.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;A retail trader may focus on short-term momentum, price action or the next market move.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;An institution, however, may be thinking about &lt;strong&gt;portfolio construction, diversification, liquidity, custody, long-term purchasing power and exposure to alternative assets.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That difference matters.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Institutional investors do not necessarily need Bitcoin to behave like a traditional safe-haven asset every day. Instead, they may be evaluating whether BTC deserves a place alongside commodities, equities, bonds and other alternative investments.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If that approach becomes more common, Bitcoin's role could gradually change.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Instead of being treated purely as a high-risk trading asset, &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/new-york-warns-ai-is-making-investment.html"&gt;BTC&lt;/a&gt; could increasingly become another instrument institutions consider when building diversified portfolios.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That does not guarantee higher prices.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It does, however, make the source and durability of Bitcoin demand much more important.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;ETF Flows Are Giving the Institutional Story More Weight&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Institutional access to Bitcoin has changed dramatically in recent years.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds have made it easier for traditional investors to gain exposure to BTC without directly managing wallets, private keys or crypto exchange accounts.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That matters because investment decisions can now happen through structures that professional investors already understand.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;And the latest ETF numbers are difficult to ignore.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;According to &lt;a href="https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/stock-market-today-dow-sp-500-nasdaq-08-27-2026/card/investors-are-piling-into-bitcoin-again-88r02djwTF9qOQUgJ88J" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;The Wall Street Journal&lt;/a&gt;, investors directed approximately &lt;strong&gt;$2.5 billion into spot Bitcoin ETFs over seven trading days&lt;/strong&gt;, marking the strongest seven-day inflow period since October, according to Dow Jones Market Data.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That does not mean every dollar represents a long-term institutional investor.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;ETF flows can include different types of investors and trading strategies.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;But the existence of sustained flows shows that Bitcoin has become much easier to incorporate into conventional investment portfolios.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Recent reporting from &lt;a href="https://www.coindesk.com/business/2026/08/25/live-updates-bitcoin-etfs-draw-a-seventh-straight-day-of-inflows-as-the-rally-holds-above-usd80-000" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;CoinDesk&lt;/a&gt; also highlighted more than $2.5 billion in spot ETF inflows across the recent streak, while noting that the durability of the buying remains an open question.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;For institutions evaluating alternative assets, that accessibility can be significant.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;The Gold Comparison Is Really About Scarcity&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Bitcoin and gold are often compared under the “digital gold” label.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;But the more useful comparison is scarcity.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Gold is valued partly because its supply is limited and difficult to increase rapidly.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Bitcoin has a hard-coded maximum supply of &lt;strong&gt;21 million coins&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The two assets are fundamentally different, but both can appeal to investors who want exposure to an asset that cannot simply be created at will by a central authority.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That becomes particularly relevant when concerns about government debt, monetary policy or currency purchasing power rise.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;In such an environment, investors do not necessarily need to choose between Bitcoin and gold.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;They can own both.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That is an important distinction.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The growth of Bitcoin as an institutional asset does not require gold to lose its role.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It simply means BTC can increasingly become part of the same broader conversation about scarce assets and portfolio diversification.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Why Bitcoin and Gold Can Move Together&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;There are several reasons the two markets can respond similarly.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Macro Uncertainty&lt;/h3&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;When investors become less comfortable with the traditional economic environment, demand can move toward alternative assets.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Gold has played that role for generations.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Bitcoin is increasingly being considered alongside it.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Dollar Concerns&lt;/h3&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;A weaker dollar or concerns about long-term currency purchasing power can support interest in scarce assets.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That does not automatically make Bitcoin bullish, but it can create a common macro driver for BTC and gold.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Institutional Portfolio Allocation&lt;/h3&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;As Bitcoin becomes easier for institutions to access, professional investors can consider it alongside commodities, equities, bonds and other alternative assets.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That creates the possibility of Bitcoin responding to macro allocation decisions that historically affected gold more directly.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;The Digital Gold Narrative&lt;/h3&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Narratives matter in financial markets.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If investors collectively start viewing Bitcoin as a form of digital scarcity, it can attract demand from investors who previously considered gold the more natural hedge.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The narrative itself does not determine price.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;But it can influence where capital is allocated.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Correlation Does Not Mean Bitcoin Has Become a Safe Haven&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;This is where investors should be careful.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Bitcoin moving with gold does not suddenly make BTC a low-risk asset.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Bitcoin remains considerably more volatile than gold.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Its market can experience sharp drawdowns even when the long-term investment thesis remains intact.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Gold, meanwhile, has a much longer history as a reserve and defensive asset.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;So the recent correlation should not be interpreted as proof that Bitcoin has finally become a conventional safe haven.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It is better understood as a sign that &lt;strong&gt;the two assets are responding to some of the same macro forces at the same time.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That distinction is important.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Correlation can strengthen for months and then disappear.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Bitcoin can also react to crypto-specific developments that have little connection to gold.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;The Institutional Question Is Bigger Than This Week's Price&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;For Bitcoin, the bigger story may not be whether BTC rises or falls over the next few trading sessions.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It is whether institutions continue treating the asset as something worth holding through different market conditions.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That is a much harder test.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;A short-term rally can be driven by momentum.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Long-term institutional adoption requires stronger conviction.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Investors need custody solutions.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;They need liquidity.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;They need regulatory clarity.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;They need investment products.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;And they need a reason to keep the allocation when the market becomes uncomfortable.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Bitcoin has made significant progress on several of those fronts.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;But the process is not finished.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Ki Young Ju's Comment Comes at an Interesting Time&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The timing of Ki Young Ju's assessment is notable.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Bitcoin has spent much of 2026 navigating a complicated market environment, with investors debating whether the current cycle is entering a new phase.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;At the same time, institutional access to Bitcoin has continued expanding through ETFs and other investment products.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That makes the institutional narrative particularly important.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If new capital continues to enter Bitcoin through &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/08/could-state-actor-use-ai-to-51-attack.html"&gt;ETFs&lt;/a&gt;, funds and other professional investment channels, the market could become increasingly influenced by traditional asset-allocation decisions.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;In that scenario, BTC may increasingly trade alongside other macro-sensitive assets.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Gold could be one of them.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;There Is Still a Major Risk&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;There is an obvious danger in interpreting the latest trend too optimistically.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Investors can move into Bitcoin and gold for different reasons.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Gold can benefit from defensive demand while Bitcoin falls because investors reduce exposure to risk.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Bitcoin can rally because of crypto-specific developments even while gold remains flat.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The fact that the assets are currently moving together does not guarantee that relationship will continue.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Institutional investors can sell just as easily as they can buy.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That is why ETF flows, liquidity, macroeconomic conditions and Bitcoin's on-chain demand will remain important indicators.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What Would Confirm a Stronger Institutional Shift?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;There are several signals worth watching.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Sustained ETF inflows&lt;/strong&gt; would suggest that demand is not simply a short-lived trading event.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Growing long-term custody balances&lt;/strong&gt; could indicate that more BTC is being absorbed by investors with longer time horizons.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Stronger institutional participation&lt;/strong&gt; would make Bitcoin increasingly sensitive to traditional financial-market conditions.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Persistent Bitcoin-gold correlation&lt;/strong&gt; would strengthen the argument that both assets are responding to similar macroeconomic forces.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;None of these indicators is perfect on its own.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Together, however, they can provide a clearer picture of whether Bitcoin is becoming more deeply integrated into traditional portfolio strategies.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Bitcoin May Be Becoming a Macro Asset&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Perhaps the most important shift is that Bitcoin is increasingly behaving like a macro asset.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That does not mean it has stopped being a cryptocurrency.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It means investors are increasingly watching the same things that influence other major assets:&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;ul&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Interest rates&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;The U.S. dollar&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Inflation&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Government debt&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Liquidity&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Institutional flows&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Global risk appetite&lt;/li&gt;
  &lt;/ul&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That is a very different market environment from the one Bitcoin occupied during its earliest years.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It also explains why the relationship with gold matters.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If Bitcoin increasingly responds to macroeconomic forces that also influence gold, the two assets may continue to move together during certain periods.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;The Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Ki Young Ju's latest comments offer a useful way to understand what is happening beneath Bitcoin's price action.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Institutional investors are increasingly able to access BTC through traditional investment products, while the asset itself is once again showing signs of moving alongside gold.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The latest ETF data adds another piece to the puzzle. Investors directed approximately &lt;strong&gt;$2.5 billion into spot Bitcoin ETFs over seven trading days&lt;/strong&gt;, according to Dow Jones Market Data cited by The Wall Street Journal.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That does not prove that every dollar represents long-term institutional accumulation.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It does, however, show that demand through traditional investment channels has become an increasingly important part of the Bitcoin market.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;None of this proves Bitcoin has become a safe haven.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;It does not guarantee that BTC and gold will continue moving together.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;And it certainly does not mean institutional investors will keep buying regardless of price.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;But it does suggest that Bitcoin's role in global portfolios may be evolving.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The market may be moving beyond the simple question of whether Bitcoin is “crypto.”&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The more important question could be whether investors increasingly see it as &lt;strong&gt;another scarce asset to own when the traditional financial landscape becomes harder to trust.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If that shift continues, Bitcoin and gold moving together may be less of a coincidence — and more of a sign that the institutional view of BTC is changing — &lt;strong&gt;and that Bitcoin may be becoming part of the broader macro conversation.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

    <title>Can You Recover Crypto Sent to the Wrong Network?</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;div class="coinai-article"&gt;

  &lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiGebxriZEz_mT5CBgDO5ICMinOqSfNeSV0zqtlSBpo-nhowd7aaJTZAKV6QF_1Toos6oXzwPwPtQ7vuk1mRhngZgQQtPvlqbRnMTXHp20dbaMw9544SpgGXMHQqKsIYiWST_n-YOrTL29GHSXPppE7sL6w88qHJemLllnpMItDTwd-Vthvx42EsHCQmuB9/s1672/can-you-recover-crypto-sent-to-the-wrong-network.jpg.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="Can You Recover Crypto Sent to the Wrong Network?" border="0" data-original-height="941" data-original-width="1672" height="360" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEiGebxriZEz_mT5CBgDO5ICMinOqSfNeSV0zqtlSBpo-nhowd7aaJTZAKV6QF_1Toos6oXzwPwPtQ7vuk1mRhngZgQQtPvlqbRnMTXHp20dbaMw9544SpgGXMHQqKsIYiWST_n-YOrTL29GHSXPppE7sL6w88qHJemLllnpMItDTwd-Vthvx42EsHCQmuB9/w640-h360/can-you-recover-crypto-sent-to-the-wrong-network.jpg.png" title="Can You Recover Crypto Sent to the Wrong Network?" width="640" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;By CoinAINews Staff&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;&lt;p&gt;
  September 6, 2026&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Sending crypto on the wrong network is one of the easiest mistakes to make in cryptocurrency—and one of the most confusing to fix.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;A transaction can show as completed on a blockchain while the crypto does not appear in the wallet or exchange account where you expected it. That does not always mean the funds are gone.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;So, can you recover crypto sent to the wrong network?&lt;/strong&gt; Sometimes, yes. But there is no universal recovery method. The answer depends on the cryptocurrency, the blockchain network used, the destination address, and whether you or the receiving platform can access the funds on that network.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;In some self-custody wallet situations, the funds may still be accessible simply by switching to the network on which the transaction actually occurred. Exchanges are different: recovery depends on the platform's supported assets, networks and recovery procedures.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Coinbase, for example, currently offers an asset-recovery process for certain eligible unsupported assets and networks, while warning that other incorrect-network transfers may be permanently lost.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What Does “Wrong Network” Mean in Crypto?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Many crypto assets exist on more than one blockchain.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Stablecoins and tokens such as USDC, DAI and other ERC-20 assets can be available across multiple networks. Ethereum.org explains that assets existing on multiple networks are not interchangeable simply because they have the same token name. The sending and receiving sides need to use a compatible network.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;For example, a user might intend to send USDC on &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/can-bitcoin-transaction-be-reversed.html"&gt;Ethereum &lt;/a&gt;but select another supported EVM network instead. If the receiving service does not support that network for the deposit, the transaction may complete on-chain without the recipient receiving a credited balance.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The important point is that &lt;strong&gt;the asset name alone is not enough&lt;/strong&gt;. You need to verify both the asset and the blockchain network.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Can Crypto Sent to the Wrong Network Be Recovered?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Sometimes—but not every wrong-network transfer is recoverable.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The biggest distinction is whether the destination is a self-custody wallet that you control or an exchange-controlled address.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;div style="margin: 20px 0px; overflow-x: auto; width: 100%;"&gt;
    &lt;table style="border-collapse: collapse; border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); min-width: 760px; text-align: left; width: 100%;"&gt;
      &lt;thead&gt;
        &lt;tr&gt;
          &lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); font-weight: 700; padding: 12px;"&gt;Situation&lt;/th&gt;
          &lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); font-weight: 700; padding: 12px;"&gt;Recovery possibility&lt;/th&gt;
          &lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); font-weight: 700; padding: 12px;"&gt;What matters&lt;/th&gt;
        &lt;/tr&gt;
      &lt;/thead&gt;
      &lt;tbody&gt;
        &lt;tr&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Wrong network to your&lt;br /&gt;own compatible wallet&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Potentially recoverable&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Whether you control the &lt;br /&gt;wallet and it supports the &lt;br /&gt;network and asset&lt;/td&gt;
        &lt;/tr&gt;
        &lt;tr&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Wrong network to an &lt;br /&gt;exchange&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Depends on the exchange&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Whether the exchange &lt;br /&gt;supports recovery for &lt;br /&gt;that asset and network&lt;/td&gt;
        &lt;/tr&gt;
        &lt;tr&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Unsupported network &lt;br /&gt;at an exchange&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;May be recoverable in limited &lt;br /&gt;cases&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Platform recovery rules &lt;br /&gt;and transaction eligibility&lt;/td&gt;
        &lt;/tr&gt;
        &lt;tr&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Wrong address controlled &lt;br /&gt;by someone else&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Usually difficult&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Whether the recipient &lt;br /&gt;can access and return the &lt;br /&gt;funds&lt;/td&gt;
        &lt;/tr&gt;
      &lt;/tbody&gt;
    &lt;/table&gt;
  &lt;/div&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Coinbase currently states that only certain assets and networks are eligible for its asset-recovery service. An ineligible asset or network cannot be recovered through that service.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Why Does Crypto Disappear After a Wrong-Network Transfer?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;In many cases, the blockchain transaction itself has not disappeared.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The transaction may be permanently recorded on the network that was actually used. The problem is that the receiving wallet or exchange may not be monitoring, supporting or crediting deposits on that network for the particular asset.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That can create a confusing situation where the sender sees a successful blockchain transaction but the recipient sees no balance.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;This is why the first step should always be identifying the exact network used rather than immediately assuming the crypto has been destroyed.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Wrong Network vs. Wrong Address: They Are Not the Same&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;These two mistakes are often confused, but they can have very different recovery possibilities.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;div style="margin: 20px 0px; overflow-x: auto; width: 100%;"&gt;
    &lt;table style="border-collapse: collapse; border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); min-width: 700px; text-align: left; width: 100%;"&gt;
      &lt;thead&gt;
        &lt;tr&gt;
          &lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); font-weight: 700; padding: 12px;"&gt;Problem&lt;/th&gt;
          &lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); font-weight: 700; padding: 12px;"&gt;What happened?&lt;/th&gt;
          &lt;th style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); font-weight: 700; padding: 12px;"&gt;Possible recovery&lt;/th&gt;
        &lt;/tr&gt;
      &lt;/thead&gt;
      &lt;tbody&gt;
        &lt;tr&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Wrong address&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Crypto was sent to a different blockchain address&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Usually cannot be reversed; recipient cooperation may be required&lt;/td&gt;
        &lt;/tr&gt;
        &lt;tr&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Wrong network&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Crypto was sent using a network different from the receiving service's expected network&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;May be recoverable depending on wallet or exchange support&lt;/td&gt;
        &lt;/tr&gt;
        &lt;tr&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;Unsupported asset&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;An asset was sent to a platform that does not support it&lt;/td&gt;
          &lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); padding: 12px;"&gt;May be recoverable in limited circumstances&lt;/td&gt;
        &lt;/tr&gt;
      &lt;/tbody&gt;
    &lt;/table&gt;
  &lt;/div&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;A wrong-network transfer should therefore not automatically be treated as the same thing as sending crypto to a completely unrelated address.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Can the Same Crypto Address Exist on More Than One Network?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Yes, particularly with EVM-compatible networks.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Ethereum.org explains that an Ethereum address can be used across EVM-compatible blockchains when the wallet type supports this functionality. The same underlying account can therefore have the same address on multiple EVM networks.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;This creates an important recovery scenario.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Imagine you control a self-custody wallet and send a token to your own &lt;code&gt;0x...&lt;/code&gt; address, but select the wrong EVM network. The funds may still exist at that address on the network you actually used. If your wallet supports that network and &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/what-happens-if-you-send-bitcoin-to.html"&gt;token&lt;/a&gt;, switching the wallet to that network can make the balance visible.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;That is not the same as reversing the transaction.&lt;/strong&gt; The original transaction remains on the blockchain where it was processed. You are simply accessing the same wallet account on the network where the asset was actually sent.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;However, users should not assume that every token will automatically appear after switching networks. The wallet must support the relevant network and asset, and some assets may require additional configuration or a compatible wallet interface.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What If the Wrong Network Was Used With a Self-Custody Wallet?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;This can be one of the more recoverable situations—provided the destination address is yours and you control the wallet's recovery credentials.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;First, find the transaction hash and identify the &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/sent-1-btc-to-wrong-coinbase-user-heres.html"&gt;blockchain&lt;/a&gt; on which the transaction was confirmed.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Then check whether your wallet supports that network and the particular asset.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If it does, switching to that network may allow the asset to appear. Some wallets may require the network or token to be added manually before the balance becomes visible.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Ethereum.org notes that wallets are interfaces for managing blockchain accounts and that the same recovery phrase can provide access to accounts across compatible networks.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Never enter your recovery phrase into a random website claiming that it can recover the transaction.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What If You Sent Crypto to an Exchange on the Wrong Network?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;This situation is more complicated.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;An exchange controls the infrastructure behind its deposit addresses. Even if the address looks technically compatible with another blockchain, the exchange may not support deposits for that asset on that particular network.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Coinbase warns that users should use the same network on both the sending and receiving sides when transferring assets supported across multiple networks. It also says it cannot recover funds lost from an incorrect network in general.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That means you should not assume that an exchange can simply “switch the network” and credit your account.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The exchange must have a technical and operational way to access the funds before recovery is possible.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Can Coinbase Recover Crypto Sent on the Wrong Network?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Coinbase is a good example of why the answer is not simply yes or no.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Coinbase currently provides an &lt;strong&gt;asset-recovery service for certain unsupported crypto transfers&lt;/strong&gt;. Only specific assets and networks qualify, and Coinbase says an ineligible asset or network cannot be recovered through the service.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The current recovery process requires information such as the transaction network, transaction ID and the Coinbase address to which the asset was sent. If the transaction qualifies, Coinbase's process can connect a self-custodial wallet to receive the recovered asset.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Coinbase also warns that assets deposited or withdrawn using an incorrect network may be permanently lost.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;So the practical answer is:&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Coinbase may recover some eligible wrong-network or unsupported-asset transfers, but it cannot recover every wrong-network transaction.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Does Coinbase Charge a Recovery Fee?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Yes, fees can apply to eligible Coinbase asset recoveries.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;According to Coinbase's current recovery documentation, recoveries with an estimated value above &lt;strong&gt;$100 incur a 5% fee on the amount over $100&lt;/strong&gt;. Network fees also apply and are deducted from the user's Ethereum balance.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;For example, the stated 5% fee is not a 5% charge on the entire recovered amount. Under the current policy, it applies to the portion above $100.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;This is a fee for Coinbase's eligible asset-recovery service—not a universal “wrong-network recovery fee” that applies to every crypto transaction or every exchange.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Because recovery rules and fees can change, users should check Coinbase's current official recovery page before starting a recovery request.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What If Coinbase Later Supports the Network?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;There have been specific cases where Coinbase later added support for a network and automatically credited certain previously affected deposits.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;But this was limited to &lt;strong&gt;specific assets and networks&lt;/strong&gt;. Coinbase's published examples include ETH, MATIC and USDC previously sent on Polygon, as well as DAI, ETH and WBTC previously sent on Optimism. Qualifying customers were credited automatically after the relevant network support was introduced.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;This should not be interpreted as a promise that every unsupported-network deposit will eventually be recovered.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Coinbase's current exchange documentation warns that unsupported-network deposits may be permanently lost, although deposits may be automatically credited if the relevant network becomes supported in the future.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;The important distinction is eligibility.&lt;/strong&gt; A platform adding support for a network does not automatically guarantee recovery of every asset previously sent through that network.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;How Long Does Wrong-Network Recovery Take?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;There is no single recovery timeline that applies to every transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;For Coinbase's current asset-recovery service, the process depends on whether the transaction qualifies and whether the transaction can be located and processed.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Because recovery policies, supported networks and eligible assets can change, readers should check the platform's current official documentation rather than relying on an old article, social-media post or forum answer.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What Should You Do Immediately After Using the Wrong Network?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;1. Stop and Do Not Send More Funds&lt;/h3&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Do not send another transaction simply because the first one has not appeared in the destination wallet.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;First determine where the original transaction went.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;2. Find the Transaction Hash&lt;/h3&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Locate the transaction ID, transaction hash or TXID in the wallet or exchange you used.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The transaction hash lets you inspect the transaction on the relevant blockchain explorer and confirm the asset, destination address and network.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;3. Identify the Actual Network&lt;/h3&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Check the blockchain on which the transaction was processed.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Do not rely only on your memory of which network you selected.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;4. Check the Destination Address&lt;/h3&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Determine whether the address belongs to you, an exchange or another person.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If it is your own self-custody wallet, check whether that wallet supports the network and asset.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;5. Check the Exchange's Official Recovery Rules&lt;/h3&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If the destination belongs to an exchange, use the exchange's official support documentation or recovery tool.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Do not rely on an unofficial Telegram account, social-media “support agent” or random recovery service.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;What Information Do You Need for Recovery?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If a recovery process exists, keep the following information ready:&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;ul&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Transaction hash or TXID&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Cryptocurrency or token name&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Amount sent&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Network actually used&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Network that was intended&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Receiving address&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Sending address&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Date and approximate time of the transaction&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Name of the exchange or wallet involved&lt;/li&gt;
  &lt;/ul&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Coinbase's current recovery process specifically asks for the transaction network, transaction ID and the address to which the asset was sent.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Does a Transaction Hash Recover Your Crypto?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;No.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;A transaction hash is an identifier used to locate and inspect a blockchain transaction. It does not give anyone the ability to reverse the transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Its value is investigative: it can show which network processed the transaction, where the asset was sent and whether the transaction was confirmed.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;That information can then help determine whether a wallet or exchange has a recovery option.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Can an Exchange Reverse a Wrong-Network Transaction?&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Usually, an exchange cannot simply reverse a completed blockchain transaction like a card payment.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The transaction has already been recorded on the blockchain. If recovery is possible, the platform generally needs to access the asset and return or credit it through a separate recovery process.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Coinbase explicitly warns that incorrect-network transfers may be permanently lost and that it cannot recover every such transfer.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Beware of Crypto Recovery Scams&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;A wrong-network mistake can create a second danger: recovery scams.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Someone may contact you claiming to be a blockchain investigator, exchange employee, hacker or recovery specialist and promise to retrieve the missing crypto for an upfront payment.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Be extremely careful.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Never give your seed phrase or private key to someone claiming that it is necessary to recover your funds.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Your recovery phrase controls access to the wallet. Giving it away can create a much larger loss than the original network mistake.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Use only the official wallet or exchange website when checking recovery options.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;How to Avoid Sending Crypto on the Wrong Network&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The easiest recovery method is preventing the mistake.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;ul&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Check the supported network before sending.&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Confirm that the sending and receiving networks match.&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Do not assume the same token name means all networks are interchangeable.&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Read the network warning displayed by your wallet or exchange.&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;For a large transfer, consider sending a small test transaction first.&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Verify the destination address before confirming.&lt;/li&gt;
    &lt;li&gt;Keep the transaction hash after sending.&lt;/li&gt;
  &lt;/ul&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Wrong-Network Crypto Recovery: The Key Differences&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;div style="margin: 20px 0px; overflow-x: auto; width: 100%;"&gt;
    &lt;table style="border-collapse: collapse; border: 1px solid rgb(204, 204, 204); min-width: 780px; text-align: left; width: 100%;"&gt;

  &lt;/div&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;Frequently Asked Questions&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Can you recover crypto sent to the wrong network?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;Sometimes. Recovery depends on the asset, blockchain network, destination and whether the wallet or exchange can access the funds. Some transfers are recoverable, while others may be permanently lost.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Is crypto sent to the wrong network always lost?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;No. If the destination is your own compatible self-custody wallet, the funds may still be accessible on the network where they were actually sent. Exchange transfers depend on the platform's recovery capabilities.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Can I recover crypto sent to my own wallet on the wrong EVM network?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;Potentially. EVM-compatible networks can use the same wallet address. If you control the wallet and it supports the network and asset, switching to the network used by the transaction may allow you to access the funds.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Can Coinbase recover crypto sent on the wrong network?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;Sometimes. Coinbase currently offers recovery for certain eligible unsupported assets and networks, but it does not guarantee recovery for every wrong-network transfer.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;How much does Coinbase charge for crypto recovery?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;For eligible recoveries above $100, Coinbase currently states that a 5% fee applies to the amount over $100. Network fees also apply. The current eligibility and fee rules should be checked before starting a recovery request.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;What if Coinbase starts supporting the network later?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;Some specific historical assets and networks have received automatic credit after Coinbase introduced support. However, this has been limited to qualifying cases and is not a guarantee for every unsupported-network transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;How long does crypto recovery take?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;There is no universal timeline. It depends on the platform, transaction, network and eligibility. Current recovery requirements should be checked directly with the relevant exchange or wallet provider.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Can a transaction hash reverse a crypto transfer?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;No. A transaction hash helps you identify and investigate a transaction. It does not provide a mechanism for reversing a confirmed blockchain transaction.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h3&gt;Should I give my seed phrase to a recovery service?&lt;/h3&gt;
  &lt;p&gt;No. Never share your recovery phrase or private key with someone claiming that it is required to recover your crypto.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;h2&gt;The Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Crypto sent to the wrong network is not automatically gone—but it is not automatically recoverable either.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The most important question is not simply whether you selected the wrong network. It is &lt;strong&gt;where the transaction went and who controls the destination&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If the funds were sent to a self-custody wallet that you control, particularly on an EVM-compatible network, the asset may still be accessible by switching to the network where the transaction actually occurred.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;If the destination is an exchange, recovery depends on that exchange's supported networks, technical capabilities and current recovery rules. Coinbase, for example, has a recovery process for certain eligible unsupported assets and networks, but also warns that other incorrect-network transfers may be permanently lost.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;And if an exchange adds support for a previously unsupported network, that does not automatically mean every old transaction will be recovered. Coinbase's documented automatic-return cases have been limited to specific assets and networks.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;The safest response after a wrong-network transfer is to &lt;strong&gt;stop, find the transaction hash, identify the actual network, verify the destination and use only the official recovery process&lt;/strong&gt;.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;p&gt;Most importantly, never hand your seed phrase or private key to someone promising guaranteed recovery.&lt;/p&gt;

  &lt;hr /&gt;

    &lt;li&gt;&lt;a href="https://help.coinbase.com/en-in/coinbase/trading-and-funding/sending-or-receiving-cryptocurrency/assets-on-multiple-networks" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;Coinbase — Assets on multiple networks&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/li&gt;

    <title>Bitcoin Apocalypse: 15 Years Ago, BTC Fell Below $5 in One of Crypto's Earliest Market Panics</title>
    <content type='html'>&lt;div class="separator" style="clear: both; text-align: center;"&gt;&lt;a href="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgZwlOfWsH3VLTHZzZU40Z-CoTH65TNxjErA9UV1QDJ-cGKJrUeUhORF1_GoSOwCOsXZfHM5b0aq19H0BVzBhSvphExVG0nIBbJFkSJUKiI_1861zbucVQYaLdWX6E_xF9wGCx32lLdd8kc0aAGaebXR6xayXORtys55WZnP352CFddm-B8IgEhUfICY6La/s1672/bitcoin-apocalypse-2011-crash-below-5.jpg.png" imageanchor="1" style="margin-left: 1em; margin-right: 1em;"&gt;&lt;img alt="Bitcoin price falls below $5 during the 2011 Bitcoin Apocalypse crash" border="0" data-original-height="941" data-original-width="1672" height="360" src="https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEgZwlOfWsH3VLTHZzZU40Z-CoTH65TNxjErA9UV1QDJ-cGKJrUeUhORF1_GoSOwCOsXZfHM5b0aq19H0BVzBhSvphExVG0nIBbJFkSJUKiI_1861zbucVQYaLdWX6E_xF9wGCx32lLdd8kc0aAGaebXR6xayXORtys55WZnP352CFddm-B8IgEhUfICY6La/w640-h360/bitcoin-apocalypse-2011-crash-below-5.jpg.png" title="Bitcoin Apocalypse: BTC Falls Below $5 in 2011" width="640" /&gt;&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/div&gt;&lt;br /&gt;&lt;h1&gt;&lt;strong&gt;&lt;span style="font-size: medium;"&gt;Fifteen years ago today, Bitcoin was trading around the $5 level, and the mood across the young cryptocurrency market was anything but optimistic.&lt;/span&gt;&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/h1&gt;

&lt;p&gt;On September 15, 2011, participants in an ongoing BitcoinTalk discussion were watching Bitcoin approach and move below the psychologically important $5 level. The thread itself had started several days earlier, on September 9, with the title &lt;strong&gt;“The Bitcoin Apocalypse 1BTC trading under $5 USD.”&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;On September 15, one participant wrote that Bitcoin was at &lt;strong&gt;$5.17 and dropping&lt;/strong&gt;. Later that same day, another post stated: &lt;strong&gt;“We're there. $4.82 now.”&lt;/strong&gt; The posts provide a rare contemporaneous record of how some early Bitcoin participants reacted to the crash. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The episode is now remembered as one of Bitcoin's earliest “apocalypse” moments. But there is an important historical distinction: &lt;strong&gt;$4.82 was not Bitcoin's lowest price of 2011.&lt;/strong&gt; Bitcoin fell further later that year, with historical data showing a November low around the $2 range. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;What made September 2011 significant was the combination of Bitcoin's dramatic fall from its June rally, the market's limited liquidity and the uncertainty surrounding a digital asset that was still in its early development.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What Was the “Bitcoin Apocalypse”?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The phrase &lt;strong&gt;“Bitcoin Apocalypse”&lt;/strong&gt; was not created years later to describe the crash. It appeared in the title of a BitcoinTalk discussion while the market was going through the sell-off.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The thread was created on &lt;strong&gt;September 9, 2011&lt;/strong&gt;, with the title &lt;strong&gt;“The Bitcoin Apocalypse 1BTC trading under $5 USD.”&lt;/strong&gt; The opening post simply asked, &lt;strong&gt;“Is this the end?”&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Several days later, on September 15, the discussion captured the continuing decline. One post at 06:41 UTC-era forum time stated that if $5 was the Bitcoin Apocalypse, the market was close, with Bitcoin at &lt;strong&gt;$5.17 and dropping&lt;/strong&gt;. Another post later that day recorded Bitcoin at &lt;strong&gt;$4.82&lt;/strong&gt;. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That makes the thread particularly valuable as historical evidence. Instead of a modern article assigning dramatic language to an old price chart, the archive shows that the “&lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/ocean-protocol-launches-inference.html"&gt;Bitcoin Apocalypse&lt;/a&gt;” label was being used by market participants during the actual decline.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Bitcoin Had Already Exploded Higher Earlier in 2011&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The September crash becomes much more significant when viewed against Bitcoin's performance earlier that year.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin began 2011 at roughly &lt;strong&gt;$0.30&lt;/strong&gt; according to historical daily data. By June, it had surged dramatically. StatMuse's historical dataset records a June 9, 2011 closing price of &lt;strong&gt;$30.06&lt;/strong&gt;, with an intraday high of $33.88 that day. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Other historical datasets can show somewhat different prices for the same period because early Bitcoin markets were fragmented and data sources can use different exchanges, timestamps and methodologies.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The broader historical fact is clear: &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/top-7-token-unlocks-this-week-zro-leads.html"&gt;Bitcoin moved&lt;/a&gt; from well below $1 at the beginning of 2011 into the roughly $30 region by June before suffering a severe correction.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(136, 136, 136); padding: 10px;"&gt;Bitcoin was still an extremely &lt;br /&gt;early-stage digital asset.&lt;/td&gt;

&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(136, 136, 136); padding: 10px;"&gt;Bitcoin experienced an &lt;br /&gt;extraordinary early &lt;br /&gt;speculative rally.&lt;/td&gt;

&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(136, 136, 136); padding: 10px;"&gt;The market panic was explicitly &lt;br /&gt;described using the “Bitcoin &lt;br /&gt;Apocalypse” label.&lt;/td&gt;

&lt;td style="border: 1px solid rgb(136, 136, 136); padding: 10px;"&gt;Bitcoin fell substantially further &lt;br /&gt;after the September episode.&lt;/td&gt;
&lt;/tr&gt;
&lt;/tbody&gt;
&lt;/table&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;Early Bitcoin prices can vary between historical datasets because exchanges, timestamps and data methodologies were not standardized.&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The September 2011 BitcoinTalk Record&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The BitcoinTalk discussion provides one of the clearest pieces of primary-source evidence surrounding the episode.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The thread was created on September 9, 2011. At that time, Bitcoin was already trading below the levels seen during its June rally. Early participants debated whether the decline represented the end of Bitcoin or simply another market correction. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;By September 15, the price had moved close to and below $5.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;At one point, a participant wrote:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;“If $5 USD is the Bitcoin Apocalypse, we're very close. $5.17 and dropping.”&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/blockquote&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Later that day, the same discussion recorded:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;blockquote&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;“We're there. $4.82 now.”&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;/blockquote&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Those posts are especially useful because they establish both the timing and the market sentiment surrounding the sub-$5 level. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Was $5 Bitcoin's Lowest Price During the September 2011 Crash?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;No.&lt;/strong&gt; The $4.82 figure is an important historical price recorded during the September episode, but it should not be described as Bitcoin's lowest price for the entire year.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin continued to fall after September.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Historical monthly data shows September closing around $5.09, followed by a much weaker October and November. The same dataset records a November low of &lt;strong&gt;$1.92&lt;/strong&gt; and a November closing price of &lt;strong&gt;$2.97&lt;/strong&gt;. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;More specifically, StatMuse records Bitcoin's November 18, 2011 close at &lt;strong&gt;$2.05&lt;/strong&gt;, after an intraday low of $1.95. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Therefore, the accurate historical interpretation is:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;September 15, 2011 was a major sub-$5 panic, but it was not Bitcoin's ultimate 2011 bottom.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This distinction matters because describing $4.82 as Bitcoin's “lowest price in 2011” would be factually incorrect.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why Was Bitcoin So Volatile in 2011?&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin's market structure in 2011 was radically different from today's cryptocurrency market.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There were fewer exchanges, far less liquidity and a much smaller number of participants. Bitcoin also lacked the institutional infrastructure that exists today, including regulated investment products, deep derivatives markets and large professional trading operations.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That meant changes in buying and selling pressure could have a much larger effect on price.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The BitcoinTalk discussion itself shows participants trying to understand what was causing the decline. Some posts speculated about large holders selling, while others suggested that buyers were simply disappearing from the market. These are historical opinions from forum participants, not independently verified explanations of the crash. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That distinction is important. The archive proves what participants were saying at the time; it does not necessarily prove why the market moved.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;From Less Than $1 to the $30 Region&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The scale of Bitcoin's 2011 price cycle was extraordinary.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Historical data shows Bitcoin starting January at around $0.30. By June, its price had moved into the $30 region, with StatMuse recording a $30.06 closing price on June 9 and an intraday high of $33.88. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin subsequently entered a prolonged decline.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;By September, the monthly data shows &lt;a href="https://www.coinainews.com/2026/09/nvidia-in-talks-to-invest-up-to-10.html"&gt;Bitcoin reaching&lt;/a&gt; a low of approximately $4.04 and closing the month at $5.09. October brought another decline, with a monthly low around $2.18. November was weaker still, with the historical dataset recording a $1.92 low and a $2.97 monthly close. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This makes the September $4.82 event part of a much longer 2011 bear-market decline rather than an isolated one-day crash.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Bitcoin Did Not End at $5&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The most interesting part of the story is what happened after the so-called “Bitcoin Apocalypse.”&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin continued operating.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The network continued processing transactions, development continued and the broader Bitcoin ecosystem gradually expanded.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That does not mean Bitcoin's survival was guaranteed in 2011. Nor does its eventual survival prove that every future Bitcoin crash will necessarily be followed by a recovery.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It simply demonstrates that a severe market decline and the failure of an underlying technology are two different questions.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin would go on to experience many additional bull and bear markets, technological developments, security incidents, regulatory challenges and periods of intense skepticism.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The September 2011 crash ultimately became one chapter in a much longer history.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;What the 2011 Bitcoin Crash Teaches Today's Investors&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Bitcoin's Extreme Volatility Is Not New&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin's reputation for dramatic price movements did not begin with the modern cryptocurrency industry. The 2011 market had already produced an enormous rally followed by a severe collapse.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Liquidity Matters&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Today's Bitcoin market is dramatically larger than the market that existed in 2011. Early price movements therefore need to be interpreted within the context of a much thinner and less mature market.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Psychological Price Levels Matter&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The BitcoinTalk discussion shows how the $5 level became psychologically significant. Round-number levels can become important during periods of extreme volatility because traders often use them as reference points.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Price and Technology Are Different Questions&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;A falling Bitcoin price does not automatically mean that the underlying network has failed. Bitcoin continued operating despite the severe 2011 decline.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Historical Recovery Is Not a Guarantee&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin's subsequent survival should not be interpreted as proof that every future crash will produce another recovery. Historical precedent provides context, not certainty.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;From the “Bitcoin Apocalypse” to a Global Digital Asset&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The contrast between September 2011 and today's Bitcoin market is extraordinary.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Fifteen years ago, Bitcoin trading below $5 was dramatic enough to inspire an “apocalypse” discussion on an early cryptocurrency forum.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Today, Bitcoin is followed by retail investors, financial institutions, policymakers and technology companies around the world.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That transformation did not happen overnight. Bitcoin went through years of development, adoption, controversy, regulatory uncertainty and repeated market cycles.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The 2011 crash therefore matters as a historical snapshot of a period when Bitcoin's long-term future was still highly uncertain.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Why the 2011 Bitcoin Apocalypse Still Matters&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Historical market events often look very different in hindsight.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Modern observers know that Bitcoin survived the 2011 crash. Investors living through the event did not have that information.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;They were watching a relatively new digital asset fall sharply after an extraordinary rally, while participants on an early Bitcoin forum were openly discussing whether the market had reached an “apocalypse.”&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;That perspective remains useful when analyzing cryptocurrency markets today.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Whether markets are rising rapidly or falling sharply, current sentiment is not necessarily a reliable guide to the long-term outcome.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The 2011 record shows how quickly expectations can change when an emerging market moves through an extreme cycle.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;The Bigger Lesson From Bitcoin's 2011 Crash&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The real lesson of the “Bitcoin Apocalypse” is not that Bitcoin always recovers from crashes.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;It is that early markets can produce extreme price movements while participants have very limited information about what comes next.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In September 2011, Bitcoin had already demonstrated extraordinary upside potential, but its subsequent decline showed how quickly market sentiment could reverse.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The fact that Bitcoin later became a globally recognized digital asset does not erase the uncertainty that existed at the time.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Instead, the BitcoinTalk archive provides a rare window into how that uncertainty looked in real time.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Bottom Line&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Fifteen years ago today, Bitcoin fell below $5 during one of the earliest major periods of panic in its market history.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The BitcoinTalk discussion titled &lt;strong&gt;“The Bitcoin Apocalypse 1BTC trading under $5 USD”&lt;/strong&gt; was actually created on September 9, 2011. On September 15, the thread recorded Bitcoin at &lt;strong&gt;$5.17 and dropping&lt;/strong&gt;, followed later that day by a post reporting &lt;strong&gt;$4.82&lt;/strong&gt;. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;But $4.82 was not Bitcoin's lowest price of 2011. The cryptocurrency fell further in the following months, with historical data showing a November low of approximately &lt;strong&gt;$1.92&lt;/strong&gt; and a November 18 closing price of &lt;strong&gt;$2.05&lt;/strong&gt;. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The importance of September 15 therefore lies in the moment itself: Bitcoin had collapsed from its extraordinary June rally, the market was still extremely young and participants were openly questioning what the future held.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Bitcoin survived that episode and continued developing.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;What was described as a “Bitcoin Apocalypse” in 2011 ultimately became one of the earliest chapters in Bitcoin's long and volatile history.&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Historical Source Note&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The primary historical source for the “Bitcoin Apocalypse” wording is the contemporaneous BitcoinTalk discussion titled &lt;strong&gt;“The Bitcoin Apocalypse 1BTC trading under $5 USD.”&lt;/strong&gt; The thread was created on September 9, 2011 and contains the September 15 posts reporting Bitcoin at $5.17 and later $4.82. &lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Direct historical thread:&lt;/strong&gt; &lt;a href="https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=42536.msg526625" rel="noopener noreferrer" target="_blank"&gt;BitcoinTalk — The Bitcoin Apocalypse 1BTC trading under $5 USD&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Historical Bitcoin prices from the early market can differ between sources because exchanges, timestamps and data methodologies were not standardized. This article therefore distinguishes the contemporaneous BitcoinTalk price reports from later historical market datasets.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Publication date: September 15, 2026&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;The bank's digital assets research team, led by Geoff
Kendrick, laid out a staged path:&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;$13 by the end of 2026**, followed by
**$41, $82, and $133&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;in subsequent years before hitting the $200
target&amp;nbsp;. The note, titled "Owning the rails," positions
Chainlink as critical infrastructure for the tokenization of real-world
assets&amp;nbsp;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;i&gt;"It is the only end-to-end platform capable of
supporting the full lifecycle of tokenized assets across both DeFi and
TradFi."&lt;/i&gt;&lt;br /&gt;
—&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;&lt;a data-preview="" href="https://www.google.com/search?ved=1t:260882&amp;amp;q=Geoff+Kendrick+Standard+Chartered&amp;amp;bbid=1063445581464181190&amp;amp;bpid=9053114080601589336" target="_blank"&gt;Geoff Kendrick&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/b&gt;, Global Head of Digital Assets Research, Standard
Chartered&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;The $4 Trillion Tokenization Bet&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;The forecast rests on a massive assumption: tokenization is
about to go mainstream.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Standard Chartered projects:&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul style="margin-top: 0cm;" type="disc"&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Tokenized
     assets on-chain&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;will grow from roughly&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;$340 billion today
     to $4 trillion by end-2028&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;DeFi
     assets&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;will surge&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;37-fold to $2.7 trillion by 2030&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l0 level1 lfo1; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Chainlink
     fees&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;could scale about&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;25 times&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;as these markets
     expand&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Kendrick expects Chainlink's token price to broadly track
fee growth, meaning the LINK forecast outpaces the bank's expected returns for
&lt;a data-preview="" href="https://www.google.com/search?ved=1t:260882&amp;amp;q=Bitcoin+price&amp;amp;bbid=1063445581464181190&amp;amp;bpid=9053114080601589336" target="_blank"&gt;Bitcoin&lt;/a&gt; ($500,000) and &lt;a data-preview="" href="https://www.google.com/search?ved=1t:260882&amp;amp;q=Ethereum+price&amp;amp;bbid=1063445581464181190&amp;amp;bpid=9053114080601589336" target="_blank"&gt;Ethereum&lt;/a&gt; ($40,000) over the same period&amp;nbsp;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Why "Owning the Rails" Matters&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Standard Chartered's core argument is that tokenized assets,
unlike crypto-native ones, are data-hungry. Tokenized funds need net asset
values, bonds require rates and payment schedules, and stablecoins need reserve
attestations&amp;nbsp;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Kendrick argues that Chainlink is currently the only
provider offering the complete package: trusted data, secure movement between
networks, privacy-preserving compliance, and integration with existing
financial systems&amp;nbsp;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Chainlink's current market position:&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul style="margin-top: 0cm;" type="disc"&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l1 level1 lfo2; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;$110
     billion+&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;in total value secured&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l1 level1 lfo2; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;~70%&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;of
     oracle-dependent DeFi value globally&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l1 level1 lfo2; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;80%+&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;on
     Ethereum network&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l1 level1 lfo2; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;$32
     trillion+&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;in transaction value enabled over seven years&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l1 level1 lfo2; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;Aave
     V3 alone accounts for approximately&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;44%&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;of Chainlink's
     secured value&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;The Institutional Roster&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Standard Chartered highlighted a growing list of traditional
finance institutions already working with Chainlink:&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;&lt;a data-preview="" href="https://www.google.com/search?ved=1t:260882&amp;amp;q=Swift+blockchain+initiatives&amp;amp;bbid=1063445581464181190&amp;amp;bpid=9053114080601589336" target="_blank"&gt;Swift&lt;/a&gt;, &lt;a data-preview="" href="https://www.google.com/search?ved=1t:260882&amp;amp;q=DTCC+tokenization&amp;amp;bbid=1063445581464181190&amp;amp;bpid=9053114080601589336" target="_blank"&gt;DTCC&lt;/a&gt;,
Euroclear, &lt;a data-preview="" href="https://www.google.com/search?ved=1t:260882&amp;amp;q=JPMorgan+digital+assets&amp;amp;bbid=1063445581464181190&amp;amp;bpid=9053114080601589336" target="_blank"&gt;JPMorgan&lt;/a&gt;, &lt;a data-preview="" href="https://www.google.com/search?ved=1t:260882&amp;amp;q=Mastercard+cryptocurrency+adoption&amp;amp;bbid=1063445581464181190&amp;amp;bpid=9053114080601589336" target="_blank"&gt;Mastercard&lt;/a&gt;, UBS, Fidelity, and S&amp;amp;P Global&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;The bank expects off-chain clients to become an increasing
share of Chainlink's fee revenue as tokenization moves from pilots to
production&amp;nbsp;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Key institutional developments:&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul style="margin-top: 0cm;" type="disc"&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l3 level1 lfo3; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Project
     Pangea:&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;Chainlink joined a pilot testing stablecoin-based FX
     settlement between Europe and South Korea, involving more than&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;50
     banks&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;representing over&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;$10 trillion&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;in assets
     under management&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l3 level1 lfo3; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Fidelity:&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;Chainlink
     is working on a project to tokenize fund data covering&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;$6.9
     billion&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;in assets&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Cross-Chain Momentum&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Chainlink's Cross-Chain Interoperability Protocol (CCIP) is
gaining traction following a high-profile exploit in April 2026&amp;nbsp;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;CCIP by the numbers:&lt;/b&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul style="margin-top: 0cm;" type="disc"&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l4 level1 lfo4; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;$7
     billion+&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;in token value migrated from legacy bridges to CCIP
     after the April exploit&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l4 level1 lfo4; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;$4.9
     billion&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;in Q2 quarterly volume, up&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;353%&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;year-over-year&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l4 level1 lfo4; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;BitGo&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;selected
     CCIP as exclusive infrastructure for Wrapped Bitcoin (WBTC)&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l4 level1 lfo4; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Aave&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;made
     CCIP its default cross-chain infrastructure&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;i&gt;"More than $7 billion in token value has migrated
from legacy bridge infrastructure to Chainlink's CCIP following a $292 million
exploit in April."&lt;/i&gt;&lt;br /&gt;
—&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;Geoff Kendrick&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;The Risks&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Kendrick also flagged three risks to the forecast&amp;nbsp;:&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ol start="1" style="margin-top: 0cm;" type="1"&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l2 level1 lfo5; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Slower-than-expected
     institutional tokenization&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;or pilots that fail to become
     production workflows&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l2 level1 lfo5; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Competition
     from specialist providers&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;in individual product categories&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
 &lt;li class="MsoNormal" style="mso-list: l2 level1 lfo5; tab-stops: list 36.0pt;"&gt;&lt;b&gt;Technical
     or configuration failures&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;that could damage confidence in the
     platform&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ol&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;The bank's coverage has moved other crypto assets in the
past — Aave jumped 15% after Standard Chartered's earlier DeFi call&amp;nbsp;.
LINK's reaction has been more muted, with the token trading around&amp;nbsp;&lt;b&gt;$8.25&lt;/b&gt;&amp;nbsp;at
the time of the report&amp;nbsp;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;o:p&gt;&amp;nbsp;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;&lt;b&gt;The Bottom Line&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/b&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;Standard Chartered's Chainlink forecast is a bet on
tokenization becoming the next major crypto narrative. If the bank is right
about the growth of tokenized assets and DeFi, Chainlink's infrastructure could
become a critical layer for tokenized finance, with the network potentially
generating greater fees as demand for data and cross-chain services grows&amp;nbsp;.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;If tokenization moves slower than expected, the $200 target
may remain just that — a target.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p class="MsoNormal"&gt;For now, the debate is sharp and the market is watching.&lt;o:p&gt;&lt;/o:p&gt;&lt;/p&gt;
